Idolatry of this kind existed in Israel, the women especially worshipping Baal-peor for the size of his obscene member, whom we can call Priapus. Hence also King Asa took away the high places from the people, and priests of this kind, and deposed his mother from her august rule, as Scripture testifies, saying: And Asa did what was right in the sight of the Lord, as David his father, and he took away the effeminate from the land, and he purged all the filth of the idols which his fathers had made. Moreover he also removed Maacah his mother, so that she should not be chief in the rites of Priapus and in his grove which she had consecrated; and he overturned its cave, and broke the most foul image, and burned it in the brook Kidron. But the high places he did not take away; nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect before God all his days. But it must be known that in the present passage he calls cadesoth the harlots, ἱερείας, that is, priestesses, made over to Priapus. In other places, however, we read cadesim for men cut off from lust, as Isaiah says: And mockers will rule over them, for which in the Hebrew is written: And cadesim will rule over them, which we have rendered 'effeminate'. But Aquila, translating ἐνηλλαγμένους, that is, changed, wished to show this: that they had changed their nature and from men had become women. Symmachus called them ἐταιρίδας, properly harlots. The Seventy, τετελεσμένους, that is, consecrated and initiated, to show that they were worshippers of idols. Theodotion, κεχωρισμένους, that is, separated from the people, men who seemed to themselves to have something more than the common crowd. We have discussed the word briefly; now let us return to the sense of the section.

And when these things occur, he says, I will remain calm, and I will not lay charges. Because of the misfortunes of the war and the troubles of the captivity, it seems right that all that will happen be predicted to the sinners. For they who once captured and overcame others will do with the captives as they like, making use of power without bridle and shamelessly attacking whomever they please, neither taking into account the law or considering what is likely or proper. But hardened and extremely wild in soul, they refuse to refrain from any kind of wretchedness. Therefore he clearly showed that the young children will be exposed to enemies because of the insult and shameless conduct of the fornicators.

Concerning the heretics the understanding is ready at hand, to whom, or of whom, it is said: If once you play the harlot, heretic, at least you, churchman, do not sin, nor go into Gilgal, the conventicles of the heretics, where the sins of all are revealed, and like swine they wallow in the mire. Nor think that you are going up to the proud and arrogant fictions of false dogmas. For there is not the house of God, but the house of the idol. Nor swear by the name of Christ, whose majesty you have polluted by mingling it with idols. For like a cow stung by the gadfly, the heretics have been struck by the burning arrows of the devil and have abandoned the knowledge of the law; therefore they will be pastured on the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and the patience of the Lord, the good shepherd, will nourish them for destruction.

If you play the harlot, Israel, let Judah at least not sin; and do not go into Gilgal; and do not go up to Beth-aven, nor swear: The Lord lives; for like a wanton cow Israel has turned aside. Now the Lord feeds them like a lamb in a broad place. LXX: But you, Israel, do not be ignorant, and Judah, do not go into Gilgal, do not go up to the house of ὢν, and do not swear: The Lord lives; for like a cow stung by the gadfly Israel has gone mad. Now the Lord feeds them like a lamb in a spacious place. For 'house of ὢν', in certain copies, and especially in Theodotion, 'house of iniquity' is read, which Aquila and Symmachus translated 'house of ἀνωφελοῦς', that is, useless, which profits nothing and by another word is called an idol. Now it is Bethel, which formerly was called house of God; after the calves were set up in it, it was called Beth-aven, that is, house of uselessness and house of the idol, which we have expressed as it is read in the Hebrew. But it seems to me that the reason why both the people of Israel in the wilderness made for themselves the head of a calf to worship, and Jeroboam son of Nebat fashioned golden calves, was this: that what they had learned in Egypt, that ἄπιν (Apis) and μνεῦιν (Mnevis), who are worshipped under the figure of oxen, are gods, they might keep in their own superstition. Let us state the sense of the section: If once, O Israel, you have been deceived by error and have mingled yourself with harlots, so that whoever filled the hand, either his own or the king's, by offering and giving him gifts, became a priest of the high places; at least you, Judah, who possess Jerusalem, and have Levites according to the law, and perform the ceremonies of the temple, ought not to follow the examples of your former sister Oholah in fornication, and worship idols along with God. Do not go into Gilgal, of which we read in this same prophet: All their wickedness is in Gilgal; in which Saul was anointed king; in which the people, coming out of the desert, first encamped and were purified by the second circumcision. From that time the error of a contrary religion grew up in a celebrated place. And do not go up to Beth-aven, that is, the place which was once called Bethel, because after golden calves were set up there by Jeroboam son of Nebat, it is called not House of God but house of the idol. For which I wonder why the Seventy translated 'house of ὢν', unless perhaps, by a common error, in place of the letter iod in the middle, which is flanked on either side by the letters aleph and nun, they supposed uau, which differs only in size. Nor swear: The Lord lives. For I do not want mention of my name to be made by your mouth, which is polluted by the remembrance of idols.

But what is the source of this hardness? It comes from gluttony and drunkenness. Who says so? Moses himself. "Israel ate and was filled, and the darling grew fat and frisky." When brute animals feed from a full manger, they grow plump and become more obstinate and hard to hold in check; they endure neither the yoke, the reins, nor the hand of the charioteer. Just so, the Jewish people were driven by their drunkenness and plumpness to ultimate evil. They kicked about and failed to accept the yoke of Christ. And they failed to pull the plow of his teaching. Another prophet hinted at this when he said, "Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer." And still another called the Jews "an untamed calf."

For as a wanton cow, casting off the yoke of the law, so Israel, that is, the ten tribes, has turned aside from the service of the Lord. For 'wanton cow' the Seventy translated παροιστρῶσαν, one stung by the oestrus and the asilus, which is commonly called the tabanus. Of this Vergil also tells in the third book of the Georgics: "whose Roman name is asilus, the Greeks turned it oestrus, so calling it; fierce, sounding harshly; terrified by it, whole herds scatter through the woods; the air, shaken, rages with bellowing, and the woods and the bank of dry Tanagrus". Since, therefore, Israel has gone mad and, struck by the spirit of fornication, has raved with incredible fury, therefore not long afterward, but while I prophesy, while breath rules these limbs, the Lord feeds them like a lamb in a broad place. Because he had taken the metaphor from the wanton cow, or from the gadfly, he keeps it in what remains, so that he calls the captivity among the Assyrians, and the dispersion of the people of Israel in the very broad land of the Medes, the pasturing of a flock and of lambs, as in a very broad plain and in a spacious land.

In another place, the prophet heapeth contumely upon Israel who had slipped his shoulder from [under] the yoke of the divine commandments: "As an ox which hath escaped from the yoke, so have the children of Israel escaped, they and their kings and their nobles." Now Israel became rebels because there was no fear [in them]; and they trod under foot the commandments because they were not mindful of what was threatened; and they despised the law because they remembered not the penalty of Him that ordained it.
13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 6 -- First Discourse on the Fear of God

Ephraim is a partaker of idols; let him go; their banquet is set apart; in fornication they have played the harlot; his protectors loved to bring disgrace; the spirit has bound him in its wings; and they will be put to shame by their sacrifices. LXX: Ephraim, a partaker of idols, has set stumbling blocks for himself, he has provoked the Canaanites; playing the harlot they have played the harlot, they have loved disgrace from their roaring; you are a whirlwind of the spirit in its wings, and they will be put to shame by their altars. Ephraim, the tribe from which came Jeroboam son of Nebat, who first set up the golden calves in Bethel and Dan, is king of the ten tribes. O Judah, then, to whom I said above: If Israel plays the harlot, let Judah at least not sin, hear my counsel, do not spurn the words of the prophet: since Ephraim is once for all a friend and partaker of idols, let him go, lest you follow his impiety, whose worship and religion and food are set apart from your banquet. For they serve idols once for all, and sacrifice to demons, and play the harlot daily; and they love their fornication; indeed, its princes and protectors, that is, the kings, loved to bring disgrace upon the people, that is: by the vice of the princes the unhappy people took up the worship of idols, whose unclean spirit has bound Israel in its wings and does not allow him to fly about freely. They will therefore be put to shame in their sacrifices, and in their confusion they will take on the disgrace of the princes. Symmachus, for what we have translated: the spirit has bound him in its wings, rendered it into Greek in this way: as if someone were to bind the wind in the wings of the wind; that is, so as to assert that both the princes and the people, or rather both the demons and Israel, are joined together, the vain with the vain and the empty with the empty. For wind and spirit among the Hebrews are called by one word, rua.

This same thing can also be referred to the heretics, and it is said to Judah, that is, to the churchman: since Ephraim, which is interpreted καρποφόρος (fruit-bearing), promises himself a false richness of doctrine and fruitful dogmas, and is once for all a friend of demons, let him go and despise him, especially since their sacrifices are set apart from your sacrifices. For this is what he says: their banquet is set apart; they have played the harlot once for all, and their princes have deceived the unhappy people; and in place of the worship of God they have steeped them in the disgrace of idols, and the spirit of the devil has bound them in its wings, they who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and cannot remain with a steady foot in the Church. They truly will be put to shame in their sacrifices, because their bread is the bread of mourning. And what is said, he has provoked the Canaanites, can in the same sense be referred to the heretics as well: that most of the heretics have invented things so foul and unspeakable, and have such unclean sacrifices, that idolatry is inferior to them. Or at least, because Canaanite is interpreted merchant or μετάβολος, that is, one who transfers, all who make the house of the Father a house of trade, and seek gains from the peoples, and transfer the truth of the Church into a lie, are to be called Canaanites.

That which the Seventy set down: he has provoked the Canaanites, is not found in the Hebrew. Yet it can be interpreted thus, so that we say that Israel had such zeal in the worship of idols that he did not imitate the Canaanites, that is, the heathen, but provoked them to imitate his own error.

The words "I will not visit your daughters when they prostitute themselves," that is, when a woman is accused of being adulterous and there is no witness, "she will make," Scripture says, "her offering of barley flour and will not pour any oil or incense." And since she is in her sorrow, the appearance of her offering will be equally sad. "And the priest," Scripture says, "will take some water from a vase of clay, and will throw some dust of the soil into the water, and will place the woman before the Lord and will make her swear." If she is innocent, she will remain unscathed and will still be fertile and will conceive; otherwise she will be torn. But in the meantime God threatens, "I will ravage Jerusalem, and there will be no one of your establishments which you cared for," and so on, because everything in the temple will be bound and delivered. "A nation that does not understand has kissed the woman of whoredom," that is, these people, who are blind and do not realize who God is, who lives and abides among them, prefer to worship idols rather than God. They foolishly kiss the calves and give themselves over to the prostitution with demons.
5: According to tropology, the people is accused so that it may not think itself free of the crime if it was led astray by kings and priests, whom we understand as the princes of the heretics. The princes themselves are also accused, because like a snare they caught the people and, though set as watchmen in the Church, led them into error. And on Mount Tabor, lofty and most beautiful, which is interpreted coming light, they laid ambushes, so as to drag all whom they had deceived down into the depth and sacrifice them to demons, and turn aside the victims into the abyss, lest they should ever come to their senses, lest they should look up to the Church, the house of God. Some think that Tabor is interpreted pit, that is, cistern; and that it fits the present sense that the heretics have dug a pit and fallen into the ditch which they made.

Hear this, O priests, and attend, house of Israel, and house of the king; listen with your ears, for the judgment is for you; since you have become a snare to the watchtower and a net spread over Tabor, and you have turned aside the victims into the depth. LXX: Hear this, O priests, and attend, house of Israel, and house of the king; perceive with your ears, for the judgment is against you, because you have become a snare to the watchtower; and like a net spread over Itabyrium, which those who take the prey have fixed fast for the hunt. The priests of the ten tribes are summoned to judgment, and the kings: not that the priests are of the tribe of Levi, but that they are called priests by the people. Hence too the priests of Baal, the four hundred and fifty prophets whom Elijah, and afterwards Jehu son of Nimshi in the presence of Jonadab son of Rechab, killed, were called priests; but Israel too, that is, the people, is summoned to judgment; and no one is excepted, so that priests and people and kings, who had led the people astray and appointed the priests, may hear together what they have done and why they are handed over to their enemies. I set you, he says, as watchmen and princes among the people, and placed you on the lofty summit of dignity, so that you might guide the wandering people. But you have become a snare, and are to be called not so much watchmen and princes as hunters. For you spread a net over Mount Tabor, which the Seventy rendered Ἰταβύριον (Itabyrium), having this custom, that they inflect Hebrew names in the Greek tongue; just as Edom, that is, Esau, and Seir they always translate Idumaea. Now Tabor is a mountain in Galilee, situated in the plains, round and lofty, and it is bounded evenly on every side. Of this mountain we read in the psalm too: Tabor and Hermon will exult in your name. This mountain the Seventy also rendered Itabyrium in Jeremiah; on it birds are commonly caught with snares.

There are some also who investigate spiritual precepts with cunning care, but what they penetrate with their understanding they trample on in their lives: all at once they teach the things which not by practice but by study they have learnt; and what in words they preach by their manners they impugn. Whence it comes to pass that when the shepherd walks through steep places, the flock follows to the precipice. Hence it is that the Lord through the prophet complains of the contemptible knowledge of shepherds, saying, "When ye yourselves had drunk most pure water, ye fouled the residue with your feet; and My sheep fed on that which had been trodden by your feet, and drank that which your feet had fouled." For indeed the shepherds drink most pure water, when with a right understanding they imbibe the streams of truth. But to foul the same water with their feet is to corrupt the studies of holy meditation by evil living. And verily the sheep drink the water fouled by their feet, when any of those subject to them follow not the words which they hear, but only imitate the bad examples which they see. Thirsting for the things said, but perverted by the works observed, they take in mud with their draughts, as from polluted fountains. Hence also it is written through the prophet, "A snare for the downfall of my people are evil priests." Hence again the Lord through the prophet says of the priests, "They are made to be for a stumbling-block of iniquity to the house of Israel." For certainly no one does more harm in the Church than one who has the name and rank of sanctity, while he acts perversely. For him, when he transgresses, no one presumes to take to task; and the offence spreads forcibly for example, when out of reverence to his rank the sinner is honoured.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 1, Chapter 2

And the victims, he says, you have turned aside into the depth, so that no one should repent, nor the slain lift up his head. Both the kings and the priests prevented the people from going to the temple at Jerusalem; therefore they are said to have turned aside the victims into the depth.

And I am the instructor of them all.

I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me, for now Ephraim has played the harlot, Israel is defiled; they will not give their thoughts to return to their God, for the spirit of fornications is in their midst, and they have not known the Lord. LXX: For I am your teacher. I have known Ephraim, and Israel has not departed from me, for now Ephraim has played the harlot, Israel is stained; they have not given their thoughts to return to the Lord their God, for the spirit of fornication is in them. But the Lord they have not known. O priests and kings, who have deceived my people; and you, O people, who have been deceived: you have sinned so grievously that you have not only slain the victims, but have sent them into the depth of hell. Do not think that by the greatness of your crime you have departed wholly from me. I am your teacher, or rather your instructor, who desire to amend, not to punish; and to save, not to destroy.

Hence the Lord is not ignorant of the princes of perverse dogmas, nor of the people; not that they are worthy of his knowledge, but that nothing escapes him of what they do in secret, of whom some have deceived and others have been deceived. Nor will they give their thoughts to repent, they who are always advancing in perdition. For the spirit of fornication with which they played the harlot in the Church and departed from the true marriage moves in their midst; therefore they have not known the Lord.

I, he says, know Ephraim, that is, Jeroboam, by whom the people was seduced, and all the kings who followed him both in rank and in crime; and Israel is not hidden from me, that is, the people of the ten tribes, because when the king played the harlot, Israel was defiled. The king first began to play the harlot away from the worship of God, desiring to adore golden calves, and the people willingly followed, and they accomplished an equal impiety with equal zeal.

Finally, they will not return to the Lord, because what they wanted they have found, and the spirit of fornication, which according to the Apostle works in the sons of unbelief, possesses their captive hearts; therefore, while he reigned, they did not know the Lord, or rather they forgot their Creator.

And the arrogance of Israel will answer in his face; and Israel and Ephraim will fall in their iniquity, Judah also will fall with them. LXX: And the injury of Israel will be humbled into his face; and Israel and Ephraim will be weakened in their iniquities, Judah also will be weakened with them. The word gaon the Seventy and Symmachus translate as injury, Aquila and Theodotion as pride. Whatever, therefore, Israel has done, whether acting proudly against the Lord or venerating idols to the injury of the Creator, will answer in his face, so that he may not go away unpunished, but that his insolence may be humbled; and that the people and the kings may fall together in their iniquity, or be weakened, so that those who were strong in crime may be compelled, now weak, to return to the Lord. And this will befall not only Israel and Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes and their kings, so that they are led into captivity; but Judah also, that is, the two tribes which reigned in Jerusalem, will follow the footsteps of the captives, so that those whose crimes they imitate they may imitate also in punishment. The heretics have pride as the mother of their iniquity, while they constantly boast that they know higher things and rave in insult against the Church. But their arrogance will be weakened, and the people and the teachers will fall together; Judah also, who seems to be in the house of God, and dwells in the Church not in mind but in body, and holds in error the same opinion as the heretics, in vain lays claim to the name of churchman, because he too must be punished with the heretics. We run quickly over what is plain, so that we may linger over the more obscure.

The heretics suppose that they appease God by a multitude of sacrifices; and churchmen, that by alms they redeem the sins in which they persist; whereas every sacrifice blots out past crimes, not present ones; therefore they do not find the Lord, who is taken away from such men and withdraws far off. These, indeed, have transgressed against God, and have begotten strange sons not to Christ but to the devil; therefore at all times their works are accursed, and all that they do the rust of bloody color lays waste, because they are next to blood and slaughter. Now rust is properly said to come down in the night dew and to stain the grain, still milky in the ear, with the color of vermilion or of red ochre; and fittingly, according to the ἀναγωγήν (anagogy), it lays waste the lots of the heretics, of whom it is said: Their lots will not profit them.

With their flocks and with their herds they will go to seek the Lord and will not find; he has been taken away from them; they have transgressed against the Lord, for they have begotten strange sons; now a month will devour them with their portions. LXX: With sheep and calves they will go to seek the Lord and will not find him; he has turned aside from them, because they have forsaken the Lord; because they have begotten strange sons for themselves, now rust will devour them, and their lots. Not only Israel and Ephraim will go with flocks and herds to seek the Lord, but Judah also, of whom it is written above: Judah also will fall with them; all of them having this one contest, that they strive to appease with victims him whom they have offended by their transgressions; and they do not find him whom they seek, because he too has departed from those who depart from him. Especially since he says elsewhere also: Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? And again: I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. And in Isaiah: Burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of lambs, and the blood of goats and bulls I do not want.

For they have transgressed against the Lord, because, playing the harlot with idols, they have begotten sons not to God but to demons. Others think that what is meant here is what is said in Ezra, a long time afterwards, when they took foreign wives, begetting children from them, and afterwards were compelled to put them away. But here it is better to take as strange sons those who were begotten in the error of idols, or those whom they led through the fire and consecrated to idols. Since, therefore, they have done this, not long afterwards, not after endless spans of years, nor, as I was formerly accustomed, foretelling things to come long after, but now and at this present time the Assyrian and the Chaldean will come; and they will devour them with their portions, or lots, that is, with the possessions which they received in the division of the land by the measure of the line. Where we said: a month will devour them, the Seventy translated rust; whereas rust, that is, ἐρυσίβη, is certainly called hasil, as they themselves also said in the prophet Joel: What the locust left, the rust has eaten, that is, hasil. But month is called hodes; accordingly Aquila translated new moons, that is, Kalends; Symmachus and Theodotion month; and the sense is: month by month the enemy will come and will lay everything waste. Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find that under King Pekah, who reigned over the ten tribes, Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians came and carried a great part of the people of Samaria away to the Assyrians; at which time among the Greeks it was the second year of the first Olympiad; and among the Latins — Rome not yet founded — Amulius was reigning at Alba in his twentieth year, he whom Romulus afterwards drove from the kingdom.

Some, following the Seventy, who said house of ὢν, have interpreted Beth-aven as the city of the sun; and, calling Christ the sun of justice, they would have his city be the Church. This displeases me; for the house of the idol, which Aquila translated useless house, cannot be referred to the Church even according to tropology. But let us say this: that the heretics, who in Gibeah and Ramah promise themselves lofty knowledge, are bidden to howl in the house of the idol, and are not before the face of Benjamin, which is interpreted son of the right hand, but behind his back, where he has no eyes. For all the boasting of Ephraim, which is interpreted fruitfulness, will shortly be in desolation; and when the day of judgment, he says, and the time of rebuke has come, I will show by deeds that my words are not empty.

Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; howl in Beth-aven, behind your back, Benjamin; Ephraim will be in desolation in the day of rebuke; among the tribes of Israel I have shown faithfulness. LXX: Blow the trumpet upon the hills, sound upon the high places, proclaim in the house of ὤν; Benjamin has fallen out of his mind, Ephraim has become a desolation in the days of rebuke; among the tribes of Israel I have shown faithful things. The months one by one, or the rust, will devour Ephraim and Israel and Judah with their portions. Therefore I command you who hear to sound not with a loud voice but with a clear horn; for clear hearing is needed, so that all who are round about may hear. Blow the horn in Gibeah, whose etymology the Seventy translated as hills; and the trumpet in Ramah, which is interpreted high places; now these are two cities in the tribe of Benjamin, neighbors to one another, that is, Gibeah, in which Saul was born, and Ramah, which is next to Gibeah, situated at the seventh milestone from Jerusalem, and which the king of Israel tried to seize, in order to shut off the going out and the coming in of the tribe of Judah. In Gibeah, therefore, and in Ramah, sound out with a clear horn and trumpet; of these the horn is a shepherd's instrument and is made of curved horn; hence it is properly called in Hebrew sophar, in Greek κερατίνη. The trumpet, however, is made of bronze or of silver, and sounds in wars and at solemn festivals. Over Beth-aven, which was once called Bethel, and is in the tribe of Ephraim, where the golden calf was, there is need not of blaring and sounding but of howling, because captivity is near. And he said beautifully that Beth-aven is behind the back of Benjamin; for where the tribe of Benjamin ends, not far off, in the tribe of Ephraim, this city was founded.

Where we translated behind your back, Benjamin, the Seventy rendered Benjamin has been moved in mind, always fitting ἔκστασιν, that is, ecstasy of mind, to Benjamin, the churchman. Hence also in the sixty-seventh (68th) psalm it is said: There is Benjamin, a youth, in ecstasy of mind. And in the blessings of Jacob, under the person of Benjamin, of which tribe the apostle Paul was, we read it written: Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and at evening he will give food. For he who in the beginning persecuted the Church afterwards bestowed the nourishment of the Gospel on believers throughout the whole world. Hence also Saul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, prophesied in ecstasy of mind all day until evening among the band of the prophets.

For this reason, then, I say and command: Blow the horn in Gibeah, and the trumpet in Ramah, and howl in Beth-aven, because the royal house of Ephraim, or Ephraim himself, that is, the dominion of Israel, will now be in desolation, and captivity is close at hand. In the day of the rebuke and punishment of the ten tribes of Israel I have shown my words to be faithful, the words I threatened through the prophets, so that what I had foretold in word I might prove in deed.

The princes of Judah have become like those who take up the boundary; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water. LXX: The princes of Judah have become like those who move boundaries; upon them I will pour out my onrush like water. When Ephraim and Israel had been led into captivity and their land reduced to a wilderness, the princes of Judah, who ought to have wept, and to have exhorted their own people to withdraw from idolatry lest they too should suffer the like, began to rejoice and be glad that the land of those tribes lay open to them to possess more widely; and they became like those who take up the boundaries of Israel, passing beyond their own borders and desiring to extend their kingdom and possession into the places that once were Israel's. Therefore the Lord says: Upon these very princes of Judah too the Babylonians will come, and will thus overwhelm them like an onrush of water, not by their own strength but by my indignation. He says also to the princes of Judah, that is, of the Church, that they ought not to exult and to reckon the perdition of the heretics their own salvation, but rather to lament that those have perished. Hence also the apostle Paul teaches churchmen not to glory over the breaking of the Jewish branches, but rather to fear lest they too be broken. And in another place: Who, he says, is made to stumble, and I do not burn? Otherwise, upon such princes, who glory in the miseries of others and think they stand precisely because others fall, the Lord will pour out his wrath like water. For wrath the Seventy translated ὅρμημα, that is, onrush; and some think it is to be taken as a blessing, according to what we read elsewhere: The onrush of the river makes glad the city of God. But it is more correctly taken as wrath — as all except the Seventy have translated —, especially since the word pouring out goes with wrath, as the prophet says to the Lord: Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your wrath take hold of them. The princes of Judah move the boundaries which their fathers set when they exchange the truth for a lie and preach something other than what they received from the apostles.

Ephraim suffering wrong, broken in judgment, because he began to go after filth. LXX: Ephraim has oppressed his adversary, has trampled on judgment, because he began to go after vain things. If Ephraim is impious, and on account of his impiety will be in desolation, how is it now said: Ephraim suffering wrong, broken in judgment? For he who suffers wrong and is broken has his judgment unjustly overborne, all the more since a just cause is set down why he was handed over to captivity. For there follows: because he began to go after filth, that is, after idols, which are compared to filth. What he says, then, is this: Ephraim is oppressed by the Assyrians, first by Pul, then by Tiglath-pileser, afterwards by Shalmaneser; not that those who oppressed him were just, and that he was therefore handed over to them, but that those who were once my people, since I abandon them, are handed over to punishment; and in this there seems to be wrong, not in the eyes of God, who passes a just sentence, but of those who endure the torments, while they are yielded up to adversaries worse than themselves. And the Lord gives the reason why in this respect they endure wrong, and are handed over to worse men, and justice is not kept toward them: because Ephraim, that is, Jeroboam, began to go after idols and to forsake God; for it was he who fashioned the golden calves. According to the translation of the Seventy, Ephraim, that is, Jeroboam, oppressed his adversary Rehoboam, that is, the tribe of Judah, and oppressed him in this, that, having deserted Jerusalem and the temple, he followed the images of Egyptian filth. Concerning the heretics the sense is plain: that by their false sophisms and by dialectical art they often oppress churchmen; but when they have done this, they follow not the cleanness of the true faith but the filth of falsehood; and, handed over to the devil and his angels, they seem to themselves to suffer wrong, and that the truth of judgment has been broken in their case. In another way: Israel is laid waste, and all his labors are plundered when the Assyrian comes, and he loses God as his protector; and he is broken in judgment for this reason, that he followed idols.

And I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like rottenness to the house of Judah. LXX: And I am like a disturbance to Ephraim, and like a goad to the house of Judah. In the Hebrew language a moth is called As; recob is rottenness and decay; of which the one consumes garments, the other wood; for which the LXX translated ταραχὴν, that is, tumult or disturbance, and goad. And it must be noted that the moth is referred to Ephraim, and rottenness to the house of Judah. Just as, therefore, the moth consumes garments, and rottenness or decay consumes wood (both of which happen over a long time), so God, giving the ten tribes, and afterwards the two, room for repentance over a long time, and calling them to salvation, while they treasure up for themselves wrath in the day of wrath, becomes as it were a moth and rottenness; not that God is a moth or rottenness, or a disturbance or a goad, but that to those who suffer punishment all these things seem so. First, therefore, Ephraim and Israel were consumed, then the house of Judah also followed; not Judah himself, but his house; otherwise there is reserved from the race of Judah the one for whom it was laid up. And he was the expectation of the nations. But when the heretics, who are understood as Ephraim, have been punished, Judah too, that is, those who remain with the Church and are held fast by either the errors or the vices of the heretics, will be subject to a like sentence.

And Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond; and Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king; and he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able to loose the bond from you. LXX: And Ephraim saw his infirmity, and Judah his pain, and Ephraim went to the Assyrians, and sent envoys to King Jareb; and he will not be able to free you, nor will he make the pain cease from you. "Envoys" is not found in the Hebrew. And where the Seventy put Jareb, we, following Symmachus, have translated "avenger"; for Aquila and Theodotion rendered "judge". That Jareb signifies avenger and judge, the name of Gideon shows: when the worshipers of Baal demanded him for punishment, because he had overthrown the grove and the altars of Baal, his father answered: Let Baal avenge himself, or let Baal judge him; and he was called, it says, Jerubbaal, that is: let Baal avenge himself. Ephraim, therefore, perceiving his infirmity, and Judah his bond, because he had been bound together with the ten tribes in sin, sought help not from God, who was able to loose them, but from the king of the Assyrians. We read that under King Menahem, who ruled over the ten tribes, Israel sent gifts to the Assyrians; and that Judah, under King Ahaz, begged the protection of Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, who, since God opposed them, were not able to free them, nor to loose the bond of captivity. We can also refer the bond, for which in the Hebrew is written mezur, and which Aquila rendered ἐπίδεσιν or συνδεσμὸν, that is, a binding together or a conspiracy, to that time when Rezin and Pekah son of Remaliah laid waste many thousands of men of the tribe of Judah, in that Judah in vain begged against the two kings the help not of God but of the Assyrians. Some, according to tropology, refer Ephraim and Judah to the heretics and to churchmen; because both they and Judah, bound together by the bonds of sins, according to what is written: Each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins, sent to Assyria and to the avenging king, that is, to the devil, of whom we read: That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger. And because they did not entreat the true helper or judge, therefore he made them remain in the pain of sickness and in the bonds of their offenses. I have read in someone's commentaries that King Jareb is interpreted as Christ. And because there follows: He will not be able to heal you, he argued from this that Christ cannot heal the heretics or the sinners among churchmen in the time of judgment, where there is no mercy, according to what is written: But in hell who will confess to you? And that he cannot heal or free them is by no means through his own weakness, but through the desert of those who have asked for help too late. Just as the Lord too is said not to have been able to do signs in his own country; and the cause why he was not able, he explains: Because, it says, they did not believe in him. Let him have said these things; let us interpret the avenging king in a bad sense. In place of what we have expounded as Jareb, that is, avenger, others wrongly read Iarim, with the letter mem, which is translated "forests"; whence Kiriath-jearim is interpreted "village of forests".

To the heretics too, and to a negligent Church, God is turned into a panther and a lion; and he will take from them the prey which they formerly snatched from the Church, so that those who had perished while free may be saved by being captured; and he will by no means dwell in the conventicles of the perverse, but will return to his place, of which he says: I am in the Father and the Father in me, and he will spurn and despise them, until they fail in their impiety and seek through repentance him by whom they had been abandoned. Others think that the place of God is heaven, to which God, offended by those who dwell on earth, returns, and will make them perish who, by the greatness of their sins, have turned the most merciful Lord into the rage of wild beasts against themselves.

For I am like a lioness to Ephraim, and like a lion's whelp to the house of Judah. I, I will seize and go; I will carry off, and there is none who may rescue. Going, I will return to my place, until you fail and seek my face. LXX: For I am like a panther to Ephraim, and like a lion in the house of Judah. And I will snatch, and go, and carry off, and there will be none who may rescue; I will go and return to my place, until they perish and seek my face. While they go to Assyria and send to the vindicating or avenging king, who will not be able to heal them nor to loose the bond that binds them, I will show that, when I oppose, all the help of men is vain; for I will be like a lioness to Ephraim, and like a lion's whelp to the house of Judah. For lioness, which in Hebrew is called sohel, the Seventy rendered panther, which is said alike in Greek and in Latin, and can be taken both as the name of a beast and as "every beast"; so that whatever is savage in beasts you may recognize in the indignation of God. Nothing is swifter than the panther, nothing stronger than the lion; in the panther is signified the swift destruction of the kingdom of Samaria by the Assyrians; and in the lion is shown the most mighty kingdom of the Chaldeans, which some time afterwards came against Jerusalem and Judah. And because he had said that he was a lioness or a panther, and a lion, he keeps the metaphor, and says: I, I will seize and go; I will carry off, and there is none who may rescue. It is asked: if, when God seizes, carries off and holds, no one can snatch from his hands, according to what is written: No one can snatch out of the hand of my Father, how was Judas snatched from the hand of God by his betrayal? To which we will briefly answer that no one can snatch from the hand of God; but that he who is held can, by his own will, fall out of the hand of God.

And as for what follows: Going, I will return to my place, by the place of God we ought to understand his magnificence and majesty; so that he no longer, by way of dispensation, descends to men, is angry, has mercy, forgets, becomes like a panther, is turned into a lion, is changed into beasts; but disregards human affairs and allows those whom he formerly protected to be subjected to their enemies, so that they may waste away, and fail, and perish, and afterwards seek the face of the Lord, and say: Make your face shine, and we shall be saved. And: Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

In their tribulation they will rise early to me: come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has seized and he will heal us; he will strike and he will cure us; he will make us live after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight; we shall know and we shall follow, that we may know the Lord. LXX: In their tribulation they will watch early for me, saying: let us go and return to the Lord our God, for he will scourge and he will heal us; he will strike and he will cure us; he will make us whole after two days; on the third we shall rise again and we shall live before him and we shall know; let us pursue, that we may know the Lord. Therefore God has handed Ephraim and Judah over to captivity, and there is none who can snatch from his hand, and he will return to his place until they fail; and they will seek his face, so that him whom they had not felt as gracious and present, they may seek again as angry and absent; and in their tribulation, when the light of repentance has risen for them, they may rise early to him, according to what we read in Isaiah: In tribulation I remembered the Lord. And in the first of the psalms of ascents: To the Lord I cried when I was in tribulation, and he heard me.

It seems that the saying refers very suitably to the mystery of Christ and the redemption through him, pointing to the conversion to God. For the face of God we seek signifies most certainly the Son himself, "who is the image, and the radiance, and the very seal of the Father's nature." Thus the true face of God and Father is the Son, inasmuch as he is recognized in him: "And who saw him, saw the Father." The psalmist thus calls him when he cries out to God of all, saying: "Cause your face to shine upon your servant." Indeed, just as from the person of those who were already transformed according to the Son through the Spirit: "The light of your face, O Lord, has been marked upon us." Or as the prophet says: "The light of our face, the anointed Lord."

"They seek early" seems to indicate here that they, as if awakened from the sleep of thoughtlessness which was in them, and further as if brought from night and darkness to light and day, will call out to one another that it is fitting to return to the Lord. This is a return to the senses of those fallen into deception and those taken up by the worship of idols. For the fruit of vigilance is at present seeking to get out of the gloom which is demonic.
6: The Holy Spirit set this forth of old, when he said in the Psalms, "O my king and my God. For to you will I pray; O Lord, in the morning you shall hear my voice. In the morning I will stand before you, and will see you." And again through the prophet the Lord says, "At dawn they will be on watch for me, saying, 'Let us go and return to the Lord our God.' " Likewise at the setting of the sun and at the end of the day necessarily there must again be prayer. For since Christ is the true sun and the true day, as the sun and the day of the world recede, when we pray and petition that the light come upon us again, we pray for the coming of Christ to provide us with the grace of eternal light.
Treatise IV. On the Lord's Prayer 35

And when they have risen early to the Lord, what will they say? Come, and let us return to the Lord. They are not content with their own salvation, but urge one another on to return to the Lord whom they had left, whom they had deserted because of their sins, by whom they had been abandoned. For he has seized and he will heal us; he who had said above: I, I will seize and go, will strike and heal us. For what we have said, "he will cure", all alike translated μοτώσει (will dress with lint); now properly μότα is the name for the little linen pads that are inserted into wounds, to eat away the putrid flesh and draw out the pus; and it belongs to the art of physicians to heal great wounds over a long time and to restore health through pain.

In the beginning he seized Adam's human nature; for he at once declared it accursed, ascribing it to death and corruption. Thus the wrath has struck, but grace plugged the wound with lint. For Christ has brought the healing. He invited [us] to know the true divine revelation; he confirmed [us] through the Spirit to observe the commandments. He showed us again to be zealous followers by placing us beyond corruption and freeing us from the previous infirmities, namely, sin and passions.

For hear what the prophet says: "God will raise us up after two days, and on the third day we shall rise again and shall live in his sight." The first day for us is the passion of the Savior, and the second, on which he descended into hell, but the third is the day of the resurrection. And therefore on the third day "God went before them, by day in a pillar of cloud, by night in a pillar of fire." But if, according to those things which we said above, the Apostle rightly teaches us that the mysteries of baptism are contained in these words, it is necessary that "those who are baptized in Christ should be baptized in his death, and be buried together with him," and rise again with him on the third day from the dead, whom also, according to that which the Apostle says: "he raised up together with himself, and made to sit together in the heavenly places." When, therefore, the mystery of the third day has been received by you, God will begin to lead you forth and Himself to show you the way of salvation.

And that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures. All things are enclosed in faith; therefore the resurrection of the Lord that was to take place on the third day was described in the person of the people. For Hosea the prophet says: After two days he will heal us, and on the third day we shall rise, and we shall live in his sight (Hos. 6:3). For none of the faithful denies that in Christ all have risen, just as in Adam all have died. In a similar way, in a psalm, under the person of man, he signifies Christ as well, saying: You have subjected all things under his feet: you have crowned him with glory and honor (Ps. 8:8).

A few of the Jews of that time were persuaded, but the world hearkened to the truth. Those who concealed the truth were buried in oblivion, but those who received it were made manifest by the power of the Savior, who rose from the dead and raised the dead himself. In the person of the risen dead the prophet Hosea says plainly, "He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, to live in his presence."

The Lord therefore strikes and cures us; for whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives; not only does he cure, but he makes alive after two days, and on the third day, rising again from hell, he raises up with himself the whole race of men. And when he has cured those who were struck, and made alive those who were cured, and raised up those who were made alive, then we shall live in his sight, we who, while he was absent, lay dead. And we shall live in his sight; we shall know him and follow him with all zeal, that we may know the Lord, by whose rising on the third day we have risen. By these words is explained what we have often already pointed out, that both Israel and Judah, that is, the ten and the two tribes, will then have one shepherd, and David as king, when they have believed in the Lord who rises again; and that the Jews vainly promise themselves dreams of a thousand years, since the salvation of all has been promised on the third day, on which the Lord rose again from hell. The Hebrews interpret the second day as the coming of their Christ, and the third day as the judgment, when they are to be saved. Granting this, let them answer us what the first day is, that is, the first coming of the Savior. And when they cannot answer, let us conclude that the first day is, according to what they themselves would have, the coming of the Savior in humility, the second in glory, the third in the guise of one who judges. But those who accept the second and the third testify that they have lost the first, because a second and a third cannot be so called without a first.

Further on, Hosea foretold the resurrection of Christ on the third day, but in the mysterious way that is proper to prophecy. He says, "He shall heal us after two days, and on the third day we shall rise again." This is the idea underlying the words of Paul [when he says], "Therefore if you have risen in Christ, seek the things that are above."

The prince of this world did not want the Lord's army to recognize the engagement of those three days, as that engagement of which the prophet said, "He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up." The first day for us is the passion of the Savior; the second day on which he descended into hell; but the third day is the day of the resurrection. So then on the third day God went before them in a pillar of cloud by day and by night in a pillar of fire, and the people were led through the Red Sea. The three days we can fittingly call the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, for the Father is a day, the Son is one, and the Holy Spirit is one, and these three are one.

This is Hosea, the first of the twelve prophets who was privileged to speak concerning the Lord Christ in these terms: When they are afflicted, let them rise early to seek me saying, Come and let us return unto the Lord our God, for he hath smitten us and he will heal us; he that hath struck us will bind us up. After two days will he heal us. On the third day we shall be raised up again and we shall live! With reference to this passage the Apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: For I delivered unto you first of all that which also I received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures. For that he was buried, and that he was raised up on the third day according to the scriptures, is not to be found anywhere else.

Nor is this the only thing that proves the dignity of the water. But there is also that which is more honorable than all—the fact that Christ, the maker of all, came down as the rain, and was known as a spring, and diffused himself as a river, and was baptized in the Jordan. For you have just heard how Jesus came to John and was baptized by him in the Jordan. Oh, things strange beyond compare! How should the boundless river that makes glad the city of God have been dipped in a little water!

Those who are thus continually engaged, are waiting entirely on the Lord, and say, ‘Let us follow on to know the Lord: we shall find Him ready as the morning, and He will come to us as the early and the latter rain for the earth.’ For not only does He satisfy them in the morning; neither does He give them only as much to drink as they ask; but He gives them abundantly according to the multitude of His lovingkindness, vouchsafing to them at all times the grace of the Spirit.

His going forth is prepared like the dawn, and he will come to us like the early rain, and the late rain to the earth. LXX: We shall find him prepared like the morning, and he will come to us like the early and the late rain to the earth. Come, he says, and let us return to the Lord, for he who has seized also will heal us, will strike and cure us, and will make us live after two days, and on the third day will raise us up; he himself and no other is prepared for us like the morning and the dawn. Of whom too is the title of the twenty-first (22nd) psalm: For the morning taking up; although in the Hebrew it is written: For the morning hart, because, having slain death and the twisting and ancient serpent, he longs to climb to the mountains; and he himself, the darkness scattered, rises for us as the sun of justice, to illuminate our blindness. And beautifully he says: his going forth is prepared. Of which, according to tropology, we read in the eighteenth (19th) psalm: And he, like a bridegroom, goes forth from his chamber. He is not only called morning, and dawn, and daybreak; but he will come to us like the early rain, and the late rain to the earth. We receive Christ as the early rain when the foundations of faith have been laid in us, and we shall receive him as the late rain when, the crops being ripe, we shall gather eternal fruits and be stored away in the Lord's granaries. Therefore the Jews, who did not receive the early rains and cast their seed without rains, will not receive the fruit of the crops in the last time. This is the rain of which the Lord makes a promise, saying: I will give you the early and the late rain. According to allegory, the early rain is given when we know in part; the late rain is given when that which is perfect comes. And the Lord is always prepared for those who rise early, who can say: I will rise at daybreak. And: O God, my God, to you I watch from the light. My soul has thirsted for you.

For I suppose that he waters in two ways upon us who received faith and have known rightly his manifestation. On the one hand, he reveals knowledge in the spirit of the old and legal, and in addition to these, prophetic teachings. In my view, this is the early rain. On the other hand, he adds to this the late [rain], the interpretation of the gospel's teachings and the most desirable grace of the apostolic preachings.

We perceive these same things to have been said also to the heretics, and to the true Judah, who is to suffer the like: that the Lord calls them to mercy and desires that they return to salvation. But they pursue the delights and refreshments of this age, like a cloud and dew that quickly passes away; to whom it is said in the Gospel: Fool, this night they require your soul of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? And that rich man clothed in purple, who despised Lazarus lying before his gates, learned that all he had enjoyed had passed away like a cloud and dew. But God always slays the prophets of the heretics, when he threatens them with eternal punishments, and takes them away from the true life, and leaves them to the death of their crimes. But let us love that cloud which is everlasting, and which protects us from the heat of this world, sitting upon which the Lord came into Egypt and broke all the images of the Egyptians. Let us love that dew of which Moses speaks: Let my words come down like the dew. And of which Isaiah says: The dead will rise again, and those who are in the tombs will be raised up; for the dew that is from you is their health. There are some who think that the prophets who were slain are holy men, because on account of a sinful people even prophets were slain and handed over to their enemies.

What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like the dew passing away in the morning; for this reason I have hewn them by the prophets, I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and your judgments will go forth like the light. LXX: What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? But your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like the dew passing away in the morning; therefore I have cut down your prophets, I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and your judgment will go forth like the light. When he says: What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? he shows the affection of a parent toward lost sons. According to what we read in Isaiah: What is there that I ought to have done further for my vineyard, and have not done for it? And in Micah: My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I been troublesome to you? Answer me, for I brought you out of the land of Egypt, I freed you from the house of servants, and I sent before your face Moses, and Aaron, and Miriam. What then shall I do to you, Ephraim, what shall I do to you, Judah? Your mercy, with which I have always had mercy on you, has passed away like a morning cloud, and like the dew rising in the morning, which is dried up when the sun has risen.

For already captivity is near, already I see you led in chains to the Assyrians and the Babylonians; I have hewn you by the prophets and threatened you with terrible words, I have brought out the scalpel, fire and cautery; so that you who despised me when I was merciful might fear me when offended; and I have slain the negligent by the words of my mouth, so that I might punish sinners by the terror of words before captivity was at hand. And all these things I have done so that the truth of the judgment with which I am about to judge you might appear, and no one might doubt that you have justly suffered what you suffer. For what is I have hewn them by the prophets, the Seventy translated: I have cut down your prophets, understanding the false prophets themselves to have been slain by the Lord; so that those who had been the cause of error, by promising prosperity, might, when slain, be turned into an occasion of salvation. And the sense is: Lest you should say: We believed the prophets; I have slain even them, so that every occasion of sinning might be taken away from you. We read in the book of Kings that three hundred prophets of the Baalim were slain under Elijah, and another countless multitude under Jehu, who overthrew the house of Ahab.

And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.  And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.  And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?  But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.  But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: [Hosea 6:6] for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

For to every one who has turned to God in truth and with a whole heart, the doors are open, and the thrice-glad Father receives his truly repentant child. And true repentance is to be no longer bound in the same sins for which he denounced death against himself, but to eradicate them completely from the soul. For on their uprooting God takes up his abode again in you. For it is said there is great and exceeding joy and festivity in the heavens with the Father and the angels when one sinner turns and repents. This is why he cries, "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice."
Who is the Rich Man that Shall Be Saved?

But he would not threaten the impenitent if he failed to pardon the penitent. This would be doubtful only if he had not revealed elsewhere the profusion of his mercy. Has he not said, "He who is fallen shall rise, and he who was turned away shall return"? He it is, most assuredly, who "will have mercy rather than sacrifice." The heavens and the angels who are there rejoice at human repentance. Look at you now, sinner, be of good heart! You see where it is that you are a cause of joy.

For the Word of God Himself tells us that He prefers the performance of His commandments to the offering of sacrifice. God proclaims this, Moses declares it to the people, Paul preaches it to the Gentiles. Do that which you understand is most profitable for the time. "I prefer mercy," it is said, "rather than sacrifice." Are they not, then, rather Christians in truth who condemn their own sin, than they who think to defend it? "The just is an accuser of himself in the beginning of his words." He who accuses himself when he has sinned is just, not he who praises himself.

Great is the principle of mercy to God. Not only his to us, but also that issuing from us to our fellow servants. In the Old Testament and the New, God lays down innumerable laws pertaining to this matter. He orders us to be benevolent continually in all quarters, through words, money and deeds. And Moses throughout—up and down, here and there—scatters words about these matters in all his legislations. And in the person of God the prophets shout, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." And all the apostles act and speak in harmony with these prophetic words. Therefore let us not neglect the matter. By mercy we greatly benefit ourselves, not the poor only. We receive much more than we provide.

Daily God calls to repentance both those who are outside the Church and those who sin while dwelling in the Church, and says to them: I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. But they offer sacrilegious bread, and give alms, and appear to pursue humility; these, then, if they are truly done, I interpret as burnt offerings. But since they have abandoned the knowledge of God, in vain, with the head of faith cut off, do they boast that they have the other members; for they have transgressed the covenant of God in the Church, just as Adam transgressed in paradise; and they show themselves imitators of their ancient parent, so that, as he was cast out of paradise, so these too may be cast out of the Church.

For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings; but they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant; there they have dealt treacherously against me. LXX: For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings; but they are like a man passing over the covenant. What follows in the Seventy: There Gilead despised me, a city that works vain things, and the rest, must be fitted to the following section; let us discuss what we have set down: I have hewn them by the prophets, I have slain them by the words of my mouth, I have threatened grievous things, so that I might have mercy on the penitent, so that I might stretch out my hand to those who have fallen and are rising. For I do not delight in sacrifices and victims, and in a multitude of burnt offerings. My victims and burnt offerings are the salvation of those who believe, the conversion of sinners.

Most of all, worship of God displays love.… For truly the compassion from beside the Father is Christ, as he takes away the sins, dismisses the charges and justifies by faith, and recovers the lost and makes [them] stronger than death. For what is good and he does not give? Therefore the knowledge of God is better than sacrifice and holocausts, as it is brought to perfection in Christ. For by him and in him we have known the Father, and we have become rich in the justification by faith.

But God said, I require mercy, and not sacrifice: and the acknowledgment of God, and not whole burnt offerings.

What is meant by mercy? and what by sacrifice? By mercy then is signified, Justification and grace in Christ: even that which is by faith. For we have been justified, not by the works of the law that we have done, but by His great mercy. And sacrifice means the law of Moses.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Whereas I [the Lord] have no need of sacrifices, I accept them out of considerateness for the limitations of your way of thinking. These two things, on the contrary, I do require: the right disposition toward me and lovingkindness toward the neighbor, these also being the first obligations I imposed, "You will love the Lord your God with your whole heart, your whole soul, your whole mind and your whole strength; and you will love your neighbor as yourself." But whereas I imposed these obligations, they resembled someone breaking agreements made by him with somebody else. In similar fashion, in fact, they despised my longsuffering and trampled on the laws given them.
Counsel disposes to mercy: for there is nothing God counsels more in Scripture than to show mercy, which he esteems above all holocausts.

A man sees the slaughter of bodies, he grieves greatly. He therefore who sees the slaughter of souls, how can he restrain himself from tears? This grief is greatly pleasing to God. The Lord says concerning this knowledge: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than holocausts." I know the infirmities of others: I ought to suffer with them.

But they have imitated Adam, so that what he had done in paradise, passing over my covenant and law, these did on earth. And there, that is, in paradise, all have dealt treacherously against me, in the likeness of the transgression of Adam. For it is no wonder if what went before in the parent is condemned in the children also.

Gilead, a city of those who work an idol, supplanted by blood, and like the jaws of robber men (or: of a robber; for it can be read either way). LXX: There Gilead despised me, a city that works vain things, and troubles the water, and your strength is that of a pirate man. We read that in Ramoth-gilead Jehu was anointed king, he who mingled blood with blood, and overthrew the house of Ahab, and before sunrise ordered heaps of the heads of his sons to be set up; in this city across the Jordan, in the possession of the tribe of Gad, an idol was consecrated; it was inhabited by priests, for it too was a city of fugitives. Therefore, the more celebrated it was and the greater its authority, because it had been assigned as the portion of the priests, so much the more was it, for Israel dwelling across the Jordan, the beginning of idolatry and of all evils, so that those who had sinned first were the first to be taken captive by the Assyrians. And since that province itself is full of robberies, he compares them to robbers: as those lie in wait for travelers, so the priests lay in wait for the simplicity of the people. Moreover, according to tropology, Gilead is interpreted 'migration of testimony'; and it despises God when it twists the testimonies of the Scriptures into perverse dogmas, and all its works are vain, and it troubles the waters of the Church, and out of the purest springs makes muddy and filthy streams, which stain rather than cleanse the baptized. And all the strength of this city is like that of a pirate man, while it imitates the devil, who in the sea of this world, through which ships pass, lies in wait for those who strive to reach the harbor. Finally, Symmachus translated more plainly, saying: And your jaws like those of a man lying in ambush. Of pirates of this kind we read in Job: There is no delay for pirates. For although in the present world they seem to vaunt themselves, and to trouble the waters, and to work vain things, and to practice piracy, yet there is no delay of the punishments, which will swiftly overtake them.

A partner of the priests who kill on the way those going from Shechem, because they have wrought wickedness. LXX: The priests hid the way of the Lord, they killed Shechem, because they wrought iniquity. Symmachus translated this passage thus: The fellowship of the priests on the way were killing Shechem. Theodotion in this way: The priests hid the way, they were killing on the back. Aquila: The partnership of the priests on the way were slaying shoulders; and when we sought their meaning according to the history from a Hebrew, it was explained to us thus: The priests of Bethel, or rather the fanatics of Beth-aven, at the times of Passover and Pentecost and Tabernacles, when one had to go through Shechem, which today is called Neapolis, to Jerusalem, where alone it was lawful to sacrifice victims, used to post robbers along the road to lie in wait for those going, so that they might worship the golden calves in Dan and in Beth-aven rather than God in Jerusalem and in the temple. But when he says: The partnership and fellowship of the priests, it signifies their conspiracy and their agreement in the bad sense. But if we read, as we have translated: partners of the priests, it must be referred, he says, to Gilead, which works an idol; and it is supplanted by blood, because it followed the impiety of the priests and is given over to robberies and blood. This is what they may say; let us say that the heretics shut off the way, so that we may not go from Shechem, that is, from good works, to Jerusalem, that is, into the Church. These are like the jaws of robber men, and they kill those who desire to go along the way of this world to the truth. Shechem is interpreted ὦμοι, that is, shoulders; in shoulders we understand work, and all the false priests hide the way, and kill men with evil works, so that they may not reach Jerusalem. And that the shoulder signifies work, this shows: Put your heart on your shoulder, that is, turn what you understand into works. And of Issachar we read that he put his shoulder under to labor, and is a farmer.

But in the house of the heretics we see a horrible thing daily, the teachers first playing the harlot, and the people who are led on by them being defiled. Judah too, that is, the Church, is commanded that it too should prepare for itself, because of its sins, a harvest, or a vintage, when the time of judgment comes. But it is pardoned, and the Lord promises it forgiveness, because whom he loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives, so that, tested and purged, he may store him in his treasuries. Some refer what is said: Judah, begin your vintage, or, set a harvest for yourself, to the good sense, so that, Israel having been punished, this one receives the fruits of its works, according to what is written: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. To us the former sense is more pleasing.

In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing; there Israel has been defiled by the fornication of Ephraim; but you also, Judah, set a harvest for yourself, when I shall turn back the captivity of my people. LXX: In the house of Israel I have seen horrible things, there the fornication of Ephraim; Israel and Judah have been defiled; begin your vintage when I shall turn back the captivity of my people. Of this crime and terrible horror Jeremiah too speaks: The heaven was astounded at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly. For what is more horrible than that the ten tribes suddenly went over to the worship of idols? Hence it is said to their metropolis: Take away your calf, Samaria, in which Ephraim first played the harlot, that is, Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim; and while he played the harlot, Israel was defiled, namely the people of Samaria, which for the most part held the common name of Israel.

Hence the word is turned to Judah also: You too, Judah, set a harvest for yourself; and the sense is: Do not think yourself secure because Israel is led away captive; you too, prepare your crops to be reaped; for not much later you will be led captive to Babylon, and the time of your reaping will come. And when the Chaldeans have reaped you, I will turn back again the captivity of my people, and under Cyrus king of the Persians and Artaxerxes I will bring my people back. And note how pointedly the captivity of Judah and its return are prophesied together; but of Israel, that is, of the ten tribes, there is silence even now, and if ever something favorable is said, it is put off to the coming of Christ.
7: When I wished to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim was uncovered, and the malice of Samaria, because they have wrought a lie; and the thief has entered, the robber plundering outside. LXX: likewise. Israel often received many wounds of idolatry, and above all that one when in the desert they cast the head of a calf and said: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Hence I, who prefer the repentance of the sinner to his death, and who afterwards say in the Gospel: The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick, have tried to heal the wounds of my people. And while I was treating these with every art, so that the wretched people might be cured, suddenly Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim arose, to make the golden calves, and the malice of Samaria, which followed the impious king, was uncovered; for both king and people wrought a lie, that is, an idol. For just as an image is contrary to God, so a lie is contrary to the truth. And the king himself entered like a thief to the people of Israel, and like a robber plundered the unhappy people of God of their help. And the sense is: When I wished to blot out the old sins of my people on account of their ancient idolatry, Ephraim and Samaria found new idols. But this too can be said: that when the Lord and Savior, after the shedding of his blood and his Church gathered from Jews as well as from Gentiles, wished to heal the sins of the people and to bring them back to repentance, suddenly Ephraim, who promise an abundance of false dogmas, and the people of Samaria, who say that they keep the commandments of God, rose up and wrought the idol of false dogmas; and through them the thief and robber, the devil, entered the Church; or else the very doctrine of the heretics entered, like a thief and a robber, of whom the Savior too says in the Gospel: All who came before me were thieves and robbers. Thieves lie in wait and deceive by hidden fraud; robbers boldly carry off what belongs to others. For those who steal, steal by night and in darkness. Hence he says pointedly that the thief entered secretly, and that the robber plunders outside. For they cannot strip those whom they have taught of the garment of Christ unless they have led them out of the Church and made them walk in the perverse way of their doctrines. By the thieves and robbers who came before the Lord we ought to understand not Moses and the prophets, who are always praised by the mouth of the Savior, but the false prophets; and afterwards the heretics, who were not sent by the Lord but came of their own will.

Therefore each one must keep his heart with all watchfulness, for when the Lord comes in the day of judgment, "He will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts," "all the thoughts of men meanwhile accusing or else excusing them," "when their own devices have beset them about." But of such a nature are the evil thoughts that sometimes they make worthy of censure even those things which seem good and which, so far as the popular judgment is concerned, are indeed worthy of praise.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11:15

And lest perhaps they say in their hearts that I have remembered all their wickedness, now their devices have surrounded them; they have been done before my face. LXX: That they may sing together as those who sing in their hearts: I have remembered all their wickednesses; now their thoughts have surrounded them, they have been done against my face. Lest perhaps, he says, they say in their hearts: God has brought old sins back upon us, and we are paying for the offenses of our fathers; they ate the sour grape, and our teeth were set on edge; for that reason I will recount in the following discourse what they have done now and at present, while I look on, and what they do daily; and I will show them their devices, or the thoughts with which they have most zealously pursued evil, and the things they have done in my presence, not fearing my face. But what we read in the Seventy: that they may sing together as those who sing in their hearts, is to be referred to this: that the thief entered, or the robber plundered outside, for this reason, lest, remaining in their former riches and garments, they should reject agreement with the thief and robber; but that, when they have been plundered, they should sing together with them and be made of one heart. Therefore let them receive what they have done, and all their thoughts or works will not merit my regard. The heretics too cannot plead old sins against God, since daily they add new impiety to their ancient works, and perish with the lost, and are bound by their own errors, and, though they think they are hiding from the Lord, are not able to escape his eyes.

In their wickedness they made the king glad, and in their lies the princes. LXX: In their wickednesses they made the kings glad, and in their lies the princes. He sets out what they did before his face: In their wickednesses they made King Jeroboam glad, and in their lies the princes who had been set over the people under Jeroboam. The heretics too, in the wickedness of their works, have made the king, the devil, glad, and in the lies of their perverse dogmas, the princes, no doubt those of this world, whose false wisdom God destroys. Among the heretics we can call king the one who first invented the heresy, and princes those who, set over the peoples of the heretics, claim for themselves a false priesthood. And at the same time it must be noted that the opposing powers and the rulers and princes of this darkness rejoice in our sins.

But where shall I find on a sudden the divine Scripture which may teach me what the "oven" is? I must call upon my Lord Jesus, that he may make me who seek to find, and open to me who knock, so that I may find in the Scriptures the "oven" where I may cook my sacrifice, so that God may receive it. And indeed I think I have found it in the prophet Hosea, where he says: "all committing adultery, like an oven heated for burning", and again: "their hearts," he says, "grew hot like an oven". The heart of man, then, is the "oven". But this heart, if vices set it ablaze or the devil inflames it, will not cook, but will burn up. But if he set it ablaze who said: "I came to cast fire upon the earth", then the loaves of the divine Scriptures and of the words of God, which I receive in my heart, I do not burn up to destruction, but cook for a sacrifice.

All are adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker; the city rested a little from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened.
