LXX: All are adulterers, like an oven burning for baking, to the scorching of the flame, from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened. Those who in their wickedness made the king glad, and in their lies the princes, are all adulterers; and like an oven they were heated by Jeroboam with the fire of idolatry, so as to bake the bread of impiety; and he, when he had sent the burning of error into their souls, like a furnace and an oven first heated with fire, rested a little, so as not to force the people but to leave them to their own will, until the whole lie was leavened; for whatever is done by compulsion is quickly undone, but what we seize upon by our will endures. Therefore here too, since he had taken the metaphor from an oven, which is heated for baking loaves, he keeps it in the rest, so as to show, in the mixing of the leaven, the consent of the whole people; by which, namely, both king and people fell with equal ardor into idolatry. No one doubts that the hearts of the heretics are heated with the fire of the devil, so that the bread of the Antichrist may be baked in them; therefore at first they rest quiet in the Church and speak in secret, and promise all things peaceable, so that the cancer may creep little by little into the peoples, and the leaven of their doctrine; which the Lord too understood when he says: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees; when it has swollen in the hearts of the deceived, then they break out into open madness; and in them is fulfilled what is said by the apostle John: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.

Although you might marry and in the face of the authority of all the Scriptures never commit adultery, why do you not with God's grace accept what is lawful? Instead you dare to offend God and commit what is unlawful. I would like to know whether those who have no wives, and neither fear nor blush to commit adultery before they are joined in wedlock, would want their spouses to be violated by adulterers before they come to marriage. Since there is no one who would patiently accept this, why does not each one observe toward his spouse the fidelity he wants observed by her? Why does one desire to take a virgin as his wife, when he himself is corrupted? Why does he wish to be united to a wife who is alive, when he is dead in soul because of adultery, according to what is written: "The soul that sins shall die"? Moreover, the apostle exclaims in terrible words, "God will judge the immoral and adulterers," and "Adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God." Furthermore, "They are all adulterers, their hearts like an oven."

Those who bent their knee to drink are those who inclined themselves totally to philosophy: and the same are inclined to an infinite number of errors, and that is how the leaven of error is warmed. As Osee writes, "the city rested a little from the mingling of the leaven, till the whole was leavened." They warm the eggs of asps, so that what has been warmed breaks out into a serpent.

Now let us pass to the spiritual understanding: Unhappy peoples who are led astray by the king, the devil, and by his princes; or who have taken up other solemn feasts from the prince of a heresy and from his leaders, leaving the Church and trampling on the truth of the faith, are accustomed to shout and say: This is the day of our king; for example, of Valentinus, of Marcion, of Arius and of Eunomius. Those set over them, hearing this, are not made drunk with wine, lest the sin be thought a light one, but they rave from the wine of which Moses writes in the song of Deuteronomy: Their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps; for these eat the food of impiety and are made drunk with the wine of iniquity. Of this the Apostle also says: Do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery. And in Proverbs we read: Let princes not drink wine, lest they forget wisdom and be unable to judge rightly. Hence, both peoples and leaders having been deceived, the prince stretches out his hand to the mockers, or the pestilent, such as were the sons of Eli, and of whom we read in the first psalm: He has not sat in the chair of the pestilent; of whom it is said: Cast out the pestilent man from the council, and strife will go out with him; whose hearts were kindled, so that they might dash down those whom they had deceived. For this, according to the Seventy, is what cataracts signify, which do not lift up on high but dash down below. And what he says: All night Ephraim was filled with sleep, shows that the heretics, sleeping, do not see the light of the sun of justice. For those who sleep, sleep at night, because their sense is weighed down. And of these we read in the psalms: They have slept their sleep and found nothing.

The day of our king: the princes began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with the mockers, because they applied their heart like an oven when he lay in wait for them. All night he slept baking them; in the morning he himself was kindled like a fire of flame; all were heated like an oven and devoured their judges; all their kings have fallen; there is none among them who cries to me. LXX: The day of your kings. The princes began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with the pestilent, because their hearts were kindled like an oven, while they were cast down headlong all night. Ephraim was filled with sleep; morning came; he was set on fire like a flame of fire. All were heated like an oven, a burning fire, and they ate up their judges. All their kings have fallen; there is not among them one who calls on me. An obscure passage, and one needing the close attention of the reader, so that we may first learn the history. Israel and the city of Samaria rested a little, having received into themselves the heat of error, until the whole lump became like leaven, and rose and burst out; and the people, swelling up, shouted at the doors of King Jeroboam and said: This is the day of Jeroboam our king, this is the feast day which our ruler has appointed for us; this we celebrate, this we sing, on this we exult and play, on this we worship the golden calves. When the people shouted, the princes were not angry, as some think; but they too began to rage from wine and to lose the understanding of their mind, to forget God and to dash themselves against the wood of idols. When the king saw this, namely that the people were shouting and saying: This is the day of our king, and that the princes, like drunken and frenzied men, did not know what they were saying, he stretched out his hand to the mockers, he joined his assent to those who mocked him with empty praises.

But where shall I find on a sudden the divine Scripture which may teach me what the "oven" is? I must call upon my Lord Jesus, that he may make me who seek to find, and open to me who knock, so that I may find in the Scriptures the "oven" where I may cook my sacrifice, so that God may receive it. And indeed I think I have found it in the prophet Hosea, where he says: "all committing adultery, like an oven heated for burning", and again: "their hearts," he says, "grew hot like an oven". The heart of man, then, is the "oven". But this heart, if vices set it ablaze or the devil inflames it, will not cook, but will burn up. But if he set it ablaze who said: "I came to cast fire upon the earth", then the loaves of the divine Scriptures and of the words of God, which I receive in my heart, I do not burn up to destruction, but cook for a sacrifice.

These mockers, when their king lay in wait for them and was leading them away from their God, offered him their heart like an oven, for him to kindle them and make them burn with the flames of idolatry. For he assented to the people for this reason: because he understood that they had turned to error with their whole mind. And what follows: All night he slept baking them; in the morning he himself was kindled like a fire of flame, signifies this: after he sent fire into the oven of their heart, and saw them raging, and that there was no one to resist his will, he slept all night, that is, he was secure; he kept himself in darkness while they were being baked and were making the bread of impiety. Hence afterwards he rose in the morning, and showed the flame of his crimes in open madness, so that they passed over, no longer by stealth but shamelessly, from the worship of God to the ceremonies of idols.

What more? All, like an oven, were heated with the fire of idolatry, and devoured their judges, so that even one who could have been good by nature and could have remembered the religion of the Lord, seeing both princes and people subject to the calves and thinking them gods, is himself also devoured by the crime. Finally, all the kings of Israel fell, and walked in the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin, and none was found who abandoned the idols and returned to God. These things we have spoken according to the tradition of the Hebrews, more boldly than knowingly, leaving the credit for what is said to its authors.

Their hearts are heated by various passions: anger, love, avarice; and they devour their judges, either whatever virtues they may be able to have in their mind, or the senses by which they distinguish evil from good. Or else it must be said that the leaders of the heretics are devoured by their own peoples, so that they themselves are devoured by the assent of those whose houses they devour for the sake of base gain. All the princes of the heretics have fallen; although they cry to the Lord, there is none who calls on his name. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call on his name; they called on the Lord, and he heard them, he who does not hear the kings and princes of the heretics, because there is none among them who cries to the Lord.

Ephraim himself was mingled among the peoples; Ephraim has become a loaf baked under the ashes, which is not turned over; strangers devoured his strength, and he did not know it. Yes, and grey hairs were spread over him, and he was unaware of it; and the pride of Israel will be humbled before his face, and they have not returned to the Lord their God, and they have not sought him in all these things. LXX: Ephraim was mingled with his peoples; Ephraim has become a loaf baked under the ashes, which is not turned over. Strangers devoured his strength, but he did not know it; and grey hairs blossomed on him, and he was unaware of it; and the insolence of Israel will be humbled before his face, and they have not returned to the Lord their God; and they have not sought him in all these things. The kingdom of the ten tribes became like all the nations, because they withdrew from the Lord; and, like a loaf baked under the ashes which is not turned over, that is, which does not repent, the Assyrians and the Chaldeans devoured its strength, and whatever strength it could have, they swallowed up. And such was its madness that it did not know it had been devoured; or at least it was unaware of the cause for which it had been handed over to those who devoured it. Finally, right up to old age, that is, right up to the last captivity, it persisted in the error it had begun.

But, to pass to another sense: though Ephraim ought to teach the peoples and draw them to his own likeness, he himself is mingled with the peoples and becomes like them; according to what was said above: As the people is, so will the priest be. Or Ephraim is mingled with the peoples and the nations, so that all heretics differ in nothing from the error of the Gentiles. And he who was once a leader in the Church has become a loaf baked under the ashes, surrounded on every side by unclean ash and the heat of the fires, so that he did not return to the Lord but persisted in the error he had begun.

Ephraim is a cake under the ashes not turned. For a cake under the ashes, that hath ashes upon it, lays the cleaner side flat to the ground, and has the upper side the fouler, in proportion as it carries the ashes upon it. And so with the mind that harbours earthly thoughts, what else does it carry upon itself but a load of ashes? But if it will be 'turned,' the clean surface, which it had kept downwards, it brings back to the top, when it has shaken off the ashes that it had upon it. If therefore we shake off from the mind the ashes of earthly thoughts, as it were we 'turn the cake under the ashes,' that that bent of our mind may henceforth go to the rear, which the ashes of grovelling thought before overlaid, and the clean face come to the top, that our right bent of mind may not henceforth be surcharged with the weight of earthly desire. Which we can never do, except we be bedewed with the grace of the Holy Spirit, in that when Almighty God 'sendeth out the waters, they will overturn the earth.'
Morals on the Book of Job, Book XI, Section 10

Demons devoured his strength, for these are the strangers and the enemies of all Christians, and he did not know it, thinking his adversaries friends, and judging those who devoured him to be his table-companions; yes, and grey hairs were spread over him, or rather they blossomed, that is, he went astray for a long time; and nonetheless he was unaware of his old age and his decrepitude, of which it is written: What grows old and ages is near to destruction. And if it is said of a just man and a churchman: A man's grey hairs are his wisdom, why should it not be said of an unjust man and a heretic: A man's grey hairs are his folly? Of this old age Daniel spoke to the elder: You who have grown old in evil days. Hence also in the book of the Shepherd — if, however, anyone cares to accept the reading of it — the Church appears to Hermas first with a grey head, then as a young girl and a bride adorned with her tresses.

Moses: Just as all young men are not alike in fervour of spirit nor equally instructed in learning and good morals, so too we cannot find that all old men are equally perfect and excellent. For the true riches of old men are not to be measured by grey hairs but by their diligence in youth and the rewards of their past labours. "For," says one, "the things that thou hast not gathered in thy youth, how shall thou find them in thy old age?" "For venerable old age is not that of long time, nor counted by the number of years: but the understanding of a man is grey hairs, and a spotless life is old age." And therefore we are not to follow in the steps or embrace the traditions and advice of every old man whose head is covered with grey hairs, and whose age is his sole claim to respect, but only of those whom we find to have distinguished themselves in youth in an approved and praiseworthy manner, and to have been trained up not on self-assurance but on the traditions of the Elders. For there are some, and unhappily they form the majority, who pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth, and in sloth, and so obtain authority not from the ripeness of their character but simply from the number of their years. Against whom that reproof of the Lord is specially aimed by the prophet: "Strangers have devoured his strength and he knew it not: yea, grey hairs also are spread about upon him, and he is ignorant of it." These men, I say, are not pointed out as examples to youth from the uprightness of their lives, nor from the strictness of their profession, which would be worthy of praise and imitation, but simply from the number of their years; and so the subtle enemy uses their grey hairs to deceive the younger men, by a wrongful appeal to their authority, and endeavours in his cunning craftiness to upset and deceive by their example those who might have been urged into the way of perfection by their advice or that of others; and drags them down by means of their teaching and practice either into a baneful indifference, or into deadly despair.
Second Conference of Abbot Moses, Chapter 13

Abraham: I will not give you my own opinion against this, but that of the blessed Antony, whereby he confounded the laziness of a certain brother (overcome by this luke-warmness which you describe) in such a way as also to cut the knot of your subject. For when one came as I said to the aforesaid old man, and said that the Anchorite system was not at all to be admired, declaring that it required greater virtue for a man to practise what belongs to perfection living among men rather than in the desert, the blessed Antony asked Where he lived himself, and when he said that he lived close to his relations, and boasted that by their provision he was set free from all care and anxiety of daily work, and gave himself up ceaselessly and solely to reading and prayer without any distraction of spirit, once more the blessed Antony said: "Tell me, my good friend, whether you grieve with their griefs and misfortunes, and in the same way rejoice in their good fortune?" He confessed that he shared in them both. To whom the old man: "You should know," said he, "that in the world to come also you will be judged in the lot of those with whom in this life you have been affected by sharing in their gain or loss, or joy or sorrow." And not satisfied with this statement the blessed Antony entered on a still wider field of discussion, saying: "This mode of life and this most lukewarm condition not only strike you with that damage of which I spoke (though you do not feel it now, when somehow you say in accordance with that saying in Proverbs:'They strike me but I am not grieved: and they mocked me but I knew it not;' or this that is said in the Prophet: 'And strangers have devoured his strength, but he himself knew it not' ), because day after day they ceaselessly drag down your mind to earthly things, and change it in accordance with the variations of chance; but also because they defraud you of the fruits of your hands and the due reward of your own exertions, as they do not suffer you to be supported by what these supply, or to procure your daily food for yourself with your own hands, according to the rule of the blessed Apostle, as he when giving his last charge to the heads of the Church of Ephesus, asserts that though he was occupied with the sacred duties of preaching the gospel yet he provided not only for himself, but also for those who were prevented by necessary duties with regard to his ministry, saying: 'Ye yourselves know that these hands have ministered to my necessities and to the necessities of those who were with me.' But to show that he did this as a pattern to be useful to us he says elsewhere: 'We were not idle among you; neither did we eat any man's bread for nothing, but in labour and in toil we worked night and day lest we should be chargeable to any of you. Not as if we had not power; but that we might give ourselves a pattern unto you, to imitate us."

Strangers have devoured his strength, and he hath known it not. For by 'strangers' are usually understood apostate angels, who devour our strength, when they consume the virtue of the mind by perverting it. Which Ephraim both endured, and knew it not, because through the temptation of malignant spirits he both lost the strength of his mind, and understood not that he had lost it. Want therefore goes before the face of Leviathan, because he spoils by his temptation the minds of the careless, before he who is tempted knows his snares.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book XXXIV, Section 6

Hence the pride of Israel will be humbled, not after a long time, but now and in the present; for this is what he means by before his face; and it was being humbled because it had lifted itself up and trusted not in God but in the size of its army, and because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble; for pride, that is, gaon, the Seventy, after their custom, translated ὕβριν, that is, outrage. And because he had said above: Ephraim has become a loaf baked under the ashes which is not turned over, and this seemed ambiguous and did not make clear enough what he meant, he now puts it more plainly: They have not returned to the Lord their God; and they have not sought him in all these things. For if they had returned to the Lord their God, they would surely have heard God speaking through Jeremiah: Return to me, and I will return to you. And though they had done so much, they did not seek him whom they had lost through their own fault.

And though the pride of the heretics is humbled, or the insolence which they daily offer to churchmen, they do not return to the Lord; but in all these things they by no means seek him, because they have been heated like an oven, and they have not sought him; they have devoured their judges, and the kings fell together; nor is there anyone who cries to the Lord. All these things they suffered so that they might seek the Lord, whom they refused to seek.

And what he says: I will strike them according to the report of their assembly, can also mean this: just as by a common counsel they all fashioned idols, so, when I am angered, they will all be laid waste together. The teachers of contrary dogmas, who have abandoned Christ, the Wisdom, and have gone out from the Church, we can rightly call a foolish and heartless dove, since, desiring earthly things, they have been handed over to the Assyrians. And when they have set out from the Church, the Lord spreads his net, woven from the testimonies of the Scriptures and the skilful discourse of wisdom, so as to bring down to low places those who lift themselves up against the knowledge of God and, like a bird, fly to the heights; and to correct them by threats and by the hearing of punishments, so that, corrected, they may not perish for ever.

And Ephraim has become like a dove led astray, without heart. They called upon Egypt, they went off to the Assyrians; and when they have set out, I will spread my net over them, I will bring them down like a bird of the sky, I will strike them according to the report of their assembly. LXX: And Ephraim was like a foolish dove without heart. He called upon Egypt, and they went off into the Assyrians as they will go. I will cast my net over them, I will bring them down like the birds of the sky; I will correct them in the hearing of their tribulation. The Lord commands in the Gospel that we be simple as doves and shrewd as serpents, so that, imitating the simplicity of doves and the shrewdness of the serpent, we may neither be able to harm others nor suffer snares from others; but by simplicity and prudence may show ourselves balanced men, because prudence without goodness is malice, and simplicity without reason is called folly. Ephraim therefore has become like a dove led astray, in Hebrew photha; by Aquila and Symmachus it is called θελγομένη or ἀπατωμένη, that is, enticed or deceived; and by the Seventy foolish or senseless; for ἄνους can express both. And he is fittingly called a dove led astray, or foolish, because there is also a dove that is wise, which says in the psalms: Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest? Whose wings are silvered, and the hinder parts of whose back are in the greenness of gold. But Ephraim, a foolish dove and without heart, is shown to be of so brutish a mind that, calling upon Egypt, he went on to the Assyrians. For he who begged the help of the Egyptians is led away captive by the Assyrians. Egypt is a staff of reed: whoever leans on it, it will at once crush him, and, broken and shattered, it pierces the hand of the one who rests upon it.

The question is asked why Ephraim is compared not to other birds but to the dove. The other birds hasten to protect their young even at the peril of their own life; and when they see a hawk, a snake, a raven or a crow approaching their nest, they fly about hither and thither, and hurl themselves at the attacker with their bites, and tear it with their claws, and testify to a parent's grief with plaintive cries; the dove alone does not grieve for its young when they are taken away, and does not look for them; and to it Ephraim is rightly compared, because he does not perceive that his people is being laid waste piece by piece, but is careless of his own safety.

Let us read Hosea the prophet, and we find his whole prophecy against Ephraim; and it is said there: "Ephraim," it says, "has become like a foolish dove." See what he says: "a foolish dove." It has abandoned the temple, and dwells in the woods. For the dove always dwells in houses. But Ephraim, my dove, has abandoned the temple, has abandoned the house, and dwells in the woods, dwells in the deserts.

And the prophet of God abuseth those who are foolish in respect of good things, and wise in respect of evil things. "Ephraim is like a silly dove, without understanding; he cometh to Egypt and he goeth to Assyria, and in the way of repentance towards Me he walketh not." Now the prophet maketh an accusation against such silliness, because it is not simplicity, but folly. And this also is the wickedness of those who are silly in respect of good things. Instead of one Redeemer, they have chosen unto themselves many helpers, and they have forsaken the path which leadeth to God, and have run after the Egyptians and Assyrians that they might come to their help. And although they have experienced many times that they were not able to redeem them from the evils in which they stood, they never became wise enough through the experience of facts to run to God's place of refuge. And the prophet likened them unto doves whose fruit others carried off, and the children of whose bowels were made servants unto others; and he considered them to be without understanding, because they possessed not the discretion through which they would have drawn nigh to God.
13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity

And so that God might show that by changing places we cannot escape his eyes, and that we are always ruled by the power of God: When, he says, they have set out into the Assyrians, even there I will spread my net, and if they have been lifted up like birds, I will bring them down from there. But I will bring them down, not to destruction, but to strike them as sons; and I will strike them not with the greatness of punishments, but with fear, so that, hearing of the punishments of old, they may be corrected by terrors alone.

And the prophet seeing that all the remedies of this life will have been applied in vain for their healing, and already as it were despairing of their life, declares: "The bellows have failed in the fire, the founder hath melted in vain: for their wicked deeds are not consumed. Call them reprobate silver, for the Lord hath rejected them." And the Lord thus laments that to no purpose has He applied this salutary cleansing by fire to those who are hardened in their sins, in the person of Jerusalem crusted all over with the rust of her sins, when He says: "set it empty upon burning coals, that it may be hot, and the brass thereof may be melted; and let the filth of it be melted in the midst thereof. Great pains have been taken, and the great rust thereof is not gone out, no not even by fire. Thy uncleanness is execrable: because I desired to cleanse thee, and thou art not cleansed from thy filthiness." Wherefore like a skilful physician, who has tried all saving cures, and sees there is no remedy left which can be applied to their disease, the Lord is in a manner overcome by their iniquities and is obliged to desist from that kindly chastisement of His, and so denounces them saying: "I will no longer be angry with thee, and thy jealousy has departed from thee." But of others, whose heart has not grown hard by continuance in sin, and who do not stand in need of that most severe and (if I may so call it) caustic remedy, but for whose salvation the instruction of the life-giving word is suffi- cient-of them it is said: "I will improve them by hearing of their suffering."

Woe to them, because they have withdrawn from me; they will be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me. I redeemed them, and they have spoken lies against me, and they have not cried to me in their heart, but they howled on their beds. LXX: Woe to them, because they have withdrawn from me; they are manifest, because they have acted impiously against me; but I redeemed them; yet they have spoken a lie against me, and their hearts have not cried to me, but they howled on their beds. While I was spreading my net to catch them, and to bring them down from their pride like a bird of the sky, and to strike them in the hearing of their distress, they withdrew and leapt away from me; for this is what ἀπεπήδησαν means, which the Seventy used in their translation. And therefore they will be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me. Where we said: they will be laid waste, in the Hebrew is written sod laem, that is, devastation to them. Symmachus translated it destruction; Theodotion, misery. Moreover, in the common edition we read it in two ways; for some manuscripts have δῆλοί εἰσιν, that is: they are manifest; others δείλαιοί εἰσιν, that is: they are fearful or wretched. They will be laid waste, therefore, and will be wretched, and always fearing and dreading, because they transgressed against God, worshiping the golden calves and abandoning him who redeemed them from Egyptian slavery and led them out with a lofty arm. But they spoke lies against the Lord, saying of the idols: These are your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt, and they did not cry to the Lord in their heart, but wallowed in the fornications of idolatry. Or, because lust and luxury follow the worship of demons, those who worshiped demons consequently wallowed like pigs in the mire of lusts. And he fittingly calls the songs of those who serve idols not hymns to God but howling. Concerning the heretics the interpretation is easy: they have everlasting woe, because they have withdrawn from God; and they are wretched, because they have abandoned their Creator, who redeemed them with his own blood; and they themselves speak lies against him, composing the impious dogmas of falsehood; and they do not cry out in their hearts, but always howl in their conventicles, which he fittingly calls beds, and the lairs of wild beasts. Such men cannot say: Every night I will wash my bed, with my tears I will water my couch; but they wallow in the filth of lusts, they give themselves to debauchery, and whatever they say, and think they are saying in praise of God, is the howling of wolves and the din of raving Bacchantes. Rarely does a heretic love chastity, and whoever pretend to love purity, like Mani and Marcion, and Arius and Tatian, and the restorers of the old heresy, promise honey with a poisoned mouth. For the rest, according to the Apostle, the things they do in secret it is shameful even to speak of.

"First I will educate them through the threat of sufferings. Then I will catch all of them like birds, placing around them a cloud of enemies like a net." And having said that, he does not forget his love for mankind but offers a dirge from fatherly love for them.

They ruminated on wheat and wine, they withdrew from me.

And I taught them and strengthened their arms; and they devised malice against me; they returned so as to be without a yoke; they have become like a deceitful bow; their princes will fall by the sword, from the fury of their tongue; this is their derision in the land of Egypt. LXX: On wheat and wine they were cutting themselves; they were taught in me, and I strengthened their arms, and they devised evils against me; they turned to nothing, they became like a bent bow; their princes will fall by the sword because of the unskilfulness of their tongue; such is their derision in the land of Egypt. Because of the abundance of all things, he says, they fell. Ezekiel too records that this happened in Sodom and Gomorrah, so that they ruminated on nothing but food and luxury; for which the Seventy translated: On grain and wine they were cutting themselves, after the example of the prophets of Baal, who, in the presence of Elijah, prayed for rain by gashing their limbs. And at the same time, to show that they were like beasts of burden, he did not say: they were eating, but: they were ruminating; and therefore they withdrew from the Lord, who says: I taught them, I gave them strength, and they raised their necks against me; not that they could do anything and harm their Creator, but, what alone they were able to do, they devised evils against me.

On wheat and wine, and the false mysteries of the body and blood of Christ, who says in the Gospel: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone. And in another place: I am the true vine. And: Unless you drink my blood. Over this wheat and wine, then, the heretics are cut asunder, and build diverse tabernacles for themselves; or they are cut off from the body of the Church, and pretend to meditate on the law of God and to ruminate on it. But in doing this they withdraw from the Lord, who taught them in the Church and gave them strength with which to fight against the adversaries.

But they devised malice against the Lord, building up most impious heresies, and returned to the state of the Gentiles, so as to be without the knowledge and the yoke of God; or they returned to nothing, not that they ceased to be, but because, in comparison with him who speaks to Moses: Go, say to the people of Israel: He who is has sent me, all who think against the Lord are said not to be. According to what we read in Esther, in the Seventy only. Do not hand over your scepter to those who are not: there is no doubt that it means idols. For if God is truth, whatever is contrary to truth is a lie, and is called nothing. This fits the heretics, who, instructed from the holy Scriptures, turn the words of the law and the prophets and the Gospel against the Lord; and they are like a deceitful or perverse bow. A deceitful and perverse bow is one that strikes the one who aims it, and wounds its own master. Or they have become like a bent bow, always ready for battle and contentions, to the subversion of their hearers. Hence their princes, that is, the heresiarchs, are struck by the Lord's sword because of the madness of their tongue, with which they blasphemed the Lord; doing in a Church falsely so called the same thing they did at the time when they dwelt in the Egypt of the world, that is, when they were Gentiles. For all the questions of the heretics and of the Gentiles are the same, because they follow not the authority of the Scriptures but the sense of human reason.

And as they were from the beginning, before I called them through Abraham and afterwards through Moses and Aaron, when they were without the yoke and the knowledge of the law and were mingled with all the nations, so even now they have returned to their former state, so as to be carried without yoke and bridle over precipices, and to be changed into a deceitful bow; so that the bow which God had bent against the adversaries they themselves turned against their own Lord, and shot against him the arrows of blasphemies. Hence their princes, who deceived the unhappy people, will fall by the sword because of the fury of their tongue, with which they dared to call the golden calves gods, so that they did in the land of promise what they had learned in Egypt, worshiping the Egyptian Apis and venerating all their monstrosities. For so also in the wilderness, when they had come out of Egypt, they derided the Lord, saying: These are your gods, Israel. And: Would that we were in the land of Egypt, where we sat by the pots of meat, and so on.
8: The devil, who longs to set his nest above the stars of heaven, we very often read called an eagle: If you are exalted like an eagle, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord. The eye too that mocks its father and despises the old age of its mother will be dug out by ravens, and the young of eagles will devour it; losing the clear light of its vision through the devil and the demons. Hence it is commanded in the law that we should not eat the eagle. This eagle, then, comes upon the conventicles of the heretics, which were once the house of the Lord; and it comes because they have transgressed his covenant and abandoned the law of God; and in vain they call upon him and say: You are my God, and we know you, we who are called Israel, seeing God, and are called by the Christian name. In vain, he says, they do these things, since they have set up kings for themselves, and acted against my will, and have as princes my adversaries, whom I do not know, because they do not deserve knowledge of me. Their silver too and their gold, and whatever they could possess by nature, words and thoughts, they turned into idols which they fashioned from their own heart; and they turned them, not in order to perish; but because they turned them, therefore they perished. For they did not do it with this purpose, that they might perish; but because they did it, therefore they perished.

Let there be a trumpet in your throat, like an eagle over the house of the Lord; because they have transgressed my covenant and violated my law. They called upon me: My God, we know you, Israel. Israel has cast away the good; the enemy will pursue him. They have reigned, and not from me: they have been princes, and I did not know it. Of their silver and gold they have made idols for themselves, that they might perish. LXX: In their bosom like earth, like an eagle over the house of the Lord, because they have transgressed my testament and acted impiously against my law. They called upon me: God, we know you; because Israel has turned away from good things. They pursued the enemy, they reigned for themselves and not through me; they have been princes, and they did not make it known to me; of their silver and their gold they have made idols for themselves, that they might utterly perish. What we have translated: let there be a trumpet in your throat, for which in the Hebrew is written alechcha sophar, Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated likewise. The Seventy alone said: in their bosom like earth, and what this means is uncertain. For some think that bosom is taken in two ways: both as the lower part of a garment, from the genitals to the feet; and as the colpus of the sea, that is, a gulf, for example of the Adriatic and the Ionian and the Propontis; and that the false teachers, who followed the blasphemy of Egypt, keep in their bosom all things that serve lust, and earthly things; or at least that in the harbor and refuge of their voyage they acquire no precious merchandise, but earthly things. But let us, following the Hebrew truth, weave on the sequence of the explanation we began. The prophet is commanded, and it is said to him: Let there be a trumpet in your throat, that is, raise your voice so that it is like a trumpet, that very many may hear, because very many have sinned. And when you have raised your voice, say this with a shout: like an eagle over the house of the Lord; and the sense is: Nebuchadnezzar will come with all his army so swiftly, so quickly, that he will imitate the flight of an eagle hastening to its prey; and he will come not to some other place but to Jerusalem, in which the temple of God stands, to destroy and overturn it. Of this eagle Ezekiel too speaks more fully: of great wings and feathers and talons, which has the course for entering into Lebanon, that is, into the temple of God, according to the prophet Zechariah, in whom it is written: Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. But this, O prophet, which I say and command you: Let there be a trumpet in your throat, so that you may cry aloud and say, like an eagle over the house of the Lord, that the king of the Chaldeans is coming, I command for no other reason than that they have transgressed my covenant and abandoned my ceremonies.

Hence in the time of necessity and distress, when the captivity comes, they will call upon me and say: My God, we know you, Israel; we who are called Israel know you and acknowledge you, and we keep the ancient name of Jacob, who pleased you, so that we are called Israel.

To them the Lord replied: How are you called Israel, when Israel has cast away the good, that is, his Lord, from whom he was called Israel? Therefore, because Israel cast away the good, the enemy, that is, the Assyrian, will pursue him and seize him, who, having abandoned me as king, asked for a king for themselves, as the other nations also had, and acted against my will. Finally, Samuel for this reason sets before them the harsh commands of a king, and says that their sons and daughters will serve kings, so that they might return to the Lord, the most merciful king; but they became princes without the will of God. And this crime was not enough for them, unless they doubled the outrage with a greater impiety, turning into idols the silver and gold which they had received for riches and adornment. Therefore Saul became king not by the will of God, but by the error of the people. And because he did not have the root of piety, as soon as he began to reign he was inflamed with impiety. What he says: They have reigned, and not from me; they have been princes, and I did not know it, can also be taken of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and of the other princes who succeeded him in power. Nor, because God, angry with Solomon, willed his kingdom to be divided, did Israel therefore do well in accepting a king. For according to the precepts of the law it ought to have asked the Lord whether he wished this to be done. For of the Savior too it is said that the Son of man must indeed be betrayed, but woe to him through whom he is to be betrayed.

Not always is the prince of the people and judge of the Church given by the judgment of God, but according as our merits demand. If our deeds are evil and we "work evil in the sight of God", princes are given to us according to our heart; and this I will prove to you from the Scriptures. For hear what the Lord says: "They made themselves a king and not by me, and a prince and not by my counsel". And this seems to be said of that Saul, whom indeed the Lord himself had chosen and had commanded to be made king; but because he had been chosen not according to the will of God, but according to the merit of a sinful people, he denies that he was appointed with his will or counsel.

When Peter is speaking to the people concerning the bishop to be ordained in the place of Judas, it says, "Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples, for the multitude was together." But we notice that the apostles observed this, not only in the ordination of bishops and of priests but also in the ordinations of deacons. Concerning this very thing, in their Acts, it is also written, "The Twelve called together the multitude of the disciples," it says, "and spoke to them."6This matter was carried on diligently and cautiously, with the whole people assembled so that no unworthy man should attain to the ministry of the altar or to the priestly rank. For the fact is that sometimes unworthy men are ordained, not according to the will of God but according to human presumption. These things that do not come from a legitimate and just ordination are displeasing to God. God himself makes this known through the prophet Hosea, saying, "They made themselves a king, but not by me."

Because He is exceedingly desirous, that we should always take refuge in Him, and in everything make our requests unto Him; and do nothing and speak nothing without Him. For men, when we trouble them repeatedly concerning our affairs, become slothful and evasive, and conduct themselves unpleasantly towards us; but with God it is quite the reverse. Not when we apply to him continually respecting our affairs, but when we fail to do so, then is he especially displeased. Hear at least what He reproves the Jews for, when He says, "Ye have taken counsel, but not of Me, and made treaties, but not by My Spirit." For this is the custom of those who love; they desire that all the concerns of their beloved should be accomplished by means of themselves; and that they should neither do anything, nor say anything, without them. On this account did God not only on that occasion, but again elsewhere, uttering a reproof, speak the same language. "They have reigned, but not by Me; they have ruled, and they made it not known to Me."

But it can be reasonably asked, How it is said in this place that the Lord makes the hypocrite to reign, when by the Prophet He complains especially of this thing, saying, They have reigned, but not of Me: they have become princes, and I know them not? For, who that thinks rightly, can say that the Lord does that of which He knows nothing? But, because God's knowledge is approval, His ignorance is disapproval. Whence He says to some whom He rejects, I know you not whence ye are; depart from Me, all ye workers of iniquity. And sometimes God's doing a thing, is His allowing in His anger that which He forbids to be done. Hence He asserted that He hardened the heart of the king of Egypt, because He, in truth, allowed it to be hardened. In a marvellous manner then does God make hypocrites to reign, and knows them not. He makes them, by suffering; He knows them not, by rejecting them. Whence it is necessary, with reference to every thing, which is desired in this life, that the Inner Will should be first enquired into. And when the ear of the heart is anxious to catch Its sound, let it know that It speaks, not in words, but in deeds. When then a post of authority is offered, it is necessary for a man first to question with himself, whether his conduct is suited to the place, whether his doings are at variance with the distinction it confers; lest, perchance, the just Ruler of all should, afterwards, not regard his prayers in tribulation, because He knows not his very entering on that high office, which is the source of all his tribulation.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book XXV, Section 41

God casts off the calves of the heretics and of Samaria, who say that they keep the precepts of the law; which calves cling to the ground and work in the earth, not in the spirit, nor lift their eyes to heaven; and therefore the fury of the Lord is kindled against them, and he wonders what this great perversity is, that they will not abandon the idols which they have fashioned for themselves, and love heretical filth instead of the cleanness of the Church. These calves Israel, who pretends that he sees God, did not receive from the other nations; but he himself forged for himself out of the holy Scriptures the depravity of his understanding, and he is the craftsman of his own god, which will quickly perish and will imitate spiders' webs, which are broken at a light touch.

What he had said above: Of their silver and their gold they have made idols for themselves, that they might perish, he now explains more plainly: Your calf is cast off, Samaria, my fury is kindled against them; either against the calves, because they had made two; or against the inhabitants of Samaria, who worshiped them. Moreover, as for what we read in the Seventy: Cast off your calf, Samaria, he exhorts its inhabitants, not of one city but of all the ten tribes, which are called Samaria — for otherwise there were no calves in the city of Samaria, but in Dan and in Bethel — to cast off the calves against which God is angry; or ἀποτρίψεται, that is, let it rub them away; so that it may little by little rub away and cleanse those which it had worshiped for a long time. And when they do not listen, he turns to others, and speaks as though to a third person: how long will they be unable to be cleansed? What madness is this, he says, that, while I give room for repentance, they refuse to turn to health?

Your calf is cast off, Samaria. My fury is kindled against them. How long will they be unable to be cleansed? For it too is from Israel; a craftsman made it, and it is not God, for the calf of Samaria will become spiders' webs. LXX: Cast off your calf, Samaria; my fury is roused against them. How long will they be unable to be cleansed in Israel? And this a craftsman made, and it is not God, because your calf, Samaria, was leading astray. In the place where we have put spiders' webs, in the Hebrew is written sababim, with the letter iod as the penultimate; not, as some falsely think, sababum, that is, with uau, which the Seventy and Theodotion translated πλανῶν, that is, leading astray and deceiving; Aquila, wandering or turned about; Symmachus, inconstant or unstable, that is, ἀκαταστατῶν; the Fifth edition, ῥεμβεύων, roving and fluctuating. We have learned from a Hebrew that sababim properly denotes the threads of spiders flying through the air, which perish even while they are seen, and are dissolved into atoms and into nothing. And to these the calf of Samaria is rightly compared, which at that time the people worshiped because of the greatness of its value, since it was of gold.

And because he had said: Cast off your calf, Samaria, he explains who this calf is: for it too is from Israel; not from others, he says, from the nations, have you received the calf, as Baal and Ashtaroth from the Sidonians, as Chemosh from the Moabites and Moloch from the Ammonites; but you yourselves, and your king Jeroboam, made in Israel what you had learned in Egypt. Or what sort of god is that which is formed by the hand of a craftsman? Finally, as the threads of spiders dissolve into the wind, so the calf of Samaria will be reduced to nothing.

For they will sow the wind and reap the whirlwind; there is no standing stalk in it, the shoot will make no flour, and if it should make any, strangers will eat it. LXX: For they have sown things corrupted by the wind, and their overthrow will receive them; a sheaf without the strength to make flour, and if it should make any, strangers will eat it. He compares the calf of Samaria to spiders' webs; therefore he keeps the metaphor in what follows, so that what he had called spiders' webs he compares to wind and whirlwind, and to stalks that do not stand; and if they do stand, they have no flour; and if, he says, they should make flour, it will be devoured by others. And since the sense is common both to the heretics and to those in Samaria who fashioned idols, it must be discussed in common. These men sow the wind, or seeds corrupted by the wind, which have no pith, which the Greeks call ἐντεριώνην, and therefore, sowing empty things, they receive what is void and empty; nay rather, sowing in the flesh, they reap corruption from the flesh, and are carried about by every wind of doctrine. And when they have sown the wind, they reap whirlwinds and storms; and first of all, no stalk, that is, no straw, will come from these seeds, nor will they be able to have any appearance of a fruitful crop. But if it should rarely happen that they seem to have something like the Church's dogma, that very shoot and ear will make no flour. Into three measures of this flour the woman of the Gospel puts leaven, so that the spirit by which we perceive, and the soul by which we live, and the body by which we walk, may be brought together into one Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle: In him we live, move and are. But if it should rarely happen to the heretics that their sowing too makes flour, from this flour will be made a loaf baked under the ashes, which is not turned over, and which strangers will eat. Hence he now also says: And if it should make flour, strangers will eat it. But we ought to understand as strangers those of whom it is written: Strange sons have lied to me. And in the eighteenth (19th) psalm: From my hidden sins cleanse me, O Lord, and from strangers spare your servant. If they have not had dominion over the righteous man, then he will be unblemished and will be cleansed from the greatest sin.

For you pluck no fruit from the idol's service, but their bundles are like ears of wheat destroyed by the wind, which show full stalks from the outside but which internally have no grain. Such is the nature of idolatry, for on the one hand it can take the image of a man or a woman, or a lion or a different animal from art, but on the other hand it is deprived of any strength or energy.

For it is infinite folly to labour painfully, and pant after the breath of applause, to apply one's self to the heavenly precepts with hard toil, but to aim at the reward of an earthly kind of recompense. For that I may so express myself, he that in return for the good that he practises looks for the applause of his fellowcreatures, is carrying an article of great worth to be sold at a mean price. From that whereby he might have earned the kingdom of heaven, he seeks the coin of passing talk. His practice goes for little, in that he spends a great deal, and gets back but very little. Whereunto then are hypocrites like but to luxuriant and untended vines, which put forth fruit from their fertility, but are never lifted from the earth by tending? All that the rich branches bud forth, stray beasts tread under foot, and the more fruitful they see it is, the more greedily they devour it, thus cast away and laid low, in that the works of hypocrites while they shew fair, come forth as if rich, but whilst they aim at human praises, it is as if they were left forsaken upon the ground. And the beasts of this world, i.e. the evil spirits, devour them, because they turn them to account to the end of perdition, and they seize upon them with greater avidity, in proportion as great things are more clearly known. Hence it is well said by the Prophet, The standing stalk, there is no bud in them, and they shall yield no meal; if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up. For the stalk is without a bud, when the life lacks the merit of virtuous habits. The stalk yieldeth no meal, when he that thrives in this world understands nothing refined, and yields no fruit of good practice.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book VIII, Sections 70-71

Israel has been devoured; now he has become among the nations like an unclean vessel. The Seventy translated "useless" for "unclean"; the rest likewise. The unclean, or useless, vessel the Hebrews call a chamber pot, which we are accustomed to use for receiving and throwing away excrement. To this uncleanness he compares the idolaters and the heretics, who are mingled with the Gentiles while they do not keep the truth of God, and, having been made a vessel unto honor, have been turned into a vessel of dishonor. For what is more unclean than a demonic spirit and the dogmas of the heretics, which have mingled them with the pagans? Such was Jeconiah, enslaved to idols, of whom God speaks through Jeremiah: Jeconiah is dishonored, like a vessel of which there is no use. On the contrary Paul, who could say: Or do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me? is called a chosen vessel, of gold and of silver, because he had wisdom and eloquence, with which he preached the Gospel of Christ. And when he says: has been devoured, or swallowed up, it signifies that, mingled with idols and with the nations, he has lost the proper name of Israel and of Christian.

As for the heretics, we do not doubt that, going to the Assyrians according to the error of their mind, they think that they are ascending, not descending. Hence it is said to them through Isaiah: What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up onto empty roofs? The prince of these Assyrians is the great mind. Hence Ephraim has sprouted within himself, judging in his presumption that he has grown. Or he has become a solitary wild ass, so as to enter not the planted fields of the Church but the deserts of the devil. He has loved gifts in return for his error, promising himself rewards, or doing everything for the sake of shameful gain. Or at least he has given gifts and payments to his lovers, the demons, and when he has done this, he will be handed over to the Gentiles. For just as the nations worship bodily images, so these men think to be gods the idols which they have fashioned out of their own heart, and therefore they will be reckoned among the number of the nations.

For they themselves have gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself. Ephraim have given gifts to lovers; moreover they have hired the nations for pay; now I will gather them, and they will rest a little while from the burden of the king and of the princes. LXX: For they themselves have gone up to the Assyrians; Ephraim has sprouted within himself, they have loved gifts; therefore they will be handed over among the Gentiles; now I will receive them, and they will rest a little, that they may anoint kings and princes. Israel, he says, has been devoured, and has become like a useless, or unclean, vessel, of which no potsherd remains in which water could be drawn, or some small bit of fire. And because he has become an unclean vessel, therefore they have gone up to the Assyrians, imitating the solitary wild ass; not at all as sheep fed by the Lord, but wickedly abusing their freedom, and led away into captivity; and the prophet bewails them and says: Ephraim have given gifts to the Assyrians and have hired their lovers for pay; of whom Ezekiel writes: To all harlots payments are given, but you have given payments to your lovers, and the contrary has happened in you.

And when they have given presents to the Gentiles, and have hired the nations for pay to help them, they will be gathered for battle, and, bound, will be led away together. And because they love to offer gifts to their adversaries, therefore for a little while they will obtain the favor of not paying tribute to the king and the princes, until they come to the Assyrians, where they will by no means pay taxes and tribute as free men, but will be reduced to the utmost slavery.

But if, he says, now and in the present age they repent, and I receive them, they will cease to set up over themselves the little king and his princes; so that we may understand the little king to be the devil, in distinction from the great king, who can have no fellowship with Belial, but, as soon as he has been received, drives the little king and his princes out of the heart of believers. According to the Hebrew, however, those who had before been scattered, and had hired the nations for pay, will be gathered into the Church of God, and will rest from the burden of the king, about whom the Apostle rebukes those cut off from the Church, saying: Without us you reign; and would that you did reign, and from the princes whom they have, set up in the synagogues of the devil.

Now the Apostle teaches that there is one altar in the Church, and one faith, and one baptism; deserting this, the heretics have fashioned for themselves many altars, not for appeasing God, but for a multitude of offenses. Therefore they do not deserve to receive the law of God, since they had earlier despised those laws which they had received. And if they have said anything from the Scriptures, it is to be compared not with the divine words, but with the thoughts of the pagans. These men sacrifice many victims and eat their flesh, deserting the one victim of Christ; nor do they eat the flesh of him whose flesh is the food of believers. Whatever they do, feigning the order and rite of sacrifices, whether they give alms, or promise chastity, or feign humility and deceive all the simple with pretended blandishments, the Lord will accept nothing of sacrifices of this kind.

For Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning; altars have become for him an offense. I will write for him my manifold laws, which have been reckoned as foreign; bring victims, bring; they will sacrifice flesh and eat it, and the Lord will not accept them. LXX: For Ephraim has multiplied altars, for sin, altars are beloved to him. I will write for them a multitude; his ordinances have been reckoned as foreign, beloved altars; for if they have sacrificed victims and eaten flesh, the Lord will not accept them. Led, he says, into captivity, they will rest for a little while from the burden of the king and the prince. And they will suffer this because Ephraim, their prince, has multiplied altars, not on which to sacrifice to the Lord, but on which to join sins to sins; and these altars, that is, places of sacrifice, will be turned for him into an offense, so that the more of them there are, the more his crimes are multiplied.

Then, as he had said above: What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? as though hesitating and seeking with what remedy he might heal the sick man, and by what counsels he might draw the sinner back to salvation. I will write for them again, he says, the laws which I had given before through Moses. But what profit is there in writing still others, when he has despised those which he received before? Is it not contempt of God when, though I commanded that there should be one altar in Jerusalem, they fashioned idols on all the mountains and hills with which to provoke the Lord?

They also made altars for this reason, not to please me, but so that, when many victims had been sacrificed, they might eat their flesh, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: Amen, amen, I say to you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. For they put all their zeal for victims into devouring the sacrifices, not into pleasing God through them; nor will the Lord accept those which they sacrificed not to him, but to their own belly and gullet.

Now he will remember their iniquity and will visit their sins; they will be turned back into Egypt.

And Israel has forgotten his Maker and has built shrines, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities; and I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour his dwellings. LXX: Now he will remember their iniquities, and will avenge their injustices; they have turned back into Egypt, and Israel has forgotten him who made him, and they have built shrines, and Judah has multiplied walled cities; and I will send forth fire upon his cities, and it will devour his foundations. Between ἀνομίαν, that is, iniquity, and sin there is this difference, that iniquities are before the law, sin is after the law; and for those who persist in their offenses, the Lord will remember their iniquity, which they had committed before the law; but their sins he will not remember, but will take vengeance on them. And he will both remember their old iniquities and visit their former sins for this reason, that they have gone back into Egypt, either asking for help or worshiping the same gods by which they had earlier been led astray, ἄπιν (Apis) and μνεῦιν (Mnevis).

But according to anagogy, those are called iniquities, that is, both ἀνομίαι and ἀδικίαι (injustices), which we committed before baptism and which have been forgiven us in baptism; but sins are those which we have done after baptism, of which it is also written in the psalm: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. All of these will be imputed to the heretics, so that both the old iniquities and the new sins are brought back upon them. For those who had gone out of Egypt through the confession of Christ have gone back into Egypt through faithlessness.

What we read according to the LXX translators, ÷ and in Assyria they ate unclean things :, is not found in the Hebrew, and therefore it must be marked beforehand with an obelus. We can, however, say that the Israelites, longing for Egypt, were taken captive by the Assyrians and there ate unclean things, according to Ezekiel, who describes them as having eaten food offered to idols in Chaldea, food so polluted with the filth of idols that it is compared to human dung. The heretics too, whose princes are the Assyrians — of whom we have often spoken — eat unclean things among them, while they are defiled by their filth.

For Israel has forgotten his Maker and has built shrines on the high places, consecrating whole hills and mountains, and shady trees, to Baal and Ashtaroth and other idols. Judah too, understanding that Israel had departed from the love of God and that their sins had been visited, was not converted to the Lord, but trusted in the fortification of his cities, which the Lord says he will destroy, devouring them down to his foundations. His: there is no doubt that it signifies Judah; although some read their foundations, that is, of the cities, in place of his.

Israel has forgotten his Maker, and, having despised the Creator, has fashioned another god for himself. Judah too, that is, the churchman, in evil works, or in a perverse interpretation of the holy Scriptures, has built himself fortified cities, not with the help of God, but with skillful falsehood; and the Lord says that he will set them on fire with the fire of his spirit, and will devour his βάρεις, that is, great houses built in the manner of towers, and will overturn the foundations badly laid, so that they may not be able to set up sacrilegious shrines against God. Some take the cities fortified by Judah in a good sense, and they try to temper what seemed contrary to this sense, I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour his dwellings, in such a way that, after what is perfect has come, what is in part is destroyed.
9: It is said also to the heretics, that they should not exult and rejoice and think themselves like the other nations. For those did not believe in God; but these, under the name of God, worship idols and play the harlot away from their God; and they multiply for themselves many threshing floors and countless winepresses, and they eat the wheat from which the bread of mourning is made, and drink the wine of Sodom, which is trodden out with the gall of asps. And because they prepare for themselves many winepresses and many threshing floors, therefore they will not eat from the true and only threshing floor, nor drink from the winepress which the Lord Jesus trod; but whatever they think they have will be corrupted by falsehood.

Do not rejoice, Israel, do not exult like the peoples, for you have played the harlot away from your God; you have loved a payment upon all the threshing floors of wheat. The threshing floor and the winepress will not feed them, and the wine will deceive them. LXX: Do not be glad, Israel, and do not rejoice like the peoples, for you have played the harlot away from your God; you have loved gifts upon every threshing floor of wheat. The threshing floor and the winepress did not know them, and the wine has deceived them. Those who have departed from God, when they have come into the depth of sins and have despaired of their salvation, will despise everything. Finally Israel too, departing from the law of God and worshiping idols, says that he is one nation out of many nations, rejoicing and congratulating himself that he has departed from the knowledge of God and is a nation mingled with the rest; and therefore he now rebukes them and says: Do not be glad, do not rejoice, and do not think that you are such as the other nations are. For one who does not know God is punished in one way, one who departs from God in another, because the servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes.

It is not fitting for you to rejoice and exult like the rest of the peoples. For they did not receive any teaching which might lead them to piety, but you, after much instruction and knowledge of God, rebelled against the knowledge which had been given to you because of the depravity of your opinion, and turned to the worship of the idols.

You have reckoned many threshing floors and winepresses as the payment for your fornication, so that you might enjoy an abundance of all things; therefore the threshing floor and the winepress will not produce wheat and wine, and the winepress will deceive them, or will deny its wine, with which they thought they would be made drunk. We read that under Ahab king of Israel, and Elijah the prophet, there was a most severe famine in Samaria, so that mothers fed on the corpses of their own sons. At that time, according to the letter, the threshing floor and the winepress did not feed them, and the wine deceived them, and they wasted away in want.

They will not dwell in the land of the Lord who have departed from the Church, and have returned in mind into Egypt, and eat the sacrifices of the Assyrians, that is, of demons; nor do they pour out to the Lord the wine with which they have been made drunk unto luxury, and neither the things they offer nor they themselves who offer please him. The sacrifices of the heretics are the bread of mourning and of tears; for all that they do will be turned into weeping. Nor will they be able to hear: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted; but on the contrary they will hear: Woe to those who laugh, for they shall mourn. Whatever they offer, they offer not to God but to the dead, namely to those who have contrived wicked heresies; and whoever eats of their victims will be defiled. The blind will be led into the pit by the blind. Whatever they do, they do for the sake of delights, to deceive the people, to devour the houses of widows. We can call the bread of mourning the deadly words with which they speak iniquity against the Lord; and this bread does not enter into the house of God; for the conventicles of the heretics are called not the house of God, but dens of robbers.

They will not dwell in the land of the Lord; Ephraim has returned into Egypt, and among the Assyrians he has eaten what is polluted. They will not pour out wine to the Lord, and their sacrifices will not please him; like the bread of mourners, all who eat it will be defiled, because their bread, their own soul, will not enter into the house of the Lord. LXX: They did not dwell in the land of the Lord; Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and among the Assyrians he ate what is unclean; they did not pour out wine to the Lord, nor did their sacrifices please him, because it is to them the bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled; because the loaves of their souls will not enter into the house of the Lord. Not only did the threshing floor and the winepress fail to feed them, and the wine lie in the land of Israel, when for three years and six months everything perished, but the inhabitants themselves also will depart from the land of the Lord; and they will be led into a foreign land, so that they may not dwell in the holy land which they have polluted with their fornications. Ephraim has returned, he says, into Egypt, and among the Assyrians he has eaten what is polluted. From this place some have added above: and among the Assyrians he has eaten what is polluted, which is not found in the Hebrew, and about which we have already spoken.

Let not the people flatter themselves as if they could be safe from contagion of sin, communicating with a sinful priest and yielding their obedience to the unjust and unlawful episcopacy of their leader, when the divine censure threatens through the prophet Hosea and says, "Their sacrifices shall be like the bread of mourning: all who eat them shall be defiled." [This] teaching obviously [shows] that all are indeed involved in sin who have been contaminated by the sacrifice of a blasphemous and unjust priest.

But when they are in Chaldea without a temple and without an altar, they will not pour out wine to the Lord, but to demons; and they will not please him, those who pour out to foreign gods, and who are held in captivity and among the Assyrians eat things sacrificed to idols, and are like the bread of mourners. For it is not lawful to eat of the sacrifices of mourners, and if anyone eats, what was offered becomes unclean. The Greeks call the suppers of mourners περίδειπνα; we can call them parentalia, from the fact that they are offered for dead parents. And not only he who has offered, but also he who has eaten of food of this kind will be unclean; for their bread, that is, the food which they offer, will not enter into the house of the Lord, which has been destroyed, which has been burned with Babylonian fire; but it will be for their own soul. And the sense is: they provide for their own gullet and their own pleasure; but polluted things do not please me.

Having collected the fruit of the vine into the wine-vats, they offered the firstlings as a libation to the demons, and not to the God who gave them. They also offered loaves of bread as firstfruits of the harvest—except that the sacrifice will become for them defiled and impure, he says, and the offerings will be considered as mourning breads (that is, disgusting, impure and odious). For what reason? For the law considered unclean anyone who approached a dead body either by blood relationship or rather by the very touching of the body. Therefore it was easy for the relatives or friends of the dead person to become unclean during mourning, since they handled the dead body and since they were willing to do for him what was customary. And whatever they touched became unclean. Therefore the mourning bread is that bread which was at hand as food for those who were mourning for the dead; for those who strive to avoid contamination with a dead body it is considered terrible even to taste this bread. Wherefore the breads themselves are defiled and rejected, even though they may have been offered as firstfruits of the harvest. "Those who eat them will become unclean." They will be useful only to their souls, that is, as a food for them.

It is said also to the heretics: When the solemn day comes, what are you going to do? For solemn day Aquila has translated time. From which it is manifest that it does not mean a festal day, but the time of retribution; for at once there follows: The days of vengeance have come, the days of your retribution have come. Behold, you have been laid waste by many enemies: the Assyrians and the Chaldeans have slaughtered you, you have fled to the world, and have been made like the other nations; there Memphis will bury you, which is interpreted from the mouth; and the sense is: you will receive according to your blasphemies, and what you have spoken you will feel in your punishments; the desirable things, that is, the dogmas which you had composed for yourselves with crafty eloquence, which is what silver signifies, the nettle will possess, which will consume you with eternal burning; and the bur or thorn will be in your tents; for thorns spring up in the hands of those who have been made drunk with the Babylonian cup. And in the Gospel we read that shameful thoughts and the cares of this world, and the vices that cling to us, are called thorns, which choke the grain as it rises among the grasses.

What will you do on the solemn day, on the day of the festival of the Lord? For behold, they have set out from the devastation; Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them; the nettle will inherit the desirable things of their silver, the bur will be in their tents. LXX: What will you do on the day of assembly and on the day of the solemnity of the Lord? Therefore behold, they will go from the misery of Egypt, and Memphis will receive them, and Michmash will bury them; destruction will possess their silver, thorns will be in their tents. When the day of captivity comes, he says, and the most savage enemy falls upon you, what is my solemnity? What victim do I hold as propitious? That he avenges me on my enemies, and puts a limit to wrong, and scourges the impious sons. What then will you do on the day of the festival of the Lord? Answer. And while they are silent, he answers himself, or rather he beholds with divine eyes what they are going to do.

Behold, he says, when misery and devastation pressed upon them, and the Assyrian and the Chaldean were eager to bind them as captives, they fled to Egypt. There Memphis will bury them, which at that time was the metropolis of Egypt, before Alexandria, which was formerly called No, received both the greatness of a city and its name from Alexander of Macedon. But what is said in the Seventy: Michmash will bury them, is not found in the Hebrew; but rather mamad, which is called desirable. From which it is clear that they were deceived by the similarity of the letters daleth and chaph, and in place of mamad, which all have translated desirable, they thought it was Michmash, a city of Egypt. We can also take what is said: For behold, they have set out from the devastation; Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them, of the tribe of Judah; when, after Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had set over the land, was killed by Ishmael, the remnant of the people fled over to Egypt with Jeremiah the prophet, and there, when the Chaldeans afterwards pursued them, they were either taken captive or buried. And by the desirable things of their silver, which the nettle possesses, we shall understand country houses and all the adornments of country houses, which are bought at the price of silver. And what follows, the bur will be in their tents, signifies a long devastation, so that where once there were houses, there burs and nettles and thorns spring up.

The days of visitation have come, the days of retribution have come; know, Israel, that you are a foolish prophet, an insane spiritual man; because of the multitude of your iniquity, and the multitude of madness. LXX: The days of vengeance have come, the days of your retribution have come, and Israel will be afflicted like a raving prophet, a man who had the spirit; because of the multitude of your iniquities, your madness has been multiplied. In this place too there is the usual error: for where we have translated: know, Israel, that is, Israelites, and in the Hebrew is read iadau, the Seventy translated: and will be afflicted, taking the letter iod for vau, and reading res for daleth; of which the one means knowledge, the other affliction or malice. Therefore the days of visitation have come, of which he had said above: What will you do on the solemn day, on the day of the festival of the Lord? The days of retribution have come. O Israel, now recognize your own words, you who used to call the prophet who told you true things, and prophesied by the Holy Spirit, a fool and insane, according to what the princes said to Jehu in Ramoth-gilead: Why did this madman come to you? Therefore, because of the multitude of your iniquities, in which you have long run riot in wickedness, recognize that it is not my prophet, but you, who are a madman, you who labored to this end, that you might trample on my words. For madness Aquila rendered ἐγκότησιν, which in Latin we can call either wrath or the memory of a grievance. The day of vengeance and retribution some interpret as the day of judgment, when Israel will be afflicted, who now boasts that he sees God, and is not ruled by the Holy Spirit, but is carried about in various directions by a demonic one, not knowing what he says, and calling the Son of God a creature, denying that the Holy Spirit is God; and again asserting that the good God is one, the creator of the world another; and their madness is manifold, because their iniquities too were very many. Whom we have called a foolish prophet, the Seventy have translated a false prophet. And lest, by often repeating the same things, we seem to distrust the reader's prudence, we briefly advise that whatever is said in this prophet about Israel and about Ephraim is to be referred to the heretics, who, truly raving, speak lies against God.
