But if he wished to mock the Hebrews, he was either foolish or unskilled: foolish, if he invented an open lie; unskilled, if he did not understand of whom these things were said. The volume itself clears him of folly, since it is composed prudently and in order; unskilled we cannot call him, whom we know from other testimonies of the Scriptures to have had knowledge of the law. It remains for us to say that the things which go before τυπικῶς (typologically) in others are referred to Christ according to truth and fulfillment; which we know the Apostle did with the two mountains, Sinai and Zion, and with Sarah and Hagar. For it is not that Sinai is not a mountain and Zion is not; that Sarah did not exist and Hagar did not exist, because the apostle Paul referred these to the two covenants. So, therefore, this which is written: Israel was a little child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son, is indeed said of the people of Israel, which is called out of Egypt, which is loved, which at that time, after the error of idolatry, was called as an infant and a little child; but it is perfectly referred to Christ. For Isaac too was a type of Christ, in that he himself carried the wood of his coming death; and Jacob, in that he had as wives Leah, sore of eye, and Rachel, the beautiful. In Leah, who was the elder, we understand the blindness of the Synagogue, in Rachel the beauty of the Church; and yet those who were in part types of the Lord Savior are not to be believed to have done in his type all the things they are related to have done. For a type indicates a part; if it went before as a whole in the type, it would no longer be a type, but ought to be called the truth of history. These things we have said briefly, as is fitting in commentaries; now let us return to the rest.

It is as a result of folly and a childish attitude that they suffer this punishment. I recalled them from Egypt and freed them from that harsh servitude, but they proved ungrateful to me and opted for the worship of the idols (referring to them as "Baals"). Though I was the one who taught them to walk, who cured them of their awkward gait, showed them paternal affection and applied all kinds of healing to them, they refused to acknowledge me, even though I protected them from manifold destruction at the hands of the invaders as if clutching them to me in love like a kind of bond. It is in love that even now I care for them and invest them in these chastisements, acting in the manner of someone striking a forward child on the cheek.

And because Israel is indeed spoken of in the singular but understood in the plural, as are people, Ephraim and Judah, since in the singular number there is a great number contained in this number, he recalls the old history: that he called them through Moses and Aaron, who called them to go out of Egypt; but they, called by them, withdrew from their face, turning their backs on him and showing the hardness of their mind by the gesture of their body. Nor was it enough for them to despise those who called them, unless they also sacrificed to Baal and burned incense to carved images, or idols. We read that they first worshipped Baal under Ahab king of Israel, who took as his wife Jezebel, daughter of the king of Sidon, and brought the Babylonian and Phoenician idol over into Samaria. Therefore he joins in one discourse sins distant in time: how first they were called out of Egypt and named sons, then in the wilderness withdrew from God, worshipping Baal-peor rather than God, and afterwards in the holy land served the Baalim and Ashtaroth and the other idols.

Otherwise: I loved them so much, and was so merciful a shepherd, that I myself carried the sick sheep on my shoulders; but they did not know that I was healing them by my passion, and that I, who am the lover of all men, was drawing them to believe with the bonds of love, according to what is written in the Gospel: No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And they thought my light yoke most heavy; and I inclined toward them, leaving the kingdoms of the heavens, so as to eat with them, having taken the form of a man; or I gave them my body to eat, I myself both the food and the guest at table.

And I was like a foster-father to Ephraim, I carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I was healing them. With the cords of Adam I will draw them, with the bonds of love. And I will be to them as one who lifts the yoke upon their jaws, and I inclined toward him that he might eat. LXX: And I bound Ephraim together, I took him up upon my arm; and they did not know that I was healing them in the corruption of men; I stretched them out in the bonds of my love. And I will be to them as a man giving slaps upon his jaws; and I will look upon him, prevailing over him. The Hebrew and the edition of the Seventy translators differ greatly from each other. Let us try, therefore, to weave the history according to the Hebrews, and ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy) according to the LXX. He who had said above: Israel was a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son, and afterwards added what wickedness he committed: They sacrificed to the Baalim and offered sacrifice to images, now relates with what love he loved Israel, according to what we read in Deuteronomy: The Lord your God carried you, as a man is wont to carry his little son, in all the way by which you walked, until you came to this place. And in another place: He spread out his wings and took him up, and carried him on his shoulders. I, he says, who was a father, became a foster-father, and I myself carried my little one in my arms, lest he be harmed in the wilderness; and lest he be terrified either by heat or by darkness, by day I was a cloud, by night a pillar of fire; so that those whom I had protected I might enlighten and heal with my light; and when they had sinned and made for themselves the head of a calf, I gave room for repentance, and they did not know that I was healing them, and closing over the wound of idolatry in the space of forty years, and restoring them to their former health.

Let us pass to the spiritual understanding, according to the Seventy translators only; lest, if we wish to expound both, according to the history and according to ἀναγωγὴν, we stretch out the size of the book. While they sacrificed to the Baalim which they had fashioned from their own heart, and, when I called, fled from my face, — for so it stands in the Seventy —, I, the most merciful Lord, bound the feet of Ephraim, that they might not flee farther from me; for this is what συνεπόδισα signifies. And I bound them with the testimonies of the Scriptures and the disputation of the teachers of the Church, so that he might hold them, bound through patience, in his arms, while they did not understand that the patience of God was the occasion of their salvation.

"Because I am kind and good, I bound the feet of Ephraim," that is, the whole Israel … although he was awkward. God himself declares why this is so: "I will take them in my arms." This image is from child raising. Those who take infants in their arms are those who bind their feet, bringing their feet together. For it is necessary, I think, that the thighs and knees of anyone who sits down should be drawn together. And in fact this is so. "I bound the feet" as, for instance, it was written about Abraham, who bound his son Isaac when he thought to bring him as a sacrifice to God. One must note that the Hebrew version and other versions do not have "I bound the feet" but rather "I became as one who nourishes Ephraim."

And I healed them because of the cords and bonds of love with which I had bound Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to myself. For in place of Adam, Aquila and Symmachus and the Seventy and Theodotion translated all men, so as to say: with the cords of men I will draw them, with the bonds of love. And what follows, I will be to them as one who lifts the yoke, for which Symmachus translated: and they thought that I was putting a yoke upon their jaw, is taken in two ways: either I took from them the yoke of all the nations round about, or they thought my law a most heavy weight of a yoke. And I gave him manna as food in the desert, for him to eat; for this is what he says: and I inclined toward him that he might eat; for which Symmachus translated: and I inclined food toward him. Not that God inclined toward him, but that he made the food of manna incline toward him.

Hence, in the corruption of men, that is, of the teachers who had deceived them, I extended the warmth of faith to those contracted by the cold of faithlessness, and bound them, resisting as they were, with the bonds of my love. And because they did not run of their own accord, but were dragged along bound with ropes, I struck their jaws a little with slaps, not punishing but correcting and amending. A judge tears the flesh, tortures with cords, torments with scourges and fire. But he who is a father strikes his wanton son with the palm of the hand. And he finely did not say: I will be beating them with slaps, but: as a man striking the jaws with the hand. And God strikes his straying sons with the threat of punishments, with the reading of the Gospel and the testimonies of the prophets. And when he has so struck on the jaw as to knock the bread and doctrine of the heretics out of the polluted mouth, then he looks upon him, while the beaten son says to him: Look upon me and have mercy on me. And again: Look and hear me, O Lord my God. And when he has looked upon him, he will prevail, or it will profit them, that is, he will overcome the adversaries and make servants out of runaways. Or he will give true and sweet food to those who formerly devoured the lies and most bitter food of the heretics.

According to the Seventy, Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, saying that he held the holy land and the Church of the Lord Savior; but by vices and sins and the perversity of his faith he always lingered in Egypt. Because, therefore, he dwelt in Egypt, the great mind, the Assyrian, will be his king; for he would not return to the Church, and, having lost power, that is, Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he has always lived in languor; and he was weak, subject to all the demons and passions; therefore the sword, that is, spiritual knowledge or the word of a churchman, laying waste and subduing, will always be at work in his cities, which he impiously built against God; and the sword itself will rest in his hands, so that, slain by another, he cannot slay another nor lift his hand against the adversary. Finally they will receive, and will devour, according to their own counsels.

He will not return into the land of Egypt, and Assyria itself is his king, because they would not be converted. The sword has begun in his cities and will consume his chosen ones; and it will eat their heads, and my people will hang in suspense for my return. But a yoke will be laid upon them all together, which will not be taken away. LXX: Ephraim will dwell in Egypt, and Assyria itself is his king, because he would not be converted. And the sword has grown weak in his cities, and has rested in his hands, and they will eat of their own thoughts; and his people hangs from its sojourning, and God will be angry over his precious things, and will not exalt him. When he says: he will not return into the land of Egypt, he shows that he desires to return but cannot go. For Israel desired to return, begging for help from the Egyptians; but he was taken in possession by the Assyrian, who captured him and ruled over him by the right of the victor; and he suffered this because he would not be converted nor repent. Or at least let us say that he returned into the land of Egypt when in the holy land he worshipped the gods of the Egyptians; or it is to be taken in the sense in which it was said above: They called upon Egypt, they went away to the Assyrians.

And so the sword has begun in his cities, or will rush in, as Aquila translated, or will wound, as Symmachus rendered. And see how great is the weight of miseries: not that fields or possessions and the countryside are laid waste, but that the enemy enters the midst of the cities and consumes his chosen ones, or his arms, as Symmachus translated, which in Hebrew is called baddau. And when the sword has consumed the chosen and the princes, or the strength of the army, and has devoured either their heads or their counsels, so that they can find no protection at all, then the wretched common people, who would not return to me, will wait for my return to them. And they will repent late, while the enemies lay everything waste. And so, because great sins must be punished with great torments, he will lay upon those of the people who are left, — their king and princes having been cut down by the Assyrian sword, — the most heavy yoke of servitude, and he will lay it on them all together, which will not be taken away according to the letter, unless it is taken away spiritually in Christ.

But the unhappy people and the untaught crowd will sigh for their ancient homeland and will feel themselves to be captive, or will hang in suspense in their sojourning, not knowing what to do and ignorant where to turn. And God is angry over their precious things, namely the gold and silver which they had received from him, of which we have often spoken, and he will by no means set free him who has fallen by his own fault. This according to the LXX; and we will fit the same sense to the Hebrew as well.

To the heretics also, and to the people deceived by them, the Lord says that unless they repent they will be set as Admah and Zeboiim, so as to have no hope of salvation. Again, as a most merciful father, he says that he changes his sentence and repents of having said such things, so as to call them too to conversion and to repentance. I will not act, he says, in my fury, I will not destroy Ephraim. As far, he says, as lies in me, as far as I desire, if he corrects his error by the truth, if he loves me more than the leaders of heresy; God, indeed, am I, and not man: I will stretch out my hand to the fallen, I will call the wandering to salvation. And because I am holy, for that reason I will not enter the city, that is, the conventicles and cities of the heretics. Those who go out of their cities I gladly receive; into their cities I will not enter.

How shall I give you up, Ephraim, shall I protect you, Israel? How shall I give you up like Admah, set you as Zeboiim? My heart is turned within me, my repentance is troubled together. I will not execute the fury of my wrath, I will not turn to destroy Ephraim, because I am God and not man; the Holy One in your midst, and I will not enter the city. LXX: What shall I do to you, Ephraim, shall I protect you, Israel? What shall I do to you? I will set you as Admah and as Zeboiim; my heart is turned in him; my repentance is troubled together. I will not act according to the wrath of my fury. I will not abandon Ephraim to be destroyed, because I am God, and not man; holy in you, and I will not enter the city. In that place where we and the LXX translated: shall I protect you, Israel? in the Hebrew is written amaggenach, which Aquila translated ὅπλῳ κυκλώσω σε, that is: I will surround you with a shield. And while we thought this was to be understood in a good sense and signified protection, from the edition of Symmachus a contrary sense is set before us, for he says ἐκδώσω σε, that is: I will hand you over. From the translation of Theodotion too, not favorable but adverse things are shown: ἀφοπλίσω σε, which signifies: I will strip you, and take from you the ὅπλον, that is, the shield with which I had protected you before; and this sense better suits the Lord when he threatens. What he says, then, is this: since they would not be converted, and Assyria became their king, and the sword will devour cities and princes and people, and a yoke will be laid upon them which will not be taken away from them; and because the sentence seemed harsh, leaving them no room at all for repentance, now God speaks to Israel with a parent's affection: What shall I do to you, Ephraim? how shall I strip you of my help? What shall I do to you? By what art shall I correct you? With what remedy shall I be able to heal you? I will set you as Admah and Zeboiim, which are two of the five cities, as we read in Genesis: Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim and Bela, which is Zoar, and in the Syrian tongue it is called Zoara. I will therefore set you and turn you into a wilderness, and destroy you down to cinders and ashes, as I destroyed Admah and Zeboiim. And when he had pronounced a harsh, nay a cruel sentence, again he is overcome by mercy through a parent's affection, and softens the severity of the judgment with a father's tenderness. For he says: My heart is turned within me; my repentance is troubled together. As soon as I said that I would set Ephraim and Israel as Admah and Zeboiim, my bowels were moved.

But if we wish to read: How shall I give you up, Ephraim, shall I protect you, Israel? it is to be understood thus: What shall I do to you? Are you worthy of protection, you who have done such things? It must also be noted that where something is said against Judah, that is, the people of God, it is not Admah and Zeboiim that are set down, but Sodom and Gomorrah. For we read in Isaiah: Hear the law of God, you princes of Sodom; and: Give heed to the word of the Lord, you people of Gomorrah. In the Gospel too, of the city which has not received the apostles, when they shake off the dust of their feet, it is said that in the day of judgment it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that city. And the prophetic word is directed to Jerusalem: Sodom has been justified by you. We are therefore given ground to suspect that Sodom and Gomorrah were the leaders in sin, and that Admah and Zeboiim followed their example; because the mighty will suffer torments mightily; and the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes. Hence churchmen too, if they are held fast by the same crimes as the heretics, will be subject not to the torments of Admah and Zeboiim, which are the lesser, but to those of Sodom and Gomorrah, which are said to be of greater crimes.

The Impassible speaks as if it suffered passion, and that which contains in Itself the cause of its own and all other bliss talks as though it could be in want and yearning. ... "How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? How shall I abandon thee, Israel? Mine heart is turned within me."

[Passage quoted, Hos. xi. 9.]

IN these words God the Word says when He has become man to those who confess Him to be a holy man, but not God: "I am God and not a holy man among you." And, then, having called Himself God, He shews the Almighty Lord and God, His Father, adding: "I will go behind the Lord." And the words: "I will not enter into the city," are of one who refuses to take part in the common and vulgar life of men, from which also He dissuades his own disciples: "Go not on a road of the Gentiles, and enter not into a city of the Samaritans."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 22

The philanthropy of God does not tolerate [abandonment]. "What can I do for you? Shall I view you as I did Sodom and destroy you like Gomorrah? My heart is upset." Here the love of God appears to imitate the passionate human being or, better yet, the affectionate mother. "My heart is upset, just as a woman would say about her child. My heart is upset just like the mother's." However, the previous metaphor was only partially adequate. "My heart is troubled in my regret"? God is troubled! Let no one ever think it! God forbid!

This which he said, I will not enter the city, and what follows according to the LXX, I will walk after the Lord, some have interpreted so as to say that the people answered the Lord, and that the sense is: Because your heart is turned within you, and you have not dealt with us according to our sins, but imitate your own clemency, and do not punish our offenses, and promise that you, holy and merciful, will dwell in our midst, therefore I too will not enter the city of evil men, nor will I be of the number of sinners; but I will walk after the Lord our God. The Hebrews, however, explain it thus, in the person of God: I will not abandon you, I will not go to another nation; nor will I enter another city.

In the same book, it is written, "I am God and not man, the holy one in the midst of thee, and I will not enter into the city," into the den, to be sure, of vices. He himself is the only one who does not enter into the city that Cain built in the name of his son, Enoch. All of this is chanted daily by the lips of the priests: ho monos anamartētos, which in our language is translated as qui solus est sine peccato.

I repented of destroying for ever my people of old; therefore I will not act according to the fury of my anger, nor will I be changed from my clemency so as to destroy Ephraim. For I do not strike in order to destroy for ever, but in order to amend. My cruelty is the occasion of repentance and of mercy. God, indeed, am I, and not man. Man punishes for this end, that he may destroy; God chastises for this end, that he may amend. The Holy One in your midst, and I will not enter the city, that is: I am not one of those who dwell in cities, who live by human laws, who think cruelty to be justice, for whom the highest law is the highest malice; but my law and my justice is to save those who have been corrected. We can also say otherwise: since Cain the parricide first built a city in the name of his son Enoch, the Lord does not enter a city of this kind, which was built by crime and blood and parricide.

"My heart recoils within me, my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute the fierceness of my anger; I will not again destroy Ephraim." God imitates a father and mother who are naturally worried and cannot turn away from their children for too long. He says that, however, not because he wills one thing now and then changes his mind. Rather, he expresses his thought in different ways, in anger and love, in threat and mercy, chastising and persuading.

The Hebrews refer these things to the coming of Christ, whom they hope is yet to come. We show that they are already accomplished, because both from Egypt and from the Assyrians, that is, from the east and the west, and from the north and the south, they have come, and daily they come, who sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And we can call sons of the sea, or of the waters, those who have been caught in the Lord's dragnet and drawn out of the sea of this world. And when they have been taken from death into life, they will be settled in their houses, which the Gospel calls barns, in which the chosen grain, separated from the chaff, is stored. It is said to be the nature of lions that when they growl and roar, all living creatures tremble, and, their step fixed, cannot move: so great is the terror, so great the dread. And so the Lord too, when he roars and thunders like a lion and utters his voice, all the birds and every winged creature will shudder, and they will go to their nests, that is, to their houses, in which the Lord will dwell with them. Let us also say it another way: when the true lion growls, the false lion, who according to the apostle Peter is our adversary, will at once fall silent, and every perverse dogma will be unable to open its mouth; and those who had before been taken captive by him, set free by the roar of the lion and its terrible threat, will follow the Lord their God. Then the sons of the sea, or of the waters, will fear, who had been begotten in the bitterness and in the salt waters of the heretics; and taking wings, they will fly like birds out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians, and they will say: Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest? So that those who had labored among the heretics may rest in the Church, and dwell in their houses, from which they had been led away by error. We know that Egypt, that is, Mesraim, is interpreted tribulation and distress; the Assyrians also, directing, or, as we judge better, rebuking. From these, therefore, the heretics will be set free when they begin to dwell in their houses and say to their evil parents: Your house will be left to you deserted.

They will walk after the Lord; he will roar like a lion, for he himself will roar; and the sons of the sea will tremble, and they will fly like birds out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will settle them in their houses, says the Lord. LXX: I will walk after the Lord; as a lion he will roar, for he himself will roar; and the sons of the waters will tremble, and they will fly like a bird out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will settle them in their houses, says the Lord. When the Lord promises prosperous things, the people will be converted to him, and will walk after the Lord, because the Lord will roar like a lion. Of this the prophet Amos also makes mention: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice. And he roars when he says: as Admah, I will set you as Zeboiim. And when he has roared, then the sons of the sea will tremble, or of the waters, as the LXX translated. For the word maim, which is written with three letters, mem, iod, mem, if it is read maim, means waters; if meiam, it is understood of the sea.

Ephraim has surrounded me in his denial, and the house of Israel in deceit; but Judah went down as a witness with God, and faithful with the saints. LXX: Ephraim has surrounded me in falsehood, and the house of Israel and Judah in impiety; now God has known them, and the holy people of God will be called. The Hebrews hand down a tale of this kind: at the exodus of Israel from Egypt, when on one side the mountain, on another the Red Sea, and on another the army of Pharaoh hemmed them in, and the people were held shut in, while the other tribes despaired of safety and wished either to return to Egypt or to fight, Judah alone faithfully entered the sea, and for this reason he also merited to receive the kingdom. And this, they say, is what is now said: Judah, a witness of the words of God, his supporter and avenger, went down with God into the sea, and among the saints was most faithful, so as to believe the words of God who commanded. That is what they say. Let us follow the sequence of the explanation we began: that Ephraim, the royal tribe, and the house of Israel, the people that served the royal tribe, surrounded him, and surrounded him in denial or falsehood, since they deny the Lord and confess idols. But Judah, that is, the two tribes, which had the temple, the law, the prophets, and kept the precepts of the law, were witnesses, and walking with God, and faithful with the saints. By the saints we can mean either the angels, or the patriarchs and prophets and the others who served at God's command. For in comparison with that time at which these things were said, when Ephraim had gone utterly astray and Israel had been deceived into the worship of idols, Judah alone had remained to be occupied in the worship and testimonies of God, and could go down with him, or be strong with the strong one. For rad means both descent and strength; for which Aquila translated ἐπικράτειαν (mastery). According to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), the heretics surround God in falsehood, nay rather in denial. For whatever they speak is denial, nay rather falsehood; and they surround him in deceit, or in the impiety of the house of Israel, while they compose with artful speech everything that they feign, and speak impiety against God. But Judah, that is, the churchman, is not proud, is not puffed up with heretical swelling, but is humbled with God, and with the choir of the saints is faithful and strong, while he builds his house upon the rock, which no storm can shake. The LXX translated very differently: that Ephraim and the house of Israel and Judah surrounded God in falsehood and in impiety, and that God is of such great clemency that he does not cut off from them the hope of salvation, but knows them and is ready to call the people a holy people and the people of God, which is now perverted by impiety. According to tropology also: that the Lord wills both heretics and sinful churchmen to be saved, and all to be called by his name. But he who is truly holy does not surround God in falsehood but in truth, as the psalmist says: You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is round about you.

And if any prefer to apply the prophecy to the people, regarding it as spoken concerning the people of Israel, let him consider the sequence of the argument, which implies that this will take place after the saying addressed as to Jerusalem itself, "And destruction shall be raised up in thy people, and all thy strong places shall depart." And those things, it says, which such and such a king suffered in a war in which he was involved, when they dashed the mother to the ground on her children, the like will I do unto you because of your wickedness. He must mean by "you" them that are called Israelites, who also were cast away with their king, by whom he implies Herod. "And you have suffered all this," it says, "because Israel is a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt have I called my son." But how can he praise and blame the same people at the same time? The real meaning supplies the explanation. The Christ is called "Israel," in other prophecies, as He is in this. Since then, it says, being obedient to Me, He took the form of a servant, and became My beloved Son, fulfilling all My will, therefore I called Him back as My true and beloved Son from the Egypt whither He descended when He became man, meaning by Egypt this earthly sphere, or possibly Egypt itself. But you, to whom the prophecy is spoken, shall suffer ruin and destruction, together with your king. Such is the prophecy. And we can see that from our Saviour's time by the siege of Jerusalem the independence and national power of the Jewish race that existed up till then was destroyed and utterly cast away. This is the third prophecy concerning Egypt, and His sojourn there.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 4

And we understand that the heretics pass away like the first light of dawn, and their king, the devil, or the heresiarch; whom in their infancy, — when they believed in the Church, and were little ones, and were reckoned under the name of Christ —, God loved; and he called them out of the tribulation and darkness of Egypt. And he called them through the apostles and the teachers of the Church. And when they had been called, he says, by my leaders, they withdrew from their face and worshipped Baal-peor, that is, they served their own vices and lust, and afterwards they sacrificed to the Baalim and to images which they had fashioned for themselves. For each of the heretics has his own gods, and whatever they have feigned they set up as a carved and a molten image.
12: Ephraim feeds on the wind and follows the burning heat; all day long he multiplies lying and devastation, and he has entered into a covenant with the Assyrians; and he was carrying oil into Egypt. LXX: But Ephraim, a most evil spirit, has pursued the burning heat; all day long he has multiplied vain and empty things, and he has made a covenant with the Assyrians; and he was trading oil in Egypt. Sacred history relates that Menahem, king of Israel, having made peace with Assyria, asked help of the Egyptians; and this is what is now said: that Ephraim feeds on winds, that is, deceives himself with vain hope, and follows καύσωνα, that is, the burning heat, and goes to the south, and does nothing else all day long but mock himself. And while he runs about this way and that, he prepares devastation and overthrow for his own cities. Is it not devastation and lying to have made a covenant with the Assyrians, and to have carried oil into Egypt? Συνεκδοχικῶς, the whole from a part: namely, that he sent gifts to the Egyptians. Although some think that oil is by no means produced in Egypt, and that the most precious oil was sent by Ephraim, whose land, Samaria, is most fertile in oil. Moreover, according to tropology, all heretics are held fast by the most evil spirit of the demons, of which it is written also in the Apostle: Against the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places. And the unclean spirit, when it has gone out of a man and has found no rest, joins to itself seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and returns to its former house. With a most evil spirit, therefore, they follow καύσωνα, that is, dryness, or the burning wind, which is hostile to flowers and destroys everything that sprouts; all day long he pursues empty and vain things, nor is he content with his own error, but he multiplies many disciples, nay rather companions of his vanity and error. He also makes a covenant with the Assyrians, whose prince is the great mind, so that whatever he has invented he may seem to have feigned wisely, with that wisdom which is destroyed by God, which the Apostle too commands us to avoid, saying: See that no one catches you through philosophy and empty seduction, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world. But he also carries oil into Egypt, or buys the wisdom of Egypt, desiring to mix with the dogmas of the Church the oil of anointing with which the prophets and priests were anointed, with which kings too were anointed. This oil the saints also have, of whom it is said: Your sons like young olive shoots around your table. And the good olive tree into which our wild olive has been grafted. But although the heretics try to mix lying with the truth, oil cannot be combined with water and the other moist and liquid things. The truth is always on top, and lying below. All other kinds, that is, heresies, which do not have, as we have said, the oil of truth, can be mixed with one another, and from many be made one body. But the oil of these, which is carried down into Egypt and descends from the holy land to the realms of Pharaoh, the prophet detests, saying: Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.

God of my heart … I didn't know how to love you, because I did not know how to conceive the existence of anything—however glorious—beyond mere matter. The soul that goes puffing and wheezing after such figments of the imagination [as fortune telling] is one that goes whoring from you and trusts what is phony and feeds on the wind. Yet while I wouldn't have this sorcerer sacrificing to demons on my behalf, I was actually sacrificing to them myself just by being involved in my superstition. For what else is to feed on the wind, if not to feed on error, and so to become the sport and plaything of the demonic?

We can understand Judah as the churchman, who is rebuked by the Lord because he is not mindful of his former benefits toward him, but daily joins sins to sins; and he sets forth what those benefits are. When the Church, he says, was bringing you to birth in faith, you supplanted your brother, the Jew or the Gentile, and received his birthright; and in your strength you were directed with the angel, either overcoming the adverse powers, or strengthened by the blessings of the angel, who is himself God; and you prevailed in figure against the angel, so that you might prevail against men, and you were strengthened. And when you had won the victory, you wept and besought the angel of the Lord, and, remembering your old sins, you found him in Bethel, that is, in the house of God, which is the Church, or in the house of ὢν, of sorrow and tears and repentance. And that we might know who this Judah was, there, he says, he spoke with us, that is, with us Christians; and from that time to the present day we are reckoned by the name of Christ, and with him directing us we are corrected.

Therefore the judgment of God is with Judah, and visitation upon Jacob; according to his ways and according to his devices he will repay him. In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was directed with the angel; and he prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and besought him; in Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us, and the Lord God of hosts. The Lord is his memorial; and you will turn to your God; keep mercy and judgment, and hope in your God always. LXX: And there is judgment for the Lord with Judah, that he may punish Jacob; according to his ways and according to his devices he will repay him. In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his labor he prevailed with God, and he was strengthened with the angel, and was able; they wept and entreated me; in the house of ὢν they found me, and there it was spoken to them. But the Lord God almighty will be his memorial, and you will turn in your God; keep mercy and judgment; and draw near to your God always. Since Ephraim once fed on winds and followed lying, and came to such madness that he wavered in doubt between two hostile nations, making peace with the Assyrians and carrying oil into Egypt, now all my judgment is with Judah, and visitation upon Jacob. Now he calls visitation scourges and punishments, so that he who repaid Ephraim what he deserved may repay Judah too, who sprang from the seed of Jacob, according to his ways and according to his devices; for he was not merely deceived by chance error and brought down by human frailty, but sought out and devised the things in which to sin and fall.

Moreover he sets forth how great benefits Judah, that is, Jacob, received, and the son is named in the father, and he recalls the ancient history, so that both the mercy of God toward Jacob and his hardness against God may be known. While he was still in Rebekah's womb, he supplanted his brother Esau, not indeed by his own strength, since he could not perceive it, but by the mercy of God, who knows and loves those whom he has predestined. And not only did he supplant his brother in the womb, but in his strength also he was directed with the angel, when at the torrent Jacob fought against the angel all night long. And because he was directed with the angel, he therefore received the name εὐθυτάτου, which in Hebrew is called isar, that is, of one directing, or directed.

There were places in Jerusalem where he taught and other places to which he retired. "In daytime he was teaching in the temple." Just this had been foretold by Hosea: "In my house did they find me, and there did I speak with them."

And he prevailed, he says, against the angel; and by the blessing of him whom he had overcome he was strengthened. He also wept and besought him, that is, the angel, saying: I will not let you go unless you bless me. And when, on the advice of his father and mother, he was fleeing to Mesopotamia, he found the same angel in Bethel, who spoke to him; he spoke with us, that is, in the father he spoke to the sons also, and in Jacob he loved Judah too; and from that time down to the present the memory of his name, which was imposed on him by the angel and by God, endures.

Where the Hebrew has: he wept and besought him; in Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us, we read in the common edition: they wept and besought me, in the house of ὢν they found me, and there it was spoken to them; ὢν is interpreted sorrow. If anyone, therefore, weeps, and repents, and entreats the Lord, he will find him in the sorrow of his heart, and when he has called upon him, he will hear him answering him.

It happened one day that the enemy of the human race met the wrestler of the eternal King on a journey and challenged him with these words: "If you would like to see what each of us can accomplish with his strength, let us have a contest." Barely finished speaking, he approached the saint and touched him in visible and corporeal reality, and for some time tried his wavering opponent, but the latter pressed Christ with prayers, and the divine aid strengthened his trembling steps and straightway caused the fugitive, apostate spirit to vanish into air. If it seems incredible to anyone that an invisible spirit can become substantial, save in the mystical sense, let it be explained to him how the divine pages narrate the struggle of Jacob with the angel too. I have this to say: that it would require less boldness for Satan to tempt a servant than the Lord, Emilian than Christ, man than God, the creature than the Creator.

Combine justice with mercy, spending in mercy what you possess with justice. It is written, "Keep mercy and justice, and draw near to thy God always." Because God loves mercy and justice, he who takes care to do mercy and justice draws near to God. It remains, then, for each to examine himself and for the rich person to take careful inventory of the private resources from which he is to offer gifts to God, to make sure that he has not oppressed a poor person, or used force against one weaker than himself, or cheated one dependent upon him, thus exercising license rather than justice. We are bidden to practice fairness and justice also toward those who serve us. Do not employ force because you are in command, and do not take advantage because it is within your power to do so.

Since these things are so, you too, O Judah, imitate your parent: weep and beseech the Lord of hosts, and turn to him. Keep mercy and judgment, and when you have done both, hope in your God always, advancing by good works to greater things.

Therefore, O churchman, you who are called Judah, and confessing, turn daily through repentance to your Lord; and if perhaps you have sinned, imitate the prophet who says: I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with my tears. And let it not suffice to have said this, but keep the commandments of God, show mercy to others, that you yourself may obtain mercy. Judge true judgment, so that in what you judge, judgment may be passed on you. And hope in your God always, or draw near to your God continually, so that, advancing in virtue at all times, you may draw near to your God.

Canaan: in his hand is a deceitful balance; he has loved calumny; and Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich, I have found an idol for myself; all my labors will not find for me the iniquity which I have sinned. LXX: Canaan: in his hand is a balance of iniquity; he has loved to oppress by power; and Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich, I have found rest for myself; all his labors will not be found for him, because of the iniquities in which he has sinned. He had admonished Judah to turn to the Lord his God, and to keep mercy and judgment, and to hope in the Lord always, or to draw near to him continually. Now the discourse turns to Ephraim, that is, to the ten tribes, whom he calls Canaan, according to what Daniel says to the elder, who was certainly of the seed of Judah: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you. And in Ezekiel we read it said to Jerusalem: Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. And in Isaiah it is said to the tribe of Judah: Hear the word of the Lord, you princes of Sodom; perceive with your ears the law of our Lord, you people of Gomorrah. In the last little verse of Zechariah too we read: And there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord. Now he says that Canaan, that is, Ephraim, has in his hand a deceitful balance, or an unjust one, though Scripture commands: Let your weights be just; and that he not only has an unjust and deceitful balance, but loves calumny and oppresses men by power.

Hence this very thing is also referred to the heretics. For Canaan can be interpreted: as if moving. And note that he said: as if moving, not moving. They are moving those whom they have deceived; as if moving, those whom they have tempted. But because these are founded upon the rock, they can be shaken by no whirlwind, nor change the footprint of their feet. In the hand of a Canaan of this sort, that is, in his works, there is a deceitful and unjust balance; for whatever the heretic speaks does not have the justice of God, and is full of deceit and frauds; whence they also love calumny, while they press down the innocent, or oppress them by power.

And lest we should think that some other Canaan is to be understood, he states more plainly who this Canaan is. Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich; and the sense is: it makes no difference whence I possess it, so long as I possess it. Very many suffer from this disease, of whom it is written: Riches gathered unjustly will be vomited up. For the ransom of a man's soul is his own riches. Hence we are commanded to make ourselves friends of the unrighteous mammon, who can receive us into the eternal tabernacles. But Ephraim, who glories and says: Yet I have become rich, I have found an idol for myself, or ἀνωφελὲς, that is, auen, which does not profit its possessor, has sweated with vain labor. Just as the belly is god to the glutton and the luxurious, so the avaricious man too worships the idol of gold, and says in his heart: I have found what I was seeking; but he will hear: Fool, this night your soul will be snatched from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? And when once, I will not say the glitter, but the blindness of riches has seized his eyes, he says: all my labors will not find my iniquity, in which I have sinned. And the sense is: whatever I sin, if I have riches, it cannot be imputed to me by those who need my help, according to what is written: And he who does iniquitous things is blessed. For the rich have many friends.

The poor churchman is oppressed by the wordiness and the subtleties of the heretics, who, after they have deceived some, are accustomed to say: we have become rich, we have a very great multitude; a crowd of disciples follows us; we have found an idol, or refreshment, for ourselves. For heresies are put together chiefly for this reason, that they may devour the houses of widows, who are always learning and never arrive at the knowledge of the truth. And beautifully: I have found, he says, an idol for myself. For all the fictions of the heretics are idols and images of the Gentiles; nor do they differ much in impiety, though they seem to differ in name. And they are accustomed to say: whatever I do, whatever I perform, cannot be imputed to me; for I have my riches, the arguments of the philosophers; I have a multitude of people, and whoever beholds it will not think that I sin.

And I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; I will yet make you sit in tabernacles as in the days of festivity; and I have spoken upon the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and in the hand of the prophets I have been likened. LXX: But I am the Lord your God, I brought you out of the land of Egypt; I will yet make you dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of solemnity, and I will speak to the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and in the hands of the prophets I have been likened. You indeed have sinned so greatly that you rejoiced in crime, and thought the multitude of your sins to be riches, and said: I have become rich, I have found an idol for myself; all my labors will not be able to find my sins. But I, the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt when you were serving Pharaoh and building cities of mud and straw, still grant you room for repentance, and by the greatness of my promises I exhort you to return to me; for I will yet make you sit in tabernacles as in the days of festivity. He calls the day of festivity Tabernacles, in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, when the sons of Israel went out of Egypt. Just as, he says, at that time I set you free from Egypt, and you dwelt in tabernacles, hastening to the holy land and to the place of the temple, so now also I will bring you out of tribulation and distresses and the impending captivity, if only you do what I have commanded.

To those also who have been led astray by the heretics it is said that they should return to the Lord, who prefers the repentance of the sinner to his death; for he is the one who brought them out of the land of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness and error of the Gentiles. And lest perhaps, remembering their sin, they should return too slowly: I will yet, he says, make you sit in tabernacles, as in the days of festivity; so that what baptism does, repentance may do, and they may dwell in the tabernacles of the Savior, that is, in the Churches, of which it is said: Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God.

For certain of these men used to see the prophetic Spirit and His active influences poured forth for all kinds of gifts; others, again, [beheld] the advent of the Lord, and that dispensation which obtained from the beginning, by which He accomplished the will of the Father with regard to things both celestial and terrestrial; and others [beheld] paternal glories adapted to the times, and to those who saw and who heard them then, and to all who were subsequently to hear them. Thus, therefore, was God revealed; for God the Father is shown forth through all these [operations], the Spirit indeed working, and the Son ministering, while the Father was approving, and man's salvation being accomplished. As He also declares through Hosea the prophet: "I," He says, "have multiplied visions, and have used similitudes by the ministry of the prophets." But the apostle expounded this very passage, when he said, "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministrations, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all. But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." But as He who worketh all things in all is God, [as to the points] of what nature and how great He is, [God] is invisible and indescribable to all things which have been made by Him, but He is by no means unknown: for all things learn through His Word that there is one God the Father, who contains all things, and who grants existence to all, as is written in the Gospel: "No man hath seen God at any time, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; He has declared [Him.]"

But that both the apostles and their disciples thus taught as the Church preaches, and thus teaching were perfected, wherefore also they were called away to that which is perfect-Stephen, teaching these truths, when he was yet on earth, saw the glory of God, and Jesus on His right hand, and exclaimed, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God." These words he said, and was stoned; and thus did he fulfil the perfect doctrine, copying in every respect the Leader of martyrdom, and praying for those who were slaying him, in these words: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Thus were they perfected who knew one and the same God, who from beginning to end was present with mankind in the various dispensations; as the prophet Hosea declares: "I have filled up visions, and used similitudes by the hands of the prophets."

How is it, then, that John says, "No one has ever seen God"? He says this so that you may know that he is speaking of a clear knowledge and a perfect comprehension of God. All the cases cited were instances of God's condescension and accommodation. That no one of those prophets saw God's essence in its pure state is clear from the fact that each one saw him in a different way. God is a simple being; he is not composed of parts; he is without form or figure. But all these prophets saw different forms and figures. God proved this very thing through the mouth of another prophet. And he persuaded those other prophets that they did not see his essence in its exact nature when he said, "I have multiplied visions, and by the ministries of the prophets I was represented." What God was saying was, "I did not show my very essence, but I came down in condescension and accommodated myself to the weakness of their eyes." However, John does not say only of humanity that "no one has ever seen God." This was proved by what I have said—I mean by the prophetic utterance that states, "I have multiplied visions, and by the ministries of the prophets I was represented."

For it is I who through all the prophets and various kinds of visions have been likened to men, and have called you to repentance. Is it not of human likeness when Moses, raising his hands on high, prays that Joshua may conquer Amalek, and the mysteries of the cross are shown in him? Is not God likened in the hands of the prophets when Jonah is in the deep three days and nights, that he may signify the Lord rising from the underworld on the third day? And we read of visions multiplied in all the prophets, when Ezekiel sees God sitting like a charioteer above the cherubim. And Isaiah: I saw, he says, the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and two seraphim around him crying to one another: holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth. And Habakkuk stood on his watchtower, to see horns in the hands of the Savior, in which his strength is hidden. Hence the psalmist too cries out: I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me. And that we may know that every prophecy in the holy Scriptures is called a vision: And all the people, he says, saw the voice of the Lord; hence the prophets also were formerly called seers.

And lest they think that the heresiarchs and leaders of their error have spoken by the spirit of God: it is I, he says, who spoke to the prophets, and not to your masters; I multiplied visions, and in the hand of my prophets, who are established in the Church, I have been likened.

If Gilead is an idol, then in vain were they sacrificing to oxen in Gilgal; for their altars too are like heaps upon the furrows of the field. LXX: If Gilead is not, then the princes sacrificing in Gilgala were false, and their altars like tortoises upon the desert of the field. Where we have translated 'to oxen', which in Hebrew are called surim, the LXX translated 'princes', who are called sarim, deceived by the likeness and ambiguity of the word. Again, where we have put 'heaps', which in Hebrew are called gallim and properly signify θῖνας, that is, mounds gathered together out of sand, which, chiefly in the desert and on the shores, are either increased or diminished as the wind blows, the LXX translated 'tortoises', for which Symmachus rendered 'heaps of stones', Theodotion 'hills'. And indeed, if you look at θῖνας, they have the likeness of great tortoises in a desert field, or on banks and shores, rising a little above the ground. What he says, then, is this: if in Gilead, of which it is written: Gilead, a city of those who work an idol, supplanted with blood, the gods are false and the religion perverse, and it is beyond the Jordan where two tribes dwell, Reuben and Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, then Gilgal too, of which we read in this same prophet: All their wickedness is in Gilgala, which is behind Beth-aven; whoever worship idols do not sacrifice oxen to the gods, but offer sacrifices to oxen, imitating the error of Samaria. For at the time when these things were prophesied, Gilead was in the kingdom of the ten tribes, and Gilgal under the rule of the two tribes, which were called Judah. Therefore both the ten tribes and the two were deceived by an equal error of idolatry, and their altars are like heaps and mounds gathered together of stones, or of sand. And since both these and those will have been led away into captivity, their once-altars, without worshippers, will have the likeness of tortoises or of mounds. But since Gilead is interpreted 'transference of testimony', and Gilgal 'wallowing place', we can say this: that the princes of the heretics transfer the testimonies of the truth into a lie, and whatever they worship is an idol, and their sacrifices have the likeness either of heaps gathered of stones or of tortoises. For just as θίνες and heaps are gathered here and there from stones and sand, so the heretics too compose images out of worldly wisdom and the subtleties of men, by fraud and falsehood. And when they have done this, they move with slow steps in one place, and cannot occupy the whole world. The tortoise, slow-footed and burdened, nay, weighed down by its own weight, does not so much walk as move, signifying the most grievous sins of the heretics, who sacrifice to their own errors in the mire and wallowing place of mud, adoring the works of their own hands, and, like oxen, toiling at everything for earthly crops.

He will not err who says that Jacob the supplanter, and Israel who sees the Lord, went before as a type of the Lord; and that Rachel, at first barren and beautiful, whom Jacob loved most, signifies the Church; but that Leah, with bleary eyes and fruitful, shows the mysteries of the Synagogue; and that he himself led the people of believers out of the darkness of this world, and came to the sweetest streams of the Jordan, that is, of baptism.

Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch. But by a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved. LXX: And Jacob withdrew into the plain of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded; and by a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved. It seems that, without reason and without prophetic order, after the idol of Gilead and Gilgal and the altars like heaps of stones, he suddenly chose to narrate the history of Genesis concerning Jacob; which is at once resolved by one who remembers having read above concerning Jacob: In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was made upright with the angel; and he prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and besought him: in Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us. This Jacob, therefore, was not strengthened by the angel in vain; but because he fought the whole night and overcame his adversary, so that from this he might learn not to fear his brother, for fear of whom he was fleeing into Syria to Laban his mother's brother; and he served seven years for a wife, Rachel; and for Leah he guarded the sheep of his father-in-law Laban for the same span of years.

And because he had once said both Jacob and Israel, he joins the father and the sons, and recalls the history that follows, when by the prophet Moses the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and the twelve tribes which were begotten of Israel were preserved, as the prophet led them out.

Ephraim provoked me to anger in his bitternesses, and his blood will come upon him, and his reproach his Lord will restore to him. LXX: likewise. Since, then, I had bestowed such great things on Ephraim that I brought him back rich and a lord, and the parent of many sons, who had been naked and an exile and alone, Ephraim deserted me, nay, provoked me to anger; and by his bitterness he made me bitter, who am sweet. Hence his blood will come upon him, that is: he himself will be the cause of his own death, according to what David says to the man who announced the death of Saul and related that the king of Israel had been slain by him: Your blood be upon your head. Not by my sentence, but by the blood of Saul will your blood be shed. And what follows: And his reproach the Lord will restore to him, agrees with that sense which Nathan speaks to David: You who have made the enemies blaspheme the name of the Lord, on account of this thing, that is, on account of this sin by which you killed Uriah, that very blasphemy and reproach, by which the Lord was blasphemed through you, will be turned upon your head. The heretics always provoke the merciful God to anger, and by the hardness of their heart they compel him who prefers the repentance of the sinner to his death to punish them; and their blood, by which they have shed both their own blood and that of many, will come upon their head; and the reproaches with which they have blasphemed the Lord, their Lord will restore to them, not that he is their Lord, but because he was once their Lord.
13: When Ephraim spoke, horror seized Israel, and he sinned in Baal, and died; and now they have added to sinning, and have made for themselves a molten image of their silver, as it were the likeness of idols; the whole is the work of craftsmen; to these they themselves say: Sacrifice men, adoring calves. LXX: According to the word of Ephraim he himself received justifications in Israel, and placed them for Baal, and died; and now he has added that he might sin, and they made for themselves a molten image of their silver, after the image of idols, molten works of craftsmen; to these they themselves say: Sacrifice men, for the calves have failed. Where the LXX translated: sacrifice men, for the calves have failed, and we rendered: sacrifice men, adoring calves, Symmachus translated: sacrifice; let men adore calves; so that the sense is: Sacrifice, that is, offer sacrifice to idols, and let the pause fall up to this point; then: let men, a rational animal, adore calves, dumb living creatures. When Ephraim spoke, then, that is, Jeroboam son of Nebat of the tribe of Ephraim, horror seized Israel, that is, the ten tribes. For 'horror', which in Hebrew is called rathath, and which Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'trembling', the LXX, intending I know not what, translated δικαιώματα, that is, justifications. And so great a horror seized Israel that he sinned and offended God in Baal, and died, losing him who says: I am the life. The soul, for, that has sinned, it shall die. And the Apostle: The widow, he says, who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives. And not only did he die in Baal, but he added sins to sins, so that from the silver which the Lord had given idols were fashioned, the works of men's hands. To these they themselves say, that is, the priests and princes who ought to have taught the people good things: Sacrifice men, adoring calves; which indeed is also said in the psalms: They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. Where, following Symmachus and Theodotion, we rendered 'adoring', Aquila translated καταφιλοῦντες, that is, kissing. For those who adore are accustomed to kiss their own hand; which Job denies having done, saying: If I have kissed my hand, putting it to my mouth, let this too be reckoned to me as the greatest iniquity. But if, as some would have it, the demons say to the people: Sacrifice men, for the calves have failed, the gluttony of those is shown who are fed on the blood of victims and the smoke of burnt offerings; for, when the victims fail, they desire men to be sacrificed to them, in whose not only death but also gore they delight.

But when the heretics speak, nay, the princes of the heretics, that is, Ephraim, horror and trembling will seize the unhappy people; and he will sin in the idols which he has fashioned from his own heart, and he dies with the people whom he has seduced.

And it is not enough for him to have fallen, unless he turns the tongue which he had received for singing of God into images of idols, and with artful eloquence composes a dogma like the truth, which is nothing else but a contrivance of human depravity. And they instruct their disciples that they too should sacrifice men, that is, steal them from the Church of God and bring them in to the heretics, and kill those whom they have deceived. What follows: For the calves have failed, has this sense: Do not seek those whom you may seduce among the Gentiles, who are called brute animals; but seize those, sacrifice those, who, set within the Church, are reckoned by the name of Christ and are called men, according to that prophetic word: But choice foods.

Such, brethren, is our life, we whose existence is so transitory. Such is the game we play upon earth. We do not exist, and then we are born, and being born we are soon dissolved. We are a fleeting dream, an apparition without substance, the flight of a bird that passes, a ship that leaves no trace upon the sea. We are dust, a vapor, the morning dew, a flower growing but a moment and withering in a moment. "Man's days are as grass: as the flower of the field, so shall he flourish." How beautifully has holy David meditated on our weakness: "Declare unto me the fewness of my days."
ON HIS BROTHER ST. CAESARIUS, ORATION 7:19

Therefore they will be like a morning cloud, and like the morning dew passing away, like dust snatched by the whirlwind from the threshing floor, and like smoke from the chimney. LXX: likewise; changing only this, which is at the end: and like vapor from locusts, or from tears, because in most manuscripts we find ἀκρίδων (of locusts) set down, in others δακρύων (of tears). Because, he says, they sacrificed men in place of calves, and adored calves, therefore they will be like a morning cloud, and like the dew passing away in the morning, like dust snatched by the whirlwind from the threshing floor, and like smoke from the chimney. All these are seen for a time and suddenly vanish, according to what he had said: Samaria has made her king pass away like foam upon the face of the water. And again: As the morning passes, the king of Israel will pass away. And that a cloud or dew passes swiftly, and dust from the threshing floor, and smoke from the chimney, no one doubts, according to what is written: As smoke fails, let them fail. But we ask why the LXX, for 'chimney', which Theodotion translated καπνοδόχην, rendered 'locusts'? Among the Hebrews 'locust' and 'chimney' are written with the same letters, aleph, res, beth, he. If it is read arbe, it means locust; if orobba, chimney; for which Aquila translated καταράκτην, Symmachus 'opening'. Now a cataract is properly the name for an opening made in a wall, through which the smoke goes out. But if someone contentious and unwilling to accept the Hebrew truth should seek the sense of 'locust', let him hear that Ephraim is compared to ἀτμῷ, that is, to a vapor, or a breath and a breathing, which comes out of the mouth of a locust so thin that it is not perceived; but if, on the contrary, he objects, why did he not liken Ephraim, who was to perish, to other things which are smaller, for example to the flea, which has all its members, head, eyes, feet, belly and the rest, which, though we do not see them with our eyes, we nevertheless perceive by sense, so much so that the mouth and teeth of the flea, which we do not see with our eyes, we feel by its bites. He must be answered that he compared the glory of those who were to perish to the vapor of the locust, or to a most thin breath, for this reason: because the locust is harmful, and so hostile to mortals that it causes famine and lays waste the tilled crops, so much so that it strips the bark from trees and vines as well, as we read more fully in the prophet Joel. And to this locust, and to the morning cloud and the dew and the dust, the heretics are compared, of whom it is also said in the catholic epistle: These are clouds without water. For they have the appearance of prophets and of apostolic clouds, to which the truth of God comes; but they do not have waters, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Lord says in the Gospel: He who believes in me, as the scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this, he says, he said of the Spirit which those who believed in him were to receive. But concerning the tears, which in the Greek tongue have some likeness to the locusts, δακρύων καὶ ἀκρίδων, the error is manifest, since some supposed 'tears' in place of 'locusts'.

For through the Lord Christ all things were created; and therefore it is His proper name that He should be the Creator. Does not both the reality and the title of His creative power belong to Him? Melchisedec is our witness, thus declaring God to be Creator of heaven and earth: "Blessed be Abraham of God most high, Who created heaven and earth." The prophet Hosea also is witness, saying, "I am the Lord thy God, that establish the heavens and create the earth, Whose hands have created all the host of heaven." Peter too is witness, writing thus, "Committing your souls as to a faithful Creator." Why do we apply the name of the work to the Maker of that work? Why do we give the same name to God and to our fellowmen? He is our Creator, He is the Creator of all the heavenly host.

But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt. In place of which one reads in the LXX: But I am the Lord your God ÷ who make firm the heaven and create the earth, whose hand created all the host of heaven, and I did not show them to you, that you might walk after them. : And I brought you out of the land of Egypt. Since these words are not found in the Hebrew, and are rendered by none of the translators, and are not read in the ancient edition of the LXX either, they must be marked beforehand with an obelus; especially since their sense is plain. Let us therefore pass on to the rest, joining the preceding section to what follows:

But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt, and you shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior but me.

I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude, according to their pastures; and they were filled and were satisfied; they lifted up their heart and forgot me. LXX: But I am the Lord your God, and I brought you out of the land of Egypt; and you shall know no God but me, and there is no savior besides me. I was pasturing you in the desert, in an uninhabitable land, according to their pastures; and they were filled to satiety, and their hearts were lifted up; therefore they forgot me. He who had said above: Jacob fled into the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch; but by a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was kept, now also recounts what he provided for them: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, who commanded you through Moses: take heed lest perhaps you eat and be satisfied, and forget your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; for there is no other God besides me, and there is no other who is able to save.

The heretics too the Lord brought out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, and out of the iron furnace, who at first served King Pharaoh and his captains; and he commanded them in the Church to know no other God except him who is the creator of all things and knows how to save those whom he made.

I, who am the founder of all things, knew you, or fed you, in the wilderness and in an uninhabitable land, where there is want of all things, where there are no waters; I gave you manna from heaven, and brought forth springs of water from the hardest rock. And they, according to what is written elsewhere: The beloved grew fat, became thick, grew broad, and kicked, now also have eaten and been satisfied, and have lifted up their heart, and have forgotten him whose benefits they ought to have remembered. For through so great a waste of desert, where not only no crops and trees and vines, but not even grass is produced, and no waters temper the heat of the sun, Israel could not for forty years have reached the land of the Jordan, unless the Lord had provided everything.

He himself knew them and fed them in the land of solitude, so that they could say: The Lord pastures me and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture there he has set me, he has brought me up beside the water of refreshment. And he gave them the bread of angels, manna from heaven, which they had never eaten in Egypt, and water from the rock that followed them. Now the rock, according to the Apostle, is Christ; and they ate and were filled, and did not endure the food of the Lord. To them the same Apostle says: Already you are satisfied, already you have become rich; without us you reign, and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you. For they ate in the holy Scriptures the bread that came down from heaven, and said with David: The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made manifest to me. And being filled and satisfied, they lifted up their heart against the Creator, and invented another god for themselves, ascribing whatever they had drunk and eaten to their own merits, not to the mercy of God. Therefore they forgot God, who had commanded them to bind the words of the law between their eyes and on their hands, and on the fringes of their cloaks, so that they might never forget their God.

And I will be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians; I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs, and I will tear apart the inner parts of their liver; and I will devour them there like a lion; the beast of the field will rend them. LXX: And I will be to them like a panther and like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians; I will meet them like a bear in want of food, and I will tear apart the inner parts of their heart; and the whelps of the forests will devour them there, the beasts of the field will tear them apart. They were filled and satisfied; they lifted up their hearts and forgot me. But I, he says, will be to them like a lioness, or a panther, of which we spoke more fully above; and like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians, when they are led captive by the Assyrians; and I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs, or in want of food; and I will tear apart all their vital organs. Those who have written on the natures of beasts say that among all wild animals nothing is more savage than a bear when she has lost her cubs or is in want of food; and he threatens not only the ferocity of the panther, the leopard and the bear, but also that of the lion and of all the beasts that are bred in the woodland pastures; and he says he will be turned into all these when they go to the Assyrians, so that, when they have suffered hard things there, they may not ascribe their miseries to the strength of their enemies, but to the power and indignation of the Lord. And at the same time let us consider that he who in the Gospel says to believers: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; for my yoke is sweet and my burden is light, now through the prophet becomes to the unbelieving and to those unwilling to repent a panther, a leopard, a bear and a lion; not only to the Israelites, who because of their idolatry were settled in the cities or mountains of the Medes, but also to the heretics, who because of the pride of their mind and the vanity of their false dogmas have forgotten their God, and have fashioned and followed foreign gods.

In fulfillment of holy Writ, the truth has resounded through the voice of the apostles, for the psalmist has sung, "Their voice has gone forth unto all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world." So also "Christ our Passover is sacrificed," for of him the prophet had foretold: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and he was mute as a lamb before its shearer, and he opened not his mouth." Who is this man? He is the man of whom the prophet at once goes on to say, "In humility his judgment was taken away; who shall declare his generation?" I recognize the realization of so much humility in a king of so much power, for he who is as a lamb that opens not its mouth before its shearer is also "the lion of the tribe of Judah." Who is this lamb and lion? He suffered death like a lamb, and he has devoured like a lion. Who is this lamb and lion? Meek yet courageous; lovable yet fearsome; innocent yet powerful; silent under judgment, yet roaring to pronounce judgment. Who is this lamb and lion—suffering like a lamb; rising up like a lion? Rather, is he not at the same time a lamb and lion in his suffering and his resurrection? Let us discern the lamb in the suffering. "He was," as we have just reminded you, "mute as a lamb before its shearer, and he opened not his mouth." Let us discern the lion in the suffering.

You have become a surfeit to me: I will by no means forgive your sins. For which Aquila translated, I have labored in bearing; Symmachus ἐκοπώθην ἱλασκόμενος, that is, I have grown weary of showing mercy; to show that he will by no means have mercy any longer, because it is one thing to kill the servants sent to them, another to kill the Son. This sense we read also in the prophet Hosea: Your destruction, O Israel; only in me is your help (Hos 13:9). Which is understood thus: You would perish, Israel, because you are saved not by your own merit but only by my help.

Your destruction, Israel; only in me is your help. Where is your king? Now above all they save you in all your cities; and your judges, of whom you said: Give me a king and princes; I will give you a king in my fury, and I will take him away in my indignation. LXX: Who will help your corruption, Israel? Where is this king of yours? And let him save you in all your cities; let him judge you, of whom you said: Give me a king and a prince; and I gave you a king and a prince, and I gave you a king in my anger, and I held him in my fury. Where the LXX translated I held, all the others rendered I took away. Unhappy Israel, and worthy of a perpetual curse, which has gone down into so great a depth of impiety that it is saved by the mercy of God alone! But in the Hebrew it can also be read in this sense: May you perish, Israel, because nothing is left to you except to be preserved by my clemency alone. In the LXX, however, the sense is different: Who will help your corruption, Israel? That is, which of those whom you thought your protectors will be able to bring help to your captivity and final servitude?

Every heretic is lost and given over to corruption; for whoever corrupts the temple of God, the Lord will destroy him; and he has help in nothing else but in the mercy of God alone, which he obtains by repentance.

Where is your king, of whom you said to Samuel: Appoint a king over us to judge us, as the other nations also have. And when he spoke against it, you answered: By no means; but there shall be a king over us, and we too shall be like all the nations, and our king will judge us, and go out before us, and fight for us. Let him, then, of whom you had promised yourself that he would fight your wars, now come to your aid in your need, and free all your cities from servitude. Where are your judges? Where are your kings? For you said: Give me a king and princes; and so I gave you Saul as king in my fury, so much so that in the days of harvest I displayed rain, contrary to the nature of the province of Judea. And I took away, he says, the king in my indignation, namely Zedekiah, so that the one I had given with fury I might take away with indignation. Others think that the king given in fury was Jeroboam son of Nebat, and the one taken away in indignation Hoshea, the last king of the ten tribes. This which we have expounded, I gave you a king in my indignation, and I took away the king, the Hebrews refer to the future tense. At that time, he says, when you were saying: Give me a king and princes, I answered you through Samuel that I would give you one in my fury and would take him away in my indignation.
