His king and judges are the devil and the demons, or all the princes of perverse dogmas, who will not be able to free them in the time of need and distress, who were given in fury and will be taken away in indignation; not that the Lord wished them to have such kings, otherwise he would not take away those whom he had given of his own accord, but because he let them go after their own wills, so that, eating, and with their flesh grown fat, they might be nauseated and vomit it out through their nostrils, and begin to hate those whom they followed with such zeal.

Praise wicked King Saul, because he also was a punishment for sinners, as the Lord says: "I gave you a king in my wrath." Praise the demon that king suffered, because it also was punishment for a sinner. Praise the blindness of heart that has befallen Israel, and do not be silent about why it is said, "Until the full number of the Gentiles should enter," although you will perhaps deny this is a punishment. If you were a lover of the inner light, you would cry out that it is not merely a punishment but a very great punishment.

But let no one who suffers such a ruler, blame him whom he suffers: because his being subject to the power of a wicked ruler was doubtless of his own desert. Let him therefore rather blame the fault of his own evil doings, than the injustice of his ruler. For it is written, "I will give thee kings in Mine anger." Why then do we scorn their being set over us, whose authority over us we endure from the anger of the Lord? If then we receive rulers, according to our deserts, from the wrath of God, we infer from their conduct, what to think in our estimate of ourselves. Although even the Elect are frequently placed under the reprobate. Whence also David for a long time endured Saul. But it is proved by the subsequent sin of adultery, that he then deserved to be thus heavily oppressed by the cruelty of him who was set over him.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 25:34

The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hidden; the pains of a woman in labor will come upon him; he is an unwise son; for now he will not stand in the crushing of the children. LXX: A gathering of iniquity is Ephraim; his sin is hidden; pains as of a woman in labor will come upon him; this is your wise son, because now he will not hold out in the crushing of the children. Just as, if something is bound up in a bag, it is kept, and is not lost to him for whom it was tied up, so every iniquity by which Ephraim has sinned against God is bound up for him, and is reserved, hidden as in a purse. Finally, when the day of vengeance has come, and the final captivity, pains as of a woman in labor will come upon him, or will seize him. A woman in labor knows long before she gives birth, from the time she conceived, that she is going to give birth, and daily awaits the extreme torments and agonies that are to come. So too Ephraim, the unwise son, of whom he had said above: Ephraim is a foolish dove, not having a heart in the crushing of his children and his people. When the day of labor and of captivity has come, he will be able neither to stand nor to endure. Instead of the unwise son, in the LXX one reads by irony: This wise son, that is: the one you thought wise, so that by contrast he may be understood as unwise. But for all the heretics their iniquity is bound up, which they have spoken on high; and their sin is hidden, while they think they hide the poisons of their heart and hold secrets, which, when the day of labor has come, will be laid open with pain and wailing. This Ephraim is an unwise son, because he has abandoned the wisdom of God, of whom it is also written in Jeremiah: His end will be foolish; and in the crushing of his children, whom he has killed, whom he has slaughtered, he will not be able to endure the wrath of God.

But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?  Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die:  And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain:  But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.  All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.  There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.  There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.  So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:  It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power:  It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.  And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.  Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual.  The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.  As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.  And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.  Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption.  Behold, I show you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,  In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.  For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.  So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.  O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? [Hosea 13:14] The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law.  But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.  Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

Now the laws of love summoned Him even as far as Death and the dead themselves, so that He might summon the souls of those who were long time dead. And so because He cared for the salvation of all for ages past, and that "He might bring to naught him that hath the power of death," as Scripture teaches, here again he underwent the dispensation in His mingled Natures: as Man, he left His Body to the usual burial, while as God He departed from it. For He cried with a loud cry, and said to the Father: "I commend my spirit," and departed from the body free, in no wise waiting for death, who was lagging as it were in fear to come to Him; nay, rather, He pursued him from behind and drove him on, trodden under His feet and fleeing, and He burst the eternal gates of his dark realms, and made a road of return back again to life for the dead there bound with the bonds of death. Thus, too, His own body was raised up, and many bodies of the sleeping saints arose, and came together with Him into the holy and real City of Heaven, as rightly is said by the holy words: "Death has prevailed and swallowed men up"; and again: "The Lord God has taken away every tear from every face."

And the Saviour of the Universe, our Lord, the Christ of God, called Victor, is represented in the prophetic predictions as reviling death, and releasing the souls that are bound there, by whom He raises the hymn of victory, and He says these words:

"From the hand of Hades I will save them, and from death I will ransom their souls. O Death, where is thy victory? O Death, where is thy sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 12

But that brazen serpent was hung up as a remedy for the biting serpents, not as a type of him that suffered for us but as a contrast. And [the brazen serpent] saved those that looked upon it, not because they believed it to live but because it was killed, and killed with it were the powers that were subject to it, being destroyed as it deserved. And what is the fitting epitaph for it from us? "O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory?" You are overthrown by the cross; you are slain by him who is the giver of life; you are without breath, dead, without motion, even though you keep the form of a serpent lifted up on a pole.

No one could know Wisdom; for no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. Therefore, He Himself revealed to John with whom Wisdom was; and for this reason, he said, not as his own, but what Wisdom had infused in him: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God. Wisdom does not know destruction, it does not know wickedness. For destruction could not hold it, who said: Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?
The Prayer of Job and David 1:9.31

And seeing the hard necessity of death, and that there is no man who lives and does not see death, the most merciful Father remembers the ancient sentence, that in Adam we all die. Or the prophet, understanding his own frailty and the condition of human flesh: Consolation, he says, is hidden from my eyes; and the sense is: I am not able to be consoled; whatever I conceive in my mind cannot soften my grief, as I see names most dear to one another severed by death; hell itself, he says, divides between brothers. Whatever, then, separates brothers is to be called hell; and above all the harlot woman, who, calling the unwise man to herself, says in the wealth of prudence: Touch gladly the hidden loaves, and the sweetness of stolen water; and the unwise man does not know that the earth-born perish with her and run into the depth of hell. For whatever is not permitted is desired the more, and what is sweet through rarity is turned into bitterness through constancy. And honey drips from the lips of the harlot woman, which for a time makes the jaws of the unwise man fat, but at the last is found more bitter than gall, and sharper even than a two-edged sword. Whoever is earth-born, and is not born from heaven, is killed by her embraces and bound with the bands of her couches; and the feet of folly lead down those who make use of her, with death, to hell. Now between death and hell there is this difference: death is that by which the soul is separated from the body; hell is the place in which souls are shut up, whether in refreshment or in punishments, according to the quality of their merits. We have said this to show that death does what the harlot woman does. For death divides brothers, and the woman does this too. Under brothers understand every bond of love, so that mother also is divided from daughter, and father from son, and brother from brother. That death is one thing and hell another, the psalmist also shows, saying: There is no one in death who is mindful of you; but in hell who will confess to you? And in another place: Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell. Where we have translated: I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell, the LXX rendered: Where is your cause, O death? where is your goad, O hell? In place of which the Apostle put: Death is swallowed up in strife? Where, O death, is your strife? Where, O death, is your sting? And expounding the force of the testimony he added: Now the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law; but thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore what he interpreted of the resurrection of the Lord, we neither can nor dare interpret otherwise. Death and hell can also be taken as the devil, who was slaughtered by the death of Christ, of whom it is also said in Isaiah: Death, growing strong, has devoured. And afterwards there follows: The Lord has taken away every tear from every face. But the two brothers divided from each other by death some understand, according to the history of that time, as Israel and Judah, so that what was then prefigured in part may now be perceived in the whole, and Israel and Judah are to be freed and redeemed together with the whole human race. In the place where the LXX rendered: where is your cause? and we said: I will be your death, Symmachus translated: I will be your stroke. The Fifth edition and Aquila: where are your words?, for in Hebrew it is written dabarach; they read dabar, that is, word, in place of deber, which is interpreted death, according to what we read in Isaiah: The Lord sent death into Jacob, and it came into Israel, that is, deber, in place of which we translated: The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it came into Israel, that is, dabar. For sting also, which we rendered bite, Symmachus translated ἀπάντημα, that is, an encounter, and Theodotion and the Fifth edition a stroke and a shutting-in.

From the hand of death I will free them, from death I will redeem them. I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell. Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he divides between brothers. LXX: From the hand of hell I will free them, from death I will redeem them; where is your cause, death? Where is your sting, hell? Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he will divide between brothers. According to both understandings, both of Ephraim, that is, of the ten tribes, and of the heretics, who could not hold out in the crushing of their children when the pains as of a woman in labor came, the Lord promises that he will free them from the hand of death and redeem them from death. Now he calls the hand of death the works by which it kills, according to what is written: Death and life are in the hand of the tongue. And the Lord freed all and redeemed them in the passion of the cross and the shedding of his blood, when his soul went down into hell and his flesh did not see corruption; and to death itself and to hell he spoke: I will be your death, O death. For this is why I died, that you might die by my death. I will be your bite, O hell, you who devoured all in your jaws.

Thus, if the glory of incorruptibility has been hidden from all people in this time, how do you, in this very same age, boast that you are able to be clothed with that very same incorruptibility? For just as sinking into sin has become for humans the beginning of corruption, so not having sin will be the beginning of incorruption. Who, therefore, concealed this prior to the judgment of God or removed it from the bosom of Christ and handed it over to you? Or do you perhaps think that a person would not merit this in the future from the hand of the Lord? That most distinguished man, Paul, teaches this and says, "But when this mortal thing has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying which is written, 'Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death is your sting?' Now the sting of death is sin." Through this the apostle shows that by no means can anyone so scoff at death and sin, until immortality follows mortality, and incorruption, corruption, and when, with the destruction of weakness, perfect virtue succeeds it; when there will not be male and female, but when all will be similar to the angels of God.

What is it the chaste person would like? That no lust at all should stir in the members against chastity. [The chaste person] wants peace but hasn't yet got it. I mean, when we get to the stage where no lusts at all rise up to be opposed, there won't be any more enemy for us to wrestle with; nor is there in that state any expectation of victory, because the triumph is being celebrated over the enemy already conquered. Listen to the apostle telling you about that victory: "The perishable must put on imperishability, and the mortal put on immortality; then will come about the saying that is written: 'Death has been swallowed up in victory.' " Now listen to the song of triumph: "Where, O death, is your striving? Where, O death, is your sting?" You have stabbed, you have wounded, you have knocked down; but the one who made me was wounded for me. O death, death! The one who made me was wounded for me, and by his death he conquered you. And that's when those who triumph over you are going to say, "Where, O death, is your striving? Where, O death, is your sting?"

Still I think it right to convict them plainly of foolishly resisting the inspired Scriptures, and to show that they completely mistook the sense of what the sacred writings teach. For come and let us see what the company of the holy prophets has spoken to us upon this point, and what are the declarations which the Lord of hosts has made by their means. He said therefore of those that sleep, "I will deliver them from the hand of the grave; I will redeem them from death: Where is your condemnation, O death? O grave, where is your sting?" Now what is meant by the condemnation of death, and by its sting also, the blessed Paul has taught us, saying, "But the sting of death is sin: and the strength of sin is the law." For he compares death to a scorpion, the sting of which is sin: for by its poison it slays the soul. And the law, he says, was the strength of sin: for so he himself again elsewhere protests, saying, "I had not known sin but by the law:" "for where there is no law, there is no transgression of the law." For this reason Christ has removed those who believe in Him from the jurisdiction of the law that condemns: and has also abolished the sting of death, even sin: and sin being taken away, death, as a necessary consequence, departed with it; for it was from it, and because of it, that death came into the world.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

For God’s mercy towards us is the more wonderful that Christ died not for the righteous nor for the holy, but for the unrighteous and wicked; and though the nature of the Godhead could not sustain the sting of death, yet at His birth He took from us that which He might offer for us. For of old He threatened our death with the power of His death, saying by the mouth of Hosea the prophet, “O death, I will be thy death, and I will be thy destruction, O hell.” For by dying He underwent the laws of hell, but by rising again He broke them, and so destroyed the continuity of death as to make it temporal instead of eternal. “For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.”

Yet again the same prophet says: From the power of the grave will I ransom them. Where is thy victory, O death! Where is thy sting, O grave!—a passage which the Apostle has used concerning the resurrection.

From this solemnity indeed the example of resurrection was given to us, the hope of the heavenly homeland was opened, and the glory of the supernal kingdom was made something we might already anticipate. Through this, the elect, who although they were in the bosom of tranquility, were nevertheless held in the confines of hell, were led back to the delights of paradise. What the Lord said before His passion, He fulfilled in His resurrection: "If I am lifted up from the earth," He said, "I will draw all things to myself." For He drew all things, He who left none of His elect in the underworld. He took away all things—that is, all the elect. For He did not restore to pardon by rising again any unbelievers or those consigned to eternal punishments for their crimes; but He snatched from the confines of hell those whom He recognized as His own in faith and in deeds. Whence rightly also He says through Hosea: "I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell." For what we kill, we cause to exist no more entirely. But from what we bite, we take away a part and leave a part behind. Therefore, because in His elect He utterly killed death, He became the death of death. But because He took away a part from hell and left a part behind, He did not utterly kill but bit hell. Therefore He says: "I will be your death, O death." As if He were saying openly: Because in my elect I utterly destroy you, I will be your death; I will be your sting, O hell, because when they have been taken away, I pierce you in part.

Whence rightly also He says through Hosea: "I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell." For what we kill, we cause to exist no more entirely. But from what we bite, we take away a part and leave a part behind. Therefore, because in His elect He utterly killed death, He became the death of death. But because He took away a part from hell and left a part behind, He did not utterly kill but bit hell. Therefore He says: "I will be your death, O death." As if He were saying openly: Because in my elect I utterly destroy you, I will be your death; I will be your sting, O hell, because when they have been taken away, I pierce you in part. What then is this solemnity which destroyed the confines of hell and opened to us the gates of the heavenly kingdom?

In spite of these words, we are so deeply affected that we fall into tears and the longing of desire crushes the beliefs of the mind. How miserable is the human lot! How vain is all our life without Christ! O death, that separates those who were joined, cruel and harsh in forcing apart those who were tied by friendship! Now, now your strength is destroyed. Now is that wicked yoke of yours broken by him who sternly threatened you in the words of Hosea: "O death, I will be your bite!" So let us with the apostle voice our taunt: "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" He who conquered you has redeemed us—he who betrayed his beloved soul into the hands of the wicked, that those who were once wicked he might make his beloved.

We have been brought to life in Christ through Christ, because Christ triumphed over death: whence death could not swallow him up, but rather the font of life swallowed up death, according to what was said: "I will be your death, O death." In no other way could we be healed and saved.

Since it was fitting for Christ to die in order to deliver us from death, so it was fitting for Him to descend into hell in order to deliver us also from going down into hell. Hence it is written (Hosea 13:14): "O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite." Secondly, because it was fitting when the devil was overthrown by the Passion that Christ should deliver the captives detained in hell, according to Zechariah 9:11: "Thou also by the blood of Thy Testament hast sent forth Thy prisoners out of the pit."
Question 52. Christ's descent into hell, Article 1

Wherefore let us direct our discourse to a second witness. And of what sort is this one? Listen to Hosea, as he speaks thus grandly: "In those days the Lord shall bring on a burning wind from the desert against them, and shall make their veins dry, and shall make their springs desolate; and all their goodly vessels shall be spoiled. Because they rose up against God, they shall fall by the sword, and their pregnant women shall be ripped up." And what else is this burning wind from the east than the antichrist that is to destroy and dry up the veins of the waters and the fruits of the trees in his times, because people set their hearts on his works? For which reason they shall serve him in his pollution.
ON THE END OF THE WORLD 4

The Lord will bring a burning wind rising from the desert, and it will dry up its veins, and lay waste its spring, and he will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel. LXX: The Lord will bring a burning wind from the desert upon them, and will dry up its veins, and lay waste its springs; he will parch its land and all the desirable vessels. I have read in the commentaries of a certain writer that the burning wind which the Lord will bring from the desert is the one that struck the house of Job at its four corners and made it fall upon his sons as they feasted, and that it is one of those winds which we read in the Gospel blow and come with whirlwind, rains and floods to overturn the house that is built upon the rock, or upon the sand. This by no means seems right to me; for it is not written in Job that the Lord brought the wind from the desert; rather, the name of the Lord is passed over in silence, so that the wind from the wilderness, which had come against the holy man of its own will, can be taken as a hostile power; and the winds that overturn the foundations of houses certainly cannot be referred to the good side. It remains that we understand the burning wind, which the Lord will bring rising from the desert, as the one of whom we also read in Habakkuk: God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Paran, which is certainly situated in the wilderness and in the south. And in the Song we read: Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday? This burning wind, then, to dry up the veins of death and parch its springs, the Lord will bring rising from the desert; but from the desert of the human race, in which even the devil, seeking rest, could not find it. Or we understand the desert as the virginal womb of holy Mary, because without human seed it sprouted no shoot, but a rod, simple and most pure and fruitful in its oneness, brought forth that flower which says in the Song of Songs: I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. And beautifully, both in Isaiah and in the present place, it is called a flower rising and a wind rising, because from the lowliness of the flesh he climbed to the heights, and led us with himself to the Father, saying in the Gospel: When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to myself. He himself will rise like a root from an uninhabitable land, and death will by no means come upon him, but he will come upon death; for death found in him no path for its power, and this is what is said in Proverbs: It is impossible to find the tracks of a serpent upon a rock. And the rock itself speaks in the Gospel: Behold, the prince of this world will come, and will find nothing in me. He will dry up the veins of death and lay waste its springs. The veins and springs and sting of death are named sins by the Apostle; and when these have been dried up, death itself also will be dried up. And what follows: He will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel, is taken in two ways: either because they are desirable to those who dwell in death, or by the desirable vessels that were held in the treasury of hell we understand the saints, whom, bound as they were, the Lord perhaps plundered and carried off from hell, and led with him into paradise like most precious vessels. For treasure the LXX translated land; there is no doubt that the land signifies death. And in the psalms we read: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. And according to the Gospel: The meek will possess the land. By contrast we must take it that the land of hell is not the land of the living but of the dead, which is plundered and laid waste when, by the death of Christ, the souls bound in hell are set free. According to tropology, in those same commentaries — of which we spoke above — we read that the burning wind is understood as the devil and the individual heresiarchs. This does not please us; for the devil cannot dry up the veins of death and the springs of error, since he himself is the source and beginning of the dead. Therefore the burning wind is to be understood as the word of the Church, which parches all the dogmas of the heretics and brings them to nothing, and plunders and scatters those who had been gathered together in death by the doctrine of the heretics.

Let Samaria perish, because she has provoked her God to bitterness; let them perish by the sword; let their little ones be dashed and her pregnant women be ripped open. LXX: Samaria will be destroyed, because she has resisted her God; they will perish by the sword, and let their sucklings be dashed against the rock, and those with child be torn apart. We have often said that the ten tribes are called Samaria from the capital city Samaria, which is now called Augusta, that is, Sebaste, from the name of Augustus. And why the city was called Samaria we read in the book of Kings. The prophet, then, commands, and, to speak more truly, speaks in the optative mood, that Samaria should perish. For though God was preparing such great goods for her, she acts against God and follows rather the images of demons. Symmachus, however, did not say let her perish, but μεταμελήσει, that is, she will repent, and she will regret her error, that she turned the sweetest God into bitterness, so that her warriors perish by the sword, her little ones and sucklings are dashed to the ground, and her pregnant women and those with child are torn apart unto death. All this we must believe befell her in the time of captivity and distress, when they lost their homeland, and those who escaped the sword were led away into perpetual servitude. Concerning the heretics the understanding is easy: they are called Samaria because they boast that they keep the precepts of God, not that they had kept his laws, but because they say that they are this, after the likeness of the schism of the Novatians, who themselves too call themselves καθαροὺς, that is, clean, though they are the most unclean of all, denying repentance, through which sins are cleansed, according to what is written: You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow. And in Isaiah: Wash yourselves, be clean. Now by washing he does not mean baptism, but all repentance, which washes away the filth of sins. Let such a Samaria, then, perish, because whatever it says fights against its God and turns his clemency into cruelty, so far that those among it who are men and have come to the full age of malice are cut down by the spiritual sword. And those who are little ones and sucklings, let them be dashed against the rock, of whom we also read in the psalm: Blessed is he who will take and dash his little ones against the rock. Her pregnant women too, and those with child, who have conceived from evil seed, will be torn apart for this reason, that they may not produce most wicked offspring. Something of the kind is also set before us in the Gospel: Woe to those who are with child and to those who nurse in those days; that is, in the days of tribulation and distress. And the warriors of Samaria are killed by the sword, and the sucklings are dashed, and those with child are torn apart, so that, the evil seed perishing and its tares burned up, the wheat alone may remain, to be stored in the Lord's barns.
14: To every perverse dogma also the prophet speaks daily, and calls its followers to repentance, saying: Return to the Lord your God, you who have fallen, or have grown weak, having lost the health of the Lord; take words with you, the true confession of faith, and say: Take away the iniquity that dwells in our heart, and receive the good of faith. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. The calves and victims, or the fruit of the lips, are to believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and in the passion and resurrection of the Lord; and whoever has offered this to him will by no means hope in the Assyrian king, of whom we have often spoken. Nor will he mount upon the horse which the Lord commands by no means to be multiplied, the horse with which Pharaoh was drowned together with his cavalry. For every heretic, through pride, mounts horses which he himself has bred in his error. And by no means will they any longer say to the works of their hands, which they themselves have fashioned with artful eloquence: our gods. The glutton's god is his belly, the covetous man worships mammon, the heretic, the dogma he has invented. Whoever deserts all these, that is, Assyria and the horse and the works of his hands, will return to the Lord, and will appease his father, by whom he had been cast off.

Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen in your iniquity. Take words with you, and return to the Lord; say to him: Take away all iniquity and receive the good, and we will render the calves of our lips. Assyria will not save us, we will not mount upon a horse; nor will we say any more: Our gods, the works of our hands; for you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you. LXX: Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have been weakened in your iniquities; take words with you and turn back to the Lord, say to him, so that you may not take up iniquity, but may receive good things; and we will render the fruit of our lips. Assyria will not save us, we will not mount upon a horse; by no means will we say any more: Our gods, to the works of our hands; he who is in you will have mercy on the orphan. Now that Samaria and its men are perishing, and its little ones and pregnant women have been slain, dashed down and ripped open, all Israel is called to repentance; so that he who has been weakened, or has fallen in his iniquities, may return to the physician and recover health, or that he who had fallen may begin to stand; and he is taught how he ought to repent.

Take, he says, words with you, that is, prayers and the confession of sins, and return to the Lord as much by words as by works; and say to him: Take away all iniquity, leave in us nothing of our sickness and of our former ruin, lest the revived seedlings of an evil seed sprout again; and receive, he says, the good. For unless you take away our evils, we cannot have a good to offer you, according to what is written elsewhere: Turn away from evil and do good; and we will render, he says, the calves of our lips. For the calves, which in Hebrew are called pharim, the Seventy translated fruit, which is called pheri, through the likeness of a deceptive word. But the calves of the lips are praises to God and thanksgiving: For a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit. Therefore, fleshly victims being already rejected at that time, the offering acceptable to God is pure confession.

A SHIP is guided to the right port by means of the helm; but the word of God pilots the soul of man, and leads him without risk of error to every thing that is necessary for salvation. For so spoke one of the holy prophets; "Take with you words:" even those which are inspired by the Holy Spirit: for no man of sense will say, that it means the words of the wise of this world. For their words lead men unto the pit of destruction, by bringing polytheism into the world, and by inciting unto carnal pleasure, and to the desire of the world's vain distractions: but the words of God point out the pathway to a better life, and beget in us an earnestness which makes us cheerfully advance unto the duty of performing all those things, by means of which we are made partakers of eternal life.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

I HEAR one of the holy prophets trying to win unto repentance those who are far from God, and saying, "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God: for you have become weak in your iniquity. Take with you words, and return to the Lord our God." What sort of words then did he, under the influence of the Spirit, command them to take with them? Or were they not such as become those who wish to repent; such namely, as would appease God, Who is gentle, and loves mercy. For He even said by one of the holy prophets, "Return you returning children, and I will heal your breaches." And yet again by the voice of Ezekiel, "Return you altogether from your wickednesses, O house of Israel. Cast away from you all your iniquities which you have committed, that they be not to you for a punishment of iniquity. For I have no pleasure in the death of the sinner, as that he should turn from his evil way and live." And the same truth Christ here also teaches us, by this most beautifully composed parable, which I will now to the best of my ability endeavour to discuss, briefly gathering up its broad statements, and explaining and defending the ideas which it contains.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Do not be surprised that I view the people of the old covenant as pitiable and woeful. When so many blessings from heaven came into their hands, they thrust them aside and were at great pains to reject them. The morning Sun of justice arose for them, but they thrust aside its rays and still sit in darkness. We [the Gentiles], who were nurtured by darkness, drew the light to ourselves and were freed from the gloom of error. They were the branches of that holy root, but those branches were broken. We had no share in the root, but we did reap the fruit of godliness. From their childhood they read the prophets, but they crucified him whom the prophets had foretold. We did not hear the divine prophecies, but we did worship him of whom they prophesied. And so they are pitiful because they rejected the blessings that were sent to them, while others seized hold of these blessings and drew them to themselves. Although they had been called to the adoption of sons, they fell to kinship with dogs; we who were dogs received the strength, through God's grace, to put aside the irrational nature that was ours and to rise to the honor of sons.

Those who say that they will render the calves of the lips, and will sing the praises of God with unceasing voice, also promise something else: that they will by no means have hope in the Assyrians, nor upon Egyptian horses, because a horse is deceptive for safety, and that they will no longer worship the works of their hands, the golden calves which they cast in Dan and Bethel; and therefore they say: By no means will we say to the work of our hands: our gods, for you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you; that is, on the people of Israel, of whom you had said: Israel is my firstborn son. And: I have begotten sons and exalted them, but they have despised me. And in another place: Foreign sons have lied to me. Now he is called an orphan because he has lost God as his father. A certain writer has explained the orphan as him who has withdrawn from an evil father, the devil, and who is therefore lifted up by the mercy of God.

Whatever we have interpreted according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy) of the coming of the Lord the Savior and of the conversion of the true Israel, this can be referred as much to heretics and Jews as to the Gentiles and to every perverse dogma, so that when they have repented they may obtain pardon. If, therefore, the fullness of the promise was fulfilled at the coming of the Savior, and is fulfilled daily in the Church, we must believe that it will be fulfilled more fully when, perfection having come, what is now in part will be done away. We must note what we have often said: that the salvation of Israel and of the return to God, and the redemption from captivity, are to be taken not carnally, as the Jews think, but spiritually, as is most truly proved.

I will heal their breaches, I will love them freely, for my fury is turned away from him; I will be like the dew. Israel will spring up like the lily, and his root will break forth like that of Lebanon; his branches will spread, and his glory will be like the olive, and his fragrance like that of Lebanon. Those who sit in his shade will be converted, they will live on wheat and will spring up like the vine. His memorial like the wine of Lebanon. Ephraim, what more have I to do with idols? I will hear him and direct him; I, like a green fir tree; from me your fruit has been found. LXX: I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, for my anger is turned away from them; I will be like the dew. Israel will flower like the lily and will send out his roots like Lebanon; his branches will spread, and he will be like a fruitful olive, and his fragrance like that of Lebanon; they will turn back and sit under his shade; they will drink and be inebriated with grain, and his memorial will blossom like the vine, like the wine of Lebanon, Ephraim. What more has he to do with idols? I have humbled him and I will strengthen him, I am like a dense juniper; from me your fruit has been found. To those who have turned to repentance and, like an orphan, acknowledge the father whom they had left, God answered: I will heal the breaches, or their dwellings, in which they had been wounded, or broken, or in which they had dwelt badly: I will love them freely; which the LXX translated ὁμολόγως, plainly and openly or without any doubt. Now the Lord loves those who love him, of whom he also says in another place: I love those who love me. For I, who before was angry with them because of the sins they had committed, will now have mercy because of my clemency.

This is our Faith. Thus did God will that He should be known by all, thus believed the three children, and felt not the fire into the midst whereof they were cast, which destroyed and burnt up unbelievers, whilst it fell harmless as dew upon the faithful, for whom the flames kindled by others became cold, seeing that the torment had justly lost its power in conflict with faith. For with them there was One in the form of an angel, comforting them, to the end that in the number of the Trinity one Supreme Power might be praised. God was praised, the Son of God was seen in God's angel, holy and spiritual grace spake in the children.

And I will be to them like the dew; so that with my dew I may quench the Babylonian furnace and the oven of the blazing fire, I who also through the patriarch Isaac spoke to my servant Jacob: Of the dew of heaven shall your dwelling be. For just as the Lord becomes to believers light, way, truth, bread, vine, fire, shepherd, lamb, door, worm, and the rest; so for us who need his mercy, and burn with the fevers of sins, he is turned into dew, he to whom Isaiah says: For the dew that is from you is their health. And in the song of Deuteronomy Moses speaks: Let my words descend like the dew. And when the Lord has sprinkled us with his dew, and has watered the dryness of our breast with his rains, we will spring up, nay, we will flower like the lily, imitating the Lord the Savior, who says in the Song of Songs: I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys; and he speaks to his bride, who has no wrinkle or spot: As the lily in the midst of thorns, so is my nearest one in the midst of the daughters. And when we have grown in the Lord, we will send out our roots like the trees of Lebanon, which sink their root into the depths as far as they rise with their top into the air, so that they are shaken by no storm, but stand firm in their steady bulk.

The branches of these trees stretch this way and that, so that the birds of heaven may come and dwell in them. And lest perhaps we should think, because he had said: his root will break forth, or: he will send out his roots like Lebanon, that he was speaking of cedars and unfruitful trees, he compares the holy man, converted to the Lord, to the fruit-bearing olive, the man who says in another place: But I am like a fruitful olive in the house of God. Its fruit the five wise virgins prepared for themselves; by it the swelling of wounds is soothed, the limbs of the sick find rest, light is kindled in darkness, those who contend in the contest are anointed. This olive will have a fragrance like that of Lebanon, or of frankincense, which is a kind of incense: ὁμωνύμως (by the same name) among the Greeks and the Hebrews both the mountain and frankincense are so called; or at least like that of Mount Lebanon, which, most fertile and green, is covered with the densest foliage of trees, so that the olive can say: We are the good fragrance of Christ.

But those who have been converted to the Lord will receive the reward of their conversion, that they may sit in his shade and say: Under his shade I rested and sat, and his fruit is sweet in my mouth. And when they have sat in his shade, those who before had been dead will live; or, according to the Seventy, they will drink and be inebriated with wheat, that is, with an abundance of all things. That inebriation here signifies not the overturning of the mind but a plenty of all things, that little verse declares, saying: You have visited the earth and inebriated it. And the banquet of Joseph, at which he is said to have inebriated his brothers. And the Lord, speaking to the apostles: Eat, friends, and drink, and be inebriated, brothers. Or, because the Lord himself is the grain and the vine, whoever believes in him is said to be inebriated. Finally there follows: And it will flower like the vine, his memorial like the wine of Lebanon. Now we can call wine of Lebanon wine mixed and seasoned with incense, so that it has a most sweet fragrance; or the wine of Lebanon is the wine poured out to the Lord in the temple, of which we read in Zechariah under the name of Lebanon: Open your gates, O Lebanon.

Since, therefore, so great an abundance of all things is to come, O Ephraim, everyone who repents and who has begun to be mine, put away idols, despise images; for I am he who humbled you, and I will exalt you; or, I will hear and direct, and I will make him like a green fir tree, so that of him it may be said in the psalm, according to the Hebrews: The fir tree is its house. Or at least, I will be like a dense juniper, so that he may rest under my shade. Of ἀρκεύθοις, that is, of junipers, according to the Seventy translators, Solomon is recorded to have made the doors of the temple, because Christ, through whom we come to the Father, has this nature, that he always flowers, always bears new fruits, and never lays aside his greenness. This juniper, for those who rest under its shade, so that they may not be struck by the burning of this world and the heat may not strike their head, as it once struck Jonah's too, gives fruits, and provides not only rest to those who sleep and sit, but also fullness to those who eat.

If any reader is "a spiritual man who judges all things and he is judged by no one," not only will he allegorize the major regions as Judea and Egypt and Babylon but also areas of the earth. And just as in Judea is Jerusalem and Bethlehem and other cities, so in Egypt when he reads, "Diospolis, Bubastis, Taphnis, Memphis, Syene," he will understand the meaning of things figuratively. "Who is wise and understands these things? Or who is understanding and will know them?"

And to such a degree does the gospel desire that there should be wise people among believers, that for the sake of exercising the understanding of its hearers, it has spoken certain truths in enigmas, others in what are called "dark" sayings, others in parables, and others in problems. And one of the prophets—Hosea—says at the end of his prophecy, "Who is wise, and he will understand these things? Or prudent, and he shall know them?"

Who is wise, and will understand these things? Understanding, and will know these things? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just will walk in them, but transgressors will fall in them. LXX: Who is wise, and will understand these things, or understanding, and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just will walk in them; but those who are impious will be weakened in them. When he says: Who is wise, and will understand these things? understanding, and will know them? he shows the obscurity of the book and the difficulty of its explanation. But if he himself who wrote it confesses that it is either difficult or impossible, what can we do, who, with bleary eyes darkened by the filth of sins, cannot gaze upon the brightest radiance of the sun, except say what is written: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who, without Christ teaching him, can know what Jezreel signifies, what his sister Not Obtained Mercy, what the third brother Not My People; who the adulteress is, who is to sit for a long time without the law of God; what the covenant with the beasts of the earth and with the birds of heaven is; who the David is to whom the people is to return, whose resurrection is on the third day and whose going forth is compared to the dawn; what the first and the last rain are; who he is whom the prophet says is to come, to show us righteousness, or in whose type Israel is led out of Egypt, and carried in arms, and led with the cords of love; who he is who slays death, and dries up its veins and parches its springs, and plunders the vessels that were kept stored in the treasury, and the rest, which it would take long to go over again? Hence whoever is holy and just will know that the ways of the Lord are right. Now we know that the ways of the Lord are the reading of the Old and New Testament, the understanding of the holy Scriptures. Whoever walks in these ways, unless he is converted to the Lord and the veil which was before the eyes of Moses has been taken away from him, will not be able to find the right road. But if he says with David: Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law, he will walk in them, and will find Christ; and he will perceive that the Jews and the heretics, whom Scripture here names either transgressors or impious, stumble in them, and are weakened and fall; according to what is written: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising of many in Israel.

You could really demonstrate that a wise and understanding person is the one with knowledge of what has been said and with zeal for the things by which it is possible for people who avoid evil and zealously practice good to be established in freedom from lower things and in enjoyment of higher things. This is because everything done by God is marked by great correctness, with which he also applies punishment to the fallen and knows how to achieve their salvation when they repent. You could also demonstrate that the righteous are those of their number who also know how to profit from each category and who develop greater self-control from the punishments, on the one hand, while taking the enjoyment of the good things stemming from repentance as a stimulus to virtue, on the other. You could also demonstrate that the impious are those who deserve troubles in every way and of every kind, gaining nothing from them, stuck fast in a downward direction, and as a result not able to understand anything of their duty.

It is only by deeply considering the matters in the divinely inspired Scriptures that we shall find the hidden truth. It would be fitting for us when looking into the dark shadows of the law to say what one of the holy prophets rightly said, "Whoever will be wise will understand these things; and whoever will be prudent will know them." "For the law is but a shadow of the good things to come, and not the exact image of the objects," as it is written. Yet the shadows bring forth the truth, even if they do not contain the whole truth in themselves. Because of this, the divinely inspired Moses placed a veil upon his face and spoke thus to the children of Israel, all but shouting by this act that a person might behold the beauty of the utterances made through him, not in outwardly appearing figures but in meditations hidden within us.
